So, I hear you took a holiday recently. Yeah, just got back. It was lovely. We went to Scotland for the holidays. Oh, Scotland? How was that? I've always wanted to visit. It was brilliant, really enjoyed it – the scenery, the food, just so much to do and see. But, and I suppose this is a part of the story, our journey back from Glasgow was... ruinous. Oh, what happened? Well, it started with a delayed train. And to cap it all off, the traffic controller's instructions were just... hilariously useless. [laughs] Sounds like a right saga. It got me thinking, though, that maybe we should plan travel a bit more carefully next time, or maybe just book those train tickets way ahead. Well, we just ended up in this awkward limbo for ages, so we decided, why not, we'll do a bit of local sightseeing right there at the jam. Got some really good photos taken as well, all things considered. But, yeah, definitely book those trains early next time. I'm all about booking stuff early. That's doesn't sound ideal but, it's good you made the most out of it. What about the food in Scotland? I've heard the Scotch cuisine is quite varied. The food was amazing. Had some of the best fish and chips at a place in Edinburgh. And haggis, if you're game for it. It's really good if you're open to trying new things. I'll pass on haggis, thanks. [laughs] Definitely to each their own. But the people were super friendly, and there's so much history, it truly was a great place to visit. Yeah, and did you watch anything on TV while you were there? Some of the best series seem to come out of the UK. Actually, I caught up on some classic sci-fi stuff. "Black Mirror" – got into that. Totally worth it, gives you food for thought during and after. "Black Mirror"? I heard it's quite... unsettling but influential.

Oh, talked to old Bobby the other day down by the butcher’s shop. You know him, don't you? He’s been around forever. What was he up to this time? Sell anything on eBay again? I wish I could get as much of a return as he does. I tried to get rid of an old settee once and got more money selling it on a buy-and-sell app than I did in eBay, but then the buyer claimed it wasn’t as described. What a hassle. Yeah, eBay’s just like the real world, innit. Everyone’s always trying to get a good deal or something for nothing. Speaking of hassle, I heard talk about the new election coming up. It’s all about money and nothing else, if you ask me. And these politicians spend it like it’s going out of style, all on their own council members or whatever. What about the rest? We’re struggling to keep our heads above water, literally in some cases. You’re right about that, but the system’s designed that way. It’s like the game’s rigged to keep us down while they’re up in the ivory tower making decisions without a care in the world for everyday people. It’s like the old days when we could actually buy a house with one man’s wage. Now, you need both and sometimes that’s still not enough. I saw on the telly last night that house prices in the London area are through the roof. And then on the other hand, people are selling houses the way we sell old trinkets now. “One day it might be worth something.” But will it be enough? We’re living in a bubble, my friends, and nobody wants to think about when it pops. While you’re on changing the subject to something more fun, did we ever go to that horse racing event next year? I heard there’s going to be a big procession of horses through the city center. Oh, yes, indeed! And maybe we could take a group of the kids from my old childcare. They could use a fun day out and learn about the horses at the same time. That sounds like a plan! Perhaps we could even book a youth hostel for the kids in Cornwall. It’s been ages since I’ve gone to that part of the country.

So tell me about the baby, did he sleep through last night? [Chuckles] Oh, that would be a yes! Well, most of the night at least. Got up twice but that's pretty good for him, really. Just two times! That's fantastic. I'm sure it's so exhausting but also wonderful at the same time. It is, absolutely. I'm still struggling to get my head around breastfeeding. The pain, the positions, it's all so new... Right, let me guess... nipple pain? [Sighs] Oh yeah, definitely that. He’s such a good feeder and sleeps a lot during the day which is a blessing. But, honestly, my partner is the star. He’s done so much; bath times, diaper changes, everything. That's amazing. I've also been thinking of trying a baby carrier so I can keep my hands free while he sleeps. Do you know any good ones that are comfy? I know a few people who swear by Ergobaby. It supposedly distributes the baby's weight well, making it comfortable for both you and the baby. But you might want to try out a few first. Right, I might go to a local baby store and test some out. That’s a great idea. And how about support groups or breastfeeding friends? Haven't joined any support groups yet, but my neighbour has a baby a few months older and she's been a lifesaver with advice. That's exactly what you need right now – someone who gets it and can offer tips or even just a listening ear.

So have you got your Ed Sheeran tickets yet? Well, no, they went off sale the minute I had dinner ready but I'm hoping to see one of his neighbors or something now, the concert’s only a month away! Oh, that must be so cool. Speaking of cool, have you heard about the plant exchange our bio class is organizing this term? I had no idea. That sounds fun. What song are you thinking about? “Perfect” or “Thinking Out Loud”, but I’m still working on getting it perfect without mistakes. Well, those are two of his best. So I finally got back to the gym. You would not believe how slumped I was feeling. Oh yeah? Are you still doing yoga? Or did you decide on something new? I started going to spinning again. So Jeannine and Frédéric are settling in well, they told me over the phone just now. You must be thrilled to have a new grandchild. How are they? Ah, yes, very much so! Born abroad though isn’t it? I find it fascinating. France has changed a lot since my youth. Have you noticed? Property prices, of course, are sky-high. But there’s also this very lively spirit of enterprise — even if it is often at odds with the bureaucracy! Yes, I've noticed. There was a time I visited France for a month, just before Covid. I was struck by the passion in the markets. And yes, the endless line for paperwork. Exactly! Though I've always found the bureaucracy even more maddening. As a historian, it's partly fascination — the sheer complexity, the historical layers — but mostly frustration. As a historian yourself, you must have similar feelings when dealing with it. But the passion for history is still there, I hope? Passion is the right word. I’ve been working on this book about the relationship between Philip of Spain and Mary Tudor for years. Visiting Spanish archives was an eye-opener — everything so meticulously recorded. It’s the bureaucrats of the time who’ve made my life easier, in a strange way. The irony is not lost on me. Speaking of archives, did you hear about the spire of Chichester Cathedral? They’re actually hosting an open day and photo exhibition. It's one of the long-standing problems around here, isn’t it? And changing the land use patterns — it’s a real challenge. I do wish we could attract more of those French visitors we occasionally get. Our local housing management’s often such a headache, but it’s not unique to us, of course. The new landlord's been a disappointment so far, hasn’t he? Some of the elder residents almost gone over to the anarchists over the constant bollard debates. Yes, the bollards. Totally taken over the local Facebook groups.

Oh my god, I don't know which GCSE options to pick for next year! Are you still deciding too? Yeah! I thought I was done with all that, but questions keep popping up. Ah, I hear that the wildlife in this area has been flourishing lately. I've noticed more birds and even some rabbits around here than I have in years. Oh, yes! I've seen a family of foxes with their kits in our back garden just last week. It's a joy to see. That's wonderful! It's great when urban and wildlife areas co-exist like that. It must be due to the efforts made to preserve local green spaces, don't you think? Indeed. It's nice to see that our local council has been supportive in these efforts. Speaking of preservation, I heard about the tractor day at the Birchanger's farm this weekend. Apparently, they were talking about the history of farming in this county. Ah, tractor day? Is that the annual event where they dust off all sorts of old farm equipment? I went a few years ago with the children. They love it. Yes, very family-friendly. But I was more interested in the history aspect. You couldn't help but appreciate how farming has changed over the decades, from what I heard. You see, I was driving back from a visit to my brother in a brand new hybrid. The build quality, the way it drives—it's a world away from what we were used to back in the '80s. It's astonishing how technology progresses so quickly. I remember the first time I used a computer back in the '90s and now...

Ah, I hear that your lad did well at school last year. Oh he did, he did. His headmaster even commented on how much he’s improved. Better late than never, isn't that the way now? But even so, it seems kids today get away with not much. You get the blundering, shambling teachers now. [laughs] Well, maybe they're getting more child-friendly, just trying not to scare them off. And the places of study now! [chuckles] My son’s new school, all modern and shiny inside. Reminds me of a fancy wardrobe more than a place for learning. Ooh, wardrobe, that’s a good one! [passes a plate] Someone should make a joke about that. Like how the modern classroom is more about presentation than substance? Ha! Oh, I’ve heard some good ones. Reminds me of when the new 'diver fresh' delivery men started showing up at our door. First thing I saw was their fancy uniform. I said, "Here comes the diving team to deliver our groceries!" Oh, good one! [laughs] Reminds me of that time when we’re trying to get a takeaway and the 'driver' needed a map to find the house. Thought it was part of the service, "Outdoor delivery, complete with a compass and local guide!" [laughs] Now, that’s side-splitting comedy right there. I just tried to tell a joke about Twitter. Do you think I'm losing my touch? What was it about? There was a cartoon of a man who spent too much time tweeting. He forgets where he’s at, starts tweeting to himself – “Self, what are we up to these days?” [thinks for a moment] Reminds me of binge-drinking – the brain has to report back to itself: “Were we even at the party, or did we post about it just in case?” [chuckles] Now, that’s spot on. Speaking of health, how’s our service up here in Norfolk? [sighs] You know, it’s getting better, but it’s still that age-old story – cuts and waiting lists. I swear, if the doctors started tweeting their appointments, we’d get a quicker response! [laughs] They might as well; some days it feels like the health service is more interested in being social media savvy than seeing patients.

Haha, so much for needing a real person for a garden. But yeah, creative solutions like that can help. What about you, have you caught up on any documentaries or shows you’ve wanted to watch? More or less together in groups doing something outrageous, probably. But speaking of the future… since we’re getting a bit of a break here, any thoughts on holidays this year? It could be fun to explore together. We could even plan a little trip around it like going to Athens, then taking a ferry to Mykonos or Santorini… Sounds like a perfect plan. So let’s make a note of that and start looking into it more seriously when we’re clear of assignments or exams.

Right okay now I'm going to make sure to put beans on's Dad's plate but today's the lentil one, okay? Right, I talked to her about the lentil beans. You know how ANON loves the brown beans. As a lecturer, I try to highlight the importance of sustainable, healthy eating and legumes fit perfectly into that category. Moreover, they're so easy for students to prepare on a budget. And they're excellent for the environment. Lentils are almost as versatile as beans in terms of the recipes you can make with them. Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 while house-sitting in Australia: So have you seen that viral video where the lecturer walks into the room and just starts the lecture and leaves? It's been doing the rounds on social media for weeks now. People can watch whenever, pause, rewind, whatever questions they need answered just pop up in the comments and he answers those and puts the answers in a "Q&A" section that's continually updated. Oh I saw that, isn't it fascinating? The concept of making lectures more digestible and on-demand. It seems like a great way to engage students who might struggle with the traditional lecture format. Exactly! I've been thinking, what if we could take that idea and translate it into an app or platform that serves as a virtual "classroom assistant"? It could have integrated quizzes, interactive modules, gamification even. That's a brilliant idea! Interactive modules could help students test their understanding and identify areas where they need more help. And gamification could make learning a lot more engaging, especially for younger students. Right, and it could also have a messaging feature where students can message the educators directly or even connect with peers for discussions or study groups. All while being accessible across devices—laptops, tablets, smartphones. Absolutely, flexibility is key, especially with the increasing use of mobile devices. Integrating technology this way could really help with reaching students who aren't physically present in a traditional classroom setting. It'd be a game-changer for online learning, wouldn't it? And we're not just talking about universities here. This could be applied across educational levels, from secondary up. The possibilities are endless. The only issue would be ensuring the content aligns with curriculum standards and is accessible to all. That’s true, it would be a logistical challenge, but the benefits would be so worth it. What about getting professors on board? Would they be open to recording lectures this way if it meant more students could access and engage with the material? Good point. You'd have to convince them that it's not a threat to their traditional teaching but rather a supplement that could enhance their reach and impact. Some might be hesitant because of the extra work, but if we could show how it helps students and increases engagement, I think most would be on board. Yeah, plus it could reduce the administrative workload for setting up and managing regular classes.

Oh hey! You've made pancakes again! Ah, yeah! I figured we could have a casual brunch together before our respective outings. That sounds perfect! Thanks for thinking of me. Food is sorted, weekend ideas are brewing, and we’re proactive about planning our futures. Seems like a good catch-up. Exactly. Now, shall we start this day with a practical focus? Alternatively, we can just enjoy our pancakes and let life figure itself out.

[smiling] Ah, thank you for coming over, it's always lovely to catch up. You're welcome, really good to see you too. How are you and all the family doing? All good, been busy with things around the house and the garden. How about you? Work been treating you well? Been all right, been busy planning for the next production cycle. Speaking of which, we should catch up on some community stuff soon. I heard there’s a local charity wanting to expand operations. That sounds interesting. Maybe there's something simple that can be done from this end. Would you... Sure, I’d love to hear your ideas. Plus, it’s good for me to see how others approach these things nowadays. Maybe we can have a family meeting and discuss. That sounds like a plan. [pauses to think] Speaking of family, how are the kids? Oh, they're growing up so fast! Your grandkids too, they’re a handful but in a good way. [chuckles] Indeed. Reminds me of when you were growing up, running around and getting into all sorts of mischief. Well, that’s part of being a kid. Though now it's more about keeping up with the latest gadgets and games. [laughs] Definitely. My time was when being new at the local library was one of the best days. Though I know today’s world is very different. What about when you have time off? Are there any plans for a break? Yeah, we can't afford a long trip this time around, but I was thinking of a short break at a local beach. The kids love it, and it’s a chance for us all to unwind. That sounds like a good idea. Just getting a bit of fresh air and some rest can make a big difference.

So what do you think of the translation we did for our History assignment? Did the old, stern professor give us any comments?      Well, honestly, I was a bit worried. But he actually praised our attempt to stick to the original meaning and praised our choice of words as creative and impressive. He did say though that it could have been even better if we'd given more thought to how medieval French societal nuances would apply to English.      Yeah, I remember him saying something about the verbal tenses and how some of our choices didn't fully embrace the medieval French idiomatic expressions. He suggested looking for more authentic phrases online in historical texts from that period.      Exactly. He also recommended this online forum where history enthusiasts and researchers share medieval language resources. We should definitely check it out. Our translation was mostly based on modern French, which, as you know, is quite different from medieval French.      True, and I noticed a few places where we could have used a more context-specific vocabulary. We might need to revisit those sections.      Absolutely. It’s also given me an idea. Maybe for the next project, we could do a comparison between modern and medieval French, using scientific methods to analyze the language evolution.      That sounds fascinating! I love how we can apply scientific methods to language evolution in our humanities studies. It makes everything much more interesting.      Right? Like using statistical analysis on word frequency and semantic change over time. I’ve always wondered how much that could reveal about the society and culture of the time.      Totally. That could be our next side project, analyzing texts together. We could even present our findings at the student symposium next year if we produce something substantial.      Sounds like a plan! We should discuss this more and maybe decide on a specific topic or corpus of texts to focus on. We could start by surveying existing research to see what others have done on that area before we begin our own project.      Agreed, let’s do that. Before lunch, I want to see if there’s a library or resource center here in France where we can access some medieval texts. We could spend some of our free time over the weekend doing some preliminary research.      Sounds good! Perhaps we could even talk to one of our French history professors or tutors here to get some insights or recommendations.

So, I was at my sister’s yesterday and she was showing me this cute little spider. It had these beautiful patterns and colors. Ooh, talked about enjoying nature. Got some of those around here. We’ve got quite a few spiders in the corner, near the basement. Yeah, tiny ones. You wouldn’t even notice them unless you’re looking for them. But my brother’s quite the fanatic about catching mice, right? Erm, yeah he set up traps. But even with keeps coming back. You get used to it in routine jobs. Hahaha. I can imagine. He always seemed so bothered by them. I’m not sure I’d be too keen if they were in my kitchen. No, not really but when you’ve got a house with old foundations, well that’s what you get sometimes. It’s surprising what you can find looking for vents and such. Let’s talk about the birds though, have you seen those pigeons on Chamberlain Street? Oh yeah, they’re quite the problem. But there are some cute ones around this time of year, you see them flirting and building nests. Not so pleasant with the mess but fun to watch sometimes. Yeah, nature’s full of surprises. I found a picture the other day on a birdwatching group – it was a little sparrow that had decided to nest right inside someone’s chimney. Looked so comfortable. Can you imagine? It’s funny how animals adapt to all contexts. And yet, mice and spiders – not so welcome in our dwellings. I know, but they do seem to have a knack for finding their way in. We’ve had a few incidents the past few weeks. My husband’s set up those sticky traps but I’m more for the humane ones. Ah, I see. The thing with those sticky traps is they’re not really species specific. You might end up catching a bird or something. Exactly, or a helpful spider. We try to let them be if they’re in a corner. But I know some people around here are always overreacting about them. Spiders are such an underappreciated species, aren’t they? Some of them are fantastic pest controllers. I know right. And the more I learn about them, the less scary they seem. It’s amazing how elegantly they move and work. So, have you ever thought of getting a bird feeder to encourage some of the more friendly birds while maybe keeping... others at bay?

To think your great grandmother nearly left Bristol for London. She met my great grandfather at a silent movie theatre. That's right. There was quite a bit of movement around that time, wasn't there? People were searching for opportunities after the war. Absolutely. She was a seamstress, and my great grandfather a butcher. Both settled and had a lovely life, with eight children! Eight! That's a big family. I can barely keep track of our own three siblings. [laughs] Indeed. Your family has had its fair share of adventurers. Your father wasn’t just any teacher, but a bit of a pioneer for his methods. He was ahead of his time. Always believed in hands-on learning and practical applications. Inspired many students, including me. [chuckles] I’m sure he did. I remember my mother talking about his classes. She thought him a bit unconventional for the time. That was his strength, I think. He encouraged curiosity and creativity. I've tried to pass that along in my own teaching. And while he may have been unconventional, in good ways, at least. [pauses to reflect] Your mother, by the way... She passed away relatively recently, didn’t she? Yes, about five years ago now. She had breast cancer, as I’m sure you heard through family grapevines. We all tried to support and be there through treatment, but... [trails off, looking reflective] I’m so sorry to hear that, dear. I do recall whispers of it. The treatment must have been very difficult. More so for her, of course. The courage she had through it all... it's hard to think about, even now. It’s funny, though—what really kept her spirits up was genealogy. She loved trying to trace our family tree on both sides. [smiles faintly] I suppose that’s why I’m so drawn to it now. Ah, yes, I remember she spoke of those long nights poring over records at the library. [nodding] Exactly. It almost became this comforting ritual for her. Maybe... maybe I’m trying to carry that forward in some way, keep her memory alive. [empathetically] That’s a beautiful tribute. I think she’d be proud to see where her curiosity has led you. We recently found some new documents about her great-grandparents. It seems they originated from a village in Wales that I didn’t know of.

Oh did you hear about that hot air balloon that went down earlier this year just over the border, in Cambridgeshire? That was quite some kind of story. Yeah, totally. A friend of a friend was actually on-board that flight. They were talking about it at the pub the other day. Apparently, it was very lucky for them. The basket got caught in those power lines, and it was a bit of a mess before they landed, but no one was seriously hurt. These power lines are everywhere here, aren't they? I almost instinctively look up and down to make sure we're not walking under any just in case we have a similar issue. Speaker_2 [chuckles]: Well, you never know when a certain lovable golden retriever might decide to go after a squirrel and inadvertently end up trying to chew through those lines. [Laughs] Exactly. Toby here might be the village's next power line or hot air balloon hazard. Oh, Toby and the wildlife round here. He's always chasing after everything from the rabbits to the odd ermine that sometimes shows up. It's good he’s got company though, we were thinking of going camping this summer. I’ve heard the local campsite is lovely – especially if you want to see all sorts of wildlife. Oh absolutely, and in all seriousness, if we go, it would be the perfect chance for Toby to really explore and "chase" his heart out. Well, there is the matter of money. The camping setup and the trips to nature reserves do add up. That's true. But I think, between our salaries as lecturers [both chuckle], we can manage it. We’re not exactly rolling in it, but we can certainly afford a few weekends of camping if we really want. True, and changing the scenery can be really good for our nerves. After all, teaching can drive you a bit up the wall some times. For sure. And just being out in the fresh air, Toby getting exercise, it's a win-win for everyone except maybe Toby when he inevitably gets too muddy. [Laughs] Oh, he'll love every second of getting dirty. Yeah, plus, the hot air balloon rides we could take if we time our trip right. They do them during certain months. Someone told me about a special wildlife observation ride that's supposed to be incredible.

Did the rain this morning catch you? Oh yes, it was torrential! I was almost late for the spin class. I wish the rain would give us a break. Now I'm never sure whether to pack a parka for my lessons or not. True. Back when I was area manager for the gyms, weather actually impacted membership. People would skip classes if it was too gloomy outside. Oh yes. Sentiment can have a surprisingly big impact on behavior. And how’s the teaching going? Actually, it’s going really well. One of my most interesting projects is a workshop I’m setting up where students are learning through reading culture-specific literature. That’s fascinating! So instead of just learning grammar and vocabulary, you integrate it into the culture itself. Absolutely. By the end of the course, I want them to see language as culture and culture as language. It’s a bit like when I read The Body Keeps the Score – it opened my eyes to the interconnectedness of everything. [nods in agreement] Have you read The School of Life – How To Do Things With Words? Hmm, not that one specifically, but in my book club we read a lot about life, society, and culture. Tools of Titans is the most recent one. It’s like a collection of tips from successful people – very enlightening and the kind that you might want to share with students. Yes, I like that style of book. Right now, I’m looking for something a bit different. I tried to get my teenage son into a certain book that I loved as a kid, but he’s more interested in The Catcher in the Rye. He and his friends love it. [laughs] Oh, we might be dealing with a rebellious spirit over there! [laughs] Exactly! At least it gets him reading. Speaking of which, I’ve been using some of the 5-Hour Rule for my own education. Try to read for at least an hour a day, just for fun or growth. I’ve found it really helps. I recently read about an interesting coaching technique using language imagery – the idea is to encourage imagination during exercise thinking of specific scenarios to enhance focus and endurance. That sounds like mindfulness. I recall that in my previous gym management, we tried a similar thing with guided mindful spins, which actually helped with performance.

Speaker_1, Speaker_2, Speaker_3, and Speaker_4. The conversation is related to household matters during a visit from Speaker_3 and Speaker_4 to Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 . Speaker_3 and Speaker_4, though retired, have a strong presence in this kind of conversations due to their extensive life experiences and close relationship with the younger family members. ---      “So how was the journey coming here? Not too bumpy?”      “Eleanor, it’s always bumpy when you’ve got Johnny here to navigate. But we made it in one piece, like the old saying goes.”      “Yeah, grandma’s making sure we all stay safe. Hence the triple checking of everything.”      “Oh, Ron here thought we were lost in the woods for a moment. Kept asking if we passed Malpass Lane already!”      “Well, Malpass Lane? That’s about the most interesting side road around here, Johnny!”      “Well, if we had lost you both, we would’ve written a new folk song about the ‘Malton Miscue’!"      “Yeah, and the world would’ve been a darker place without us, I’m sure!”      “So, shall I get you both a cup of tea? You can't have come from Hull without us getting you that, right?”      “Aye, that’d be wonderful, thanks dear. Nothing like a proper cuppa after that trip.”      “And a biscuit. Do we have any digestives? If not, jelly babies will do quite nicely too.”      “Let me check the cupboard. Ah, there are some digestives left from… well, from a previous adventure.”      “Well, it looks like our visitors truly know what they want. I’ll get the tea and biscuits right away.”      “You know, in my day, we had to make do with what we had, no fancy tea came with fancy biscuits.”      “In my day, it was often just bread and butter. But this is lovely, thank you. Reminds me of those early mornings before market when we’d have a quick cuppa in the back room.”      “Grandma, did you ever lose something at the market? You must’ve had a system back then to keep track of everything, right?”      “Oh, successful markets relied less on systems and more on the sheer ability to juggle dozens of items and still finding that one thing you need in your apron pocket.”      “And those market days were never complete without a good story being shared over a loss. Someone would always find something, like my hat, hidden in under a bin of potatoes.”

How's the schedule looking for the weekend's gig? Got all the various components accounted for. There's the usual squeeze time. But, dear, I heard that pub you've been wanting to try out just opened down there. Maybe we could stop before the gig. Ah, that sounds like a plan. I’m starving. While you’re dealing with the car telling you where to turn, she’s stuck staring at her phone. She’s probably more likely to just say “Google, where?” Either way, it’s invaluable. Saved us countless times already on our travels. It's wild how technology progresses. Again and again, the navigation. Sat-navs almost gone the way of the VHS. But maybe someday they’ll have planes with complete freedom to divert without any issues. Dreaming of aviation utopia aren't we? But, actually, I heard about company that’s using AI for wildlife monitoring.

What did you order? I was clearly slumped out when the lady talked to me and the tea and croissants just sounded right. A full English, as usual, though I kind of regret ordering questions because this kind of day always seems to drain my appetite. Oh absolutely. I'm still struggling to actually want to eat. I had a girl call me last night for my advice on design for keepsakes for kids. She’s working on a public space project and wants to include interactive, durable elements for kids. That's a brilliant idea, very commendable in thinking about inclusivity and durability. How is she struggling exactly? Well, from what she shared earlier - she’s having a bit of a hurdle with her boss over the interactivity aspect. He wants it to be more ‘grown-up appealing’ she said. Ah, that old chestnut. You know, this kind of thing comes up all the time - the balance between making a space kid-friendly without making it look...‘childish’. It's tricky. Exactly, I told her to emphasize the learning aspect, while also showcasing how these interactive elements could be subtle, blending into the overall aesthetic yet still engaging. She should probably show him some good examples of successful public spaces with interactive elements that aren’t just, you know, ‘playgrounds in disguise’. For sure. I gave her some pointers but told her to maybe highlight projects like the Somerset House doesn’t come to mind, it's a bit too inconsistent for that, but more projects like the interactive water fountains at the South Bank or something similar. She’d also do well to remind him that durability isn’t always matched with ‘grown-up’ design aesthetics. Hell, some of the most durable public installations I’ve seen are quite whimsical looking and kids love them. Right? Like those fantastical street art murals or public sculptures that are out of this world? Exactly. If he’s still being stubborn, maybe suggest a compromise - run some mock-ups for a focus group of both kids and adults. Show the benefits in action and it might be harder to dismiss. Good idea. I hope she takes that approach. Did you catch any part of that new project brief for the community housing architectures course we’re teaching or planning? I saw it quickly before the meeting. It’s focusing on communal living this year, with a hype around sustainable and accessible designs, aiming for universal design principles.

Oh hello! You look a bit frazzled after work. Can I put the kettle on? What kind of tea would you like today? Oh, a cup of Earl Grey, thanks, Mum. Just trying to process today’s morning traffic. I swear, East Coast is backwards. Everyone’s driving like they’re in a game of Mario Kart. Well, try not to let it stress you out. You've been thinking about your driving test, right? Yeah, but whenever I'm driving home or to work, I just see so many examples of what not to do. Like, why does the guy in front of me not use their mirrors? It's like they're in a film noir, staring intently at the road ahead while entirely disregarding their surroundings. That's unfortunately quite common. For me, it's always about focusing and anticipating. Remember when you were little and we did those "what if" scenarios while driving? Yes! I think that really helped. I try to picture the other drivers, like, what they might do next, so I can prepare. But sometimes it feels overwhelming, all these people not following the rules. I understand. Just remember that your manners and general courtesy are much better than what you see from some other drivers. You don't have to follow their example. But it's good you're thinking critically about your own driving. Thanks, Mum. I just hate seeing things like people using their phones or just lack of general courtesy. Makes me worry for when I'm out on my own. Well, when you do get your licence, just take your time and be patient. Everyone has to learn, and changing the habits of other drivers is unfortunately beyond us. I know. Plus, I want to do well. I’ve been practicing in quiet areas and working on my manoeuvres. Hopefully, one day we'll actually get some decent driving lessons in school. Yeah, that’s something they could definitely improve. Anyway, let's set a date for those more advanced driving sessions I was telling you about? Maybe next Thursday? Yeah, Thursday works. Thanks, Mum. I feel better now. Always here to chat and support you. We can even invite Dad to be part of a driving etiquette discussion after tea. Oh, please no. Just tea and a sense of normalcy right now! Of course, of course. Tea is coming right up.

Speaker_1 applying for a media post and Speaker_2 giving advice and helping to prepare. So Helen, tell me more about this job opening – what is it again? Oh, it's a producer and journalist role at BBC Radio, but it's based in Birmingham. I'm pretty excited about it, as it combines two things I absolutely love – languages and media. Birmingham? That's a bit of a commute from Hertfordshire but worth looking into. What particularly drew you to this role? I think I can really use my language skills in a way that just teaching students wouldn't allow. Plus, the excitement of working in radio – from researching stories to interviewing people. Ah, I hear you used to work in Germany at exhibitions, Mr. Jenkins. That must have been quite an experience. Indeed it was, my dear. It was the early 70s, and technology was beginning to really pick up. I was part of the team that developed those new printing systems. Inventing was just one part of the job; marketing them to people who didn't quite get what they did was quite a challenge. I can imagine. I used to deal with antiques for my gallery, and I'd occasionally have clients who wanted something medieval when in reality, it was early 20th-century. Similar problem but different realm entirely. The Germans were early adopters of new technology. Our systems, back then, were quite radical. We had to explain how digital printing—this "ink on paper from little dots" thing—wasn't just a fad but a game changer. It's remarkable how we both worked in industries that required us to explain the abstract in tangible ways. I often felt like a lecturer for the uninitiated, while I suspect you were equally tasked with convincing people that a future without paper copies and typewriters was a good thing. Exactly! And the fun part was that we had the 'luxury' of being in a space where most people hadn't seen anything like it before, so we got to leave lasting impressions quite literally. I love that, "leaving lasting impressions." I could've been speaking about art. One man's impression of the Sistine Chapel might be entirely different from another's. Or explaining that a 'rare' print wasn't that rare because it was a modern edition of something classic. I recall one time when I had to gently explain to a potential buyer that the 'century-old' vase was made in the 1950s. Oh, classic move. I've had my fair share of those situations too. While you were dealing with the modern and abstract technological advancements, I was stuck in the past—trying to unearth the real stories behind the pieces in my gallery. Funny how both of our industries taught us the art of patience in explanations. And of course, the international show circuit in Germany wasn't just about tech. It was about storytelling too. Every piece we showed had a history, just as every art piece does. I started to see the printing systems as art in a way—a piece of technology that would change how people communicated, told stories.

I've actually been considering including it in one of my courses on intercultural communication. That's an excellent idea! We could develop it into a case study. So the course could integrate theoretical discussions with the practical experience of playing the game, discussing cultural aspects related to the game’s theme, and how drinking—or not drinking—in different cultures influences communication and social bonding.

After a week without internet or advanced gadgets, you come back thinking differently about what you truly need versus what's just convenient.      And there’s also the health benefits. It’s well documented now that nature has a positive impact on physical and mental well-being. The cold, the exertion of hiking in the snow... it’s harder than summer camping but also incredibly rewarding.      That’s a good point. I’ve heard of something called ‘forest bathing’ which is really just about spending time in nature and letting it effect your well-being.      Yes, and when you combine that with winter camping, you get also this unique sense of solitude and being part of a very small community of people who appreciate the same thing.

I've been meaning to watch that film "The Match Factory Girl" but I need to find the right time to watch it because it can be quite intense. Oh yeah, I've seen it and it's certainly not for the faint-hearted. The cinematography and the way they handle the darkness is phenomenal actually, quite groundbreaking I'd say. But yeah very heavy for sure. Yeah, I've heard it's very bleak and raw but that's actually why I'm interested in it. I'm fascinated by how the film explores themes of isolation and individuality in such a stark light. Absolutely. And the performance by Kati Outinen is stunning. She brings such a depth of emotion to her character without needing words. It's incredible how much they convey through body language and facial expressions. Exactly! It's a film that really speaks to me about the lack of options and the suffocating constraints on women's lives in those kinds of contexts or even just in general. Definitely. It's universal yet intensely specific at the same time. I find the way it ties into other works by Kaurismäki really interesting. The whole thematic thread of the underclass and the silenced is also really compelling. Agreed. It's very Ahmatovian in some ways, despite being a Finnish film, dealing with the quiet desperation in everyday life. I hadn't thought of that connection but that's a great analysis. I was more reminded of something like a Lena Dunham "Tiny Furniture" vibe or even some of the films by Kelly Reichardt if one was to do an indie film version. But yes the Ahmatovian theme is a great tie, especially the focus on marital or partnership failures and the tragic heroines trapped in systems they can't change. Oh, Reichardt and Dunham’s works are great points of reference. You can definitely see those influences in the storytelling methods and themes—almost a shared understanding of vulnerabilities that are both deeply personal and universally relatable. Exactly, and so much of it comes back to the mundane ways people survive and cope with oppressive systems whether those are social economic or emotional. It's more about the brutal reality of being just another person going through their day and trying to find purpose. I think that's why works like "The Match Factory Girl" hit so hard; it's not just a particular issue but a general commentary on being trapped in a cycle where you're reduced to your function rather than your humanity.

Well young one, talked about stories and phrases, and we thought we could maybe invent one together? Speaker_2 and Speaker_3, in unison: Yeah! Can we build it with Lego? Of course! A story about a magical Lego kingdom sounds exciting. What kind of magical powers can Lego bricks have? They can make things come true! If you build it, it happens in real life. Speaker_3, excitedly: Like in our Lego game! If we build the tower, we can win the level. Exactly like that! But let's suppose the kingdom wasn’t just about magic but about following a promise—like the Brownie Promise, perhaps. What's the Brownie Promise again, mum? It’s about being kind and helpful, just like when we help build your Lego kingdom here. And what if those Lego bricks or even PlayStation games could teach us about that? Like if we're kind and cooperative in our game, the kingdom doesn’t crumble? Brilliant! That would be the magic: the more you help and cooperate, the stronger your kingdom becomes. And at the end, maybe you get to type out your promise with a typewriter . Speaker_3, laughing: Excel? For promises? But mummy, can we play some PlayStation when we finish? Yeah, it's almost bedtime, but we can do it after! Alright, after you finish building your story setup here, we can have ten minutes of PlayStation together as your bedtime treat, as long as it’s a cooperative game that follows our Lego kingdom’s promise. Yes! And next time, can we write it all down? Like a real book? We could! It might be a good practice for using advanced features of Excel to format it for us. Let's say we learn how to make tables, headers, and even a simple cover page. Can we use the Legos to make the cover too? Again like our kingdom could have towers and bricks and... And maybe we can put little sayings we want to remember, like from the Brownie Promise? Absolutely! “In thinking of others, we build happiness together.” That could be a great motto for our Lego kingdom or any game we play. So the story's already starting... the Lego kingdom was founded on the promise of helping each other. And whoever breaks that promise might have to rebuild the tower from scratch! And maybe the story’s also about remembering that even if games end or we fall apart, we can always rebuild and start again, like with our Lego bricks.

Ah, I see you’re enjoying the homemade jam first thing in the morning. Makes me think; these are actually from Jeannie’s fruit farm out in the countryside. She’s doing quite well with her various berries. Indeed. She and I used to visit her father's – do you remember his old farm just outside Shipley? It was always something to see. A whole abandoned village next to it, just a ghostly reminder of how things can change over time. Oh, I do remember! As kids, we’d explore those medieval ruins in our imagination. Wondering what life was like there. And these days I often have similar thoughts when stuck in traffic thanks to all those roadworks. Reminds me of the deserted places from your childhood. Indeed! And speaking of journeys, you were going to share about your wife finding some excellent looking herbs in a local shop. Ah, that’s right. Off we went to this little shop in the old market area. She fell in love with a few rare varieties – For me, it’s always about bringing a bit of the countryside indoors through these little things. These busy lives with phones blipping and junk mail piling up. I completely understand. I found myself reading the junk mail the other day while waiting for the coffee to brew. Can’t imagine why anyone would send me an ad for furniture polish! Exactly! But the herbs, I mean – they’re a different story altogether. There’s something so grounding about nurturing something that grows and smells good. Makes the day-to-day more bearable. Absolutely, and if one’s planning to sell the old house – like I just had to do in Bradford, a few lovely pots of greenery can really help brighten up the place. Brighten it up, or maybe distract the potential buyers from noticing the cracks on the wall? Or maybe it’ll remind them of that lovely old garden I used to have. The eternal optimism of a seller, I suppose. It does work though! You’ll probably hear the same advice from estate agents. Speaking of which, I went through all those old family photos. I found a picture of my grandmother. She always wore such elegantly scruffy clothes. Always a bit of flair, but never too formal. I remember those visits to Windsor. We’d often remark on how your grandmother always managed to look both tidy and a bit rough around the edges – like she might’ve just stepped out of the garden into town.

Right, so I’ve drastically reduced my intake of processed foods because of the new medication questions. It kind of makes me feel like a new person. That’s a great decision! I’ve been thinking about doing something similar, perhaps going a bit more plant-based? Our diet is mostly okay, but even so, it could be improved with whole foods over processed. You’ve noticed any difference? Actually, I’ve been using social media less just since the New Year, despite being a copywriter. It’s weird to think how much of our digital lives can shape our food choices based on ads and whatnot. Exactly! Hence the change. But now I’m trying to balance the advice with being on top of family and work. How about your department’s work schedule? Are you all set for the quarter ahead? Almost. We’re still ironing out a couple of details, but it should be a decent balance of this and that. Also, planning our family trip for Easter is keeping me busy. We’re thinking of Spain this time—loads of recommendations? Any tips on where to go? Spain is great! We’ve traveled there a couple of times. The first time was a bit chaotic because we didn’t know where to go or how to get there, but it’s silly how easy it is once you’ve done it once. I know, right? Directions can get quite complicated if you don’t speak the language well. I’ve learned to use Google Maps obsessively to avoid getting lost. Except, one time on holiday, I followed it to a dead-end in the middle of nowhere just because I didn’t want to ask locals for help. Haha! Good thing you ended up okay. It proves the importance of being adventurous but also prepared. For directions, I always look up places first and make a list. Also, I find that Facebook’s group for travel enthusiasts is super helpful – people post real-time tips and advice. That’s a good tip! Facebook groups can be quite useful for those kinds of things. For animals – we’ve considered getting a pet after this trip, perhaps. Did one of you ever go through the ups and downs of having a pet? Oh, we did once, a rescue cat came into our lives. It was fun but also really challenging, especially with work.

So tell me about that TV show you've been devouring. I have to admit I still don't quite understand what's going on but clearly it's got you deep into it. Oh yeah, "The Committee". Right? It's so good. Hmm, yeah, heard rumors. It kind of got me stuck because sometimes I feel like my narrative brain isn't quite getting into the swing of it but I see where you're coming from. Exactly! It's like it expects you to piece it together backwards. You get hints here and there and suddenly it just blasts a fact, and you're like, oh wait, what? Exactly, that's been my experience. Though, let me tell you, even if I was stuck, I read that the writer uses this technique because it reflects the way we consume news and information these days. Precisely, I love that about it. It's so meta, you know? And despite the complexity, it speaks to things we're experiencing in current affairs in this kind of...I don't know, indirect way. It's brilliant. I can see that it would be quite thought-provoking. But between that and everything else going on, has it felt heavy for you lately? Yeah, it’s definitely felt like a lot. I mean, we can't even plan anything properly with current events being so...fluid. Aye, right, it feels like every day is a new uncertainty. Reminds me, have you sorted your upcoming internship yet? Or is it still in "provisional plan" land? Actually it's still up in the air. I kind of went back and forth on whether to take on the survey programming or just focus on studies for a bit. Seems like the company's waiting on some grants so... Mm. Okay. Speaking of uncertain plans, how’s home life? Or should I ask? It's probably too confronting given everything. It's been okay, really. Accommodation’s still a bit of a mess because of rent prices but otherwise I'm managing. Just trying to keep on top of everything, you know? I hear you. It does seem like a constant juggling act. And with the finances being the way they are, I bet managing them adds another level of anxiety. Yeah, and I'm trying to be patient with it but sometimes it feels like we're all just floating until our paychecks are confirmed or rejected each month.

", "", etc. Hi sis, talked to you recently? Got some updates on my life. Yeah, it's been a while, but I've been keeping up with you on socials. So, how's your new exercise routine going? So, did you hear about the new budget cut at work? Yeah, they're going to have to lay off some of the project leads if it keeps up. I'm lucky that my part in the team is somewhat secure, but it's still unsettling. That's so frustrating. They're really cutting back on all the money for research and development. It seems counter-productive if you ask me. Exactly! Like, they're always talking about innovation, but then you have to watch them cancel your funding. It just doesn't make any sense. I feel like the whole "austerity" thing has gone on way too long. It's like, they never thought there'd be an end to it. True. But, you know, it's not all bad. I've been listening to a lot of Gilbert and Sullivan musicals lately, and I find it really helps to take my mind off of this sort of stuff. I can see that. "Iolanthe" is great for that sort of thing. The satire is still relevant today, if you think about it. Absolutely. "Hereward the Wake's" line about the budget for the expedition... "Hundred, fifty, twenty, one... and in practice, as good as none" is scarily familiar. That’s brilliant. I never thought of it that way. Well, maybe things will turn out okay. The budget might be tight, but we've made some decent progress with the current team setup. Hopefully, yeah. And who knows, maybe we'll get a lucky break or a new project that comes through. Or maybe they'll just suddenly decide that engineers are too important to cut corners on. You'd think so, right? I'm sure we'll figure something out. You know, it's funny, but I've found that listening to music or going for a walk here helps me handle work stress. Same here. The gardens are great for that. Where else can you just walk and listen to birds and not have to think about spreadsheets or project timelines? Exactly. Nothing thinking about bridges needing to be just so or that the HMS Paranth has to be reduced to like, this year's budget version... Don't even get me started on naval analogies in budget planning... I hear ya. Anyway, let's not worry too much right now. We've got this beautiful view, and I've got tickets for "Hamilton".

So tell me about that new development. I heard they've started tearing things apart over by the old factory. Yeah, it's been a mess. It's supposed to be these fancy new studios for film production. They're promising all sorts of jobs and improving the area, but it's a right mess at the moment. I used to see those old crates when I was taking students around on tours. Any chance of keeping some of those old buildings as part of it? The developers say that rebuilding keeps it "modern and efficient." I personally think it's a bit of waste seeing all those new builds when there's history right there. I used that history lesson in my literature course last semester to highlight how urban development can change the cultural identity of a place. Was a good way to get them thinking about the impact of changes. Ah, you’re one of the reasons I do this painting with you. It’s also creative and therapy. Plus, the view when it’s done will be nice. You ever thought about acting yourself? Someone should make a film about us and what we’ve seen over the years. Now that's a thought. I did some acting in college. It was fun but I wasn’t the best. I prefer seeing plays written by local writers at the theatre up the road. You should. Well, they keep talking about making Liverpool the next big film destination. Maybe I’ll show up at an audition someday. Or at least try painting as a hobby. I'm glad you're keeping it creative. I’ve been thinking of switching some of my lessons to focus on the local plays and the writers that come from here. It hits home more for the students. That sounds cool. Something real to latch onto, you know? More so than some American film that doesn’t really represent Liverpool. Speaking of representation, have you checked out this couple selling second-hand art supplies on Facebook? No, but I often look for second-hand stuff myself. I find some of the most valuable pieces for teaching in unexpected places. Yeah, for sure. I scored a painting from someone just moving out. Saved me a bundle. Might be rubbish but it’s a good conversation piece. That’s almost as good as some of the second-hand books I get.

Oh, did you see that?? That's definitely not a usual sight. No, I talked to her! She was just down on her luck. We gave her a bit of money. Still, though, the roadside surprises you meet – always something new. I knew my map was out of date, but I did not expect that socialism-era road block sign... right in the middle of nowhere. Oh my, how time flies keeps changing backwards and forwards with these medieval castles and modern oddities blurring along the road. It really makes you see – we're all just passing through, carrying our own stories. I think about that a lot, especially when I read about the history places we're passing by – the people making the journey, the traders, the armies... Exactly! It's all about the journey for me now – creative and otherwise. After deciding to clear the clutter and just focus on experiencing life, it's funny how much less expensive it's been. I'm with you. I mean, we're seeing some beautiful scenes, but if we're honest the cabin doesn't need much. Less is more while on the move. It’s interesting, we’re sort of hitchhikers ourselves, relying on the kindness of strangers for camping spots and the like. Like that guy yesterday who invited us to stay at his farm for the night in return for helping with his cows. You always end up doing more work on your holidays! But it was nice weren’t it? Kind of like that community kind of living again. Yes, and seeing how people live here really puts things into perspective. More focus on togetherness and less focus on, well, the clutter we were so used to at home. It's also confronting though – the poverty, the cultural differences, but changing the world takes time. We just try to do our little part by spreading a bit of knowledge and kindness. And food is such a huge part of it, isn't it? All these different tastes! That borscht last night was such an experience. And the almost unintelligible café menus in the countryside... We had to order based on complete guesswork, and then were surprised by the flavor. Yeah, but it's fun! And it brings us closer – the shared confusion, trying new things... reminds me of hitchhiking back in the day when you took whatever the road threw at you.

Are we still on track for the Hay festival? I don't want to miss it. Yes, we are. But let’s discuss directions before we talk about the festival. We need to make a left at the next roundabout, then take a straight road for about 2 miles. After that, you can see the sign for Hay-on-Wye. Oh, that’s okay. I’ve been there last year for the Festival. The excitement is seeing all those book lovers and writers in one place. It’s like a whole different world. Exactly! And this year, I heard they have even more authors coming. And maybe a few of my favourite authors? I need to check the schedule. If it’s anything like your last year, you might even spot someone famous around town! Did I tell you about this one time when I went and saw… Ah, can this wait a bit? We need to plan our shopping list for tonight. I’ve heard about the train strike affecting deliveries to some areas. Oh, the train strike’s affecting our plans? That’s disappointing, really. Oh, by the way, do we have enough space in the car for all the books we’ll probably bring back? The last trip, we had to fit in an extra box for all the fiction I picked up. Well, unless you plan to return a carful of books back for us to read, we’ll have to be a bit selective. But, seriously, so much to read, so little time! Indeed, we’ll have to be. Also, let’s check if there are any new stores in the town worth visiting. And since we are close to Preston, maybe we can stop by some of the bigger supermarkets before returning home. Might help with supplies, especially if the train strike keeps causing delays. That sounds like a plan. And with the exams over and the pregnancy progression well, maybe some of that pressure also lifts off our shoulders a bit.

Speaker_1 :   “You know, I always loved Monty Python. That was the first real show that made it into the living room the way we never thought it would. The jokes, the sketches... I don’t think I understood most of it the first time. But it just had this... togetherness feel. We’d gather around the TV and watch. It was fun!”   Speaker_2 :   “I can remember that! It was something new. You and Grandpa would sit there, quoting lines for days after. You sure had a way of making sense of it all.   Speaker_3 :   “Does that mean you like funny stuff today, Gran? Like, do you watch anything funny now on the telly or...?”      “I like a good laugh. Not as much stuff these days, perhaps, but there’s still classics. And the grandkids. I laugh so much when you two are around. You’ve got sense of humor.”      “And I do hope you know there are still good comedies. Lots of them. The way... I remember when any mention of clearing out felt like a bit of a disaster. Now it feels so... peaceful. A time to share, reflect. How about you, Tom? Do you have a favorite comedian or show?”      “I love Ricky Gervais! He’s got some good stuff, like The Office, which seems really old to me, but I get it. And some of the jokes on TikTok are pretty good too. Do you think they’re as funny as Python?”      “Oh, no, but different. The world’s a different place. The Office’s funny cause you know it’s real, like. Same with Python. Real life, exaggerated just enough. But now it’s quick, bite-sized. Which I’m trying to get used to.      “It’s just the condensed version of all our different senses of humor. And frankly, it's impressive how they pack so much into a short video.”      “Indeed. I’m just glad I got to see things change. Strange but... necessary. Though, clearing out this room does make me think of mental illness – how clutter can be overwhelming. Even with all we talked about earlier, clearing out is therapeutic actually. Helps me remember what’s important, who I am beyond things.”      “That’s beautifully put, Mum. And it’s something we all need sometimes – to clear space not just physically but mentally. I’m sure your stories and advice will always be some of our most valuable possessions, even if the physical things have to go.

So you've just got this new beast from the company? Yep, had to do a presentation for my design group and the old laptop was struggling. Nice! Is it as good as they say? I was thinking of getting one for video editing. Oh, video editing? It’ll handle that easily. I've just had to set up some software for work - it wasn’t as straightforward as I hoped, but overall, I'm impressed. The graphics card really makes a big difference. What software are you using for your work? Any tips? I'm going to be diving deep into Adobe soon. For the most part, it’s just Illustrator and Photoshop. But this laptop also comes with some great software for those, and I’ve been using Clip Studio Paint For comics. Really smooth workflow. One tip is to keep it well-managed - software updates can eat up a lot of memory if you're not careful. Speaking of things to update - you noticed the weather’s been weird lately? Planning on hiking over the weekend if the weather permits. Anything you’re into? Yeah, really missed hiking since everything closed down. Hopefully, the forecast is on our side. You know, when I was doing my dissertation, I would often go for long walks just to clear my head. Ah, I know that feeling. I grew up less into hiking and more into fixing old tech. I just found this old computer at a yard sale the other day - a real beast from the 2000s. That’s cool! While you’re dealing with the past, I’m dealing with YouTube. Trying to plan out content for next month – it’s tougher than I thought. Content planning? Reminds me of trying to find a new recipe to replace my mom's old chicken dish. It took forever. Or me trying to recover data from an old hard drive. I swear, it was like a mystery to solve. Exactly! So, have you all seen those new YouTube videos on retro tech? They’re so interesting. Watching hacks and builds from back in the day can inspire interesting design ideas. Oh, totally into that. I even started repairing an old Game Boy just as a hobby. Gave me some new design ideas too. I didn’t know about that! Maybe we should do a bit more of that. I fixed up an old TV over the summer; it’s amazing what a bit of TLC can do.

Oh, did I mention my first year's flatmate was called Amélie; and she was super cool and all about art and addiction recovery? Addiction recovery? What do you mean? Well, you know, she used to have a really bad relationship with booze. But she’s turned her life around now. She even wrote a book about her struggles with addiction and art therapy. That’s actually very cool. I never knew about her backstory. Yeah, keeps it pretty low-key, but she’s become this amazing artist and advocate for addiction recovery, using her art as a way to heal. Wow, I used to have a friend in London who struggled with something like that too. He would get stuck in this cycle of self-destruction and then try to get better. It’s really hard to watch sometimes. It is. But sometimes I feel like society doesn't really address how deep-seated these issues can be. We treat it like someone just needs to “get over it” or “manage it”, but it can really affect someone's identity or sense of self. Absolutely. And maybe it's partly because it's still stigmatized as this "personal failing" rather than a serious health issue. Exactly. For a lot of people, it's also linked to their dreams and aspirations, you know? If they keep spiraling out of control or focusing on survival rather than their ambitions, then it feels like their whole identity can get lost. It can, and it also happens a lot with fitness stuff and "beauty ideals". People feel like they need to reach this certain level of physical "perfection" to be valid or successful. It's like their whole worth is tied to how they look or perform. Totally, and it’s so damaging! And, as a friend, it’s so hard to watch someone you love struggle with that. You want to help but sometimes you feel powerless. And it's so easy to get caught up in that narrative ourselves. You start to view friendships based on who's struggling versus who's succeeding. Like, "I can't handle this person's issues today, let's just take a break." And it's not about them, it's about us feeling overwhelmed or not wanting to deal with the complexity. Right, and that’s just not fair or real. You know, relationships are supposed to be about supporting each other through all of it.

Mum, Dad, did you hear about the Dorset Steam Fair's online ticket sales? Yeah, I saw it on the local Facebook group. Looks like it's going to be quite an event. Indeed. I just wish the old days when you could get in for a sixpence would return. Haha, those were the days indeed! But actually, I've been thinking, we should get tickets early. Seems like it always gets very busy and it can be a bit tricky for me with the mobility issues to get around, especially if the tents are not well spaced. Absolutely, we should make sure they're disabled-friendly this time, right? Yeah, actually, while we're at it, let's also make sure they have good facilities for Dad and Grandma. It's not just about the tickets, it's about everyone being able to enjoy it comfortably. Exactly! We could contact them directly and ask. It's easier to get the info upfront rather than expecting or hoping for the best. That's a great idea! Also, when we’re planning the tickets, we should consider the extra costs involved with parking and food while we're there. Good point. I found a website the other day that showed average food prices at such events, and honestly, it was a bit of a shock. We should probably plan for that. True, and maybe we can even pick up some things from the house, sandwiches or whatnot, and save a bit. Or we could also look if there's the possibility to park elsewhere for a bit cheaper and then walk. Yeah, let’s consider all that. Also, Dad, any preferences on what stalls or areas we should check out? I noticed there's usually a funfair for the kids as well. Oh, I always loved the vintage car exhibits! But I guess changing times call for adapting. We could sit together where there's a bit of shade and a clear view. And of course, we'll need to make sure the picnic area is accessible. I know how much you all like having a proper sit-down meal together. Right, so perhaps we can go ahead and book tickets for a Thursday or Friday, maybe? I heard those days are less crowded. Yeah, Thursday seems good. We've got all day, and it allows some flexibility with the day afterward if we need it.

[The grandmother] Oh, I do love this place! I've been meaning to move out of the city for years. You two live in this lovely part of Yorkshire too. How do you find the change, though?      [The mother/adult in the group] It's got its moments, but we've grown quite fond of it. The region has a lot to offer actually, especially when you’re close to nature. Our children love it for playing outdoors even in winters—it’s not as extreme as most people think.      [The teenage son] Yeah, and the air is much cleaner here, definitely makes a difference. I do miss Twitter though. [laughs] Sports is happening, and I wish I could just check in without my mum laughing at my password!      [The uncle/a distant relative who is a writer] Ah, I hear you on the technology front. Twitter’s also creative for artists like me, but I barely have the time to juggle social media and writing. It’s like every minute's a battle for attention. I’m actually thinking of joining forces with a local artisan this summer. You ever tried their homemade pasta?      [Grandmother] Oh, I’d love that! And yet, they say the forecasts have been wrong quite a few times this year.      That’s true. The unpredictability matches our lives, doesn’t it? Constantly changing plans based on the weather. I did see some of that. Makes you think. I often wonder if we’re moving too quickly into a world where virtual experiences replace the physical, like churches being recorded instead of attended. So tell me about that cycle ride. You said you went from Almondsbury to Banbury. Oh yes! Well it was my early days before I even thought of becoming a dentist but I had this bike and one lazy summer. I always wondered how the NHS benefits were used by our health professionals in your time. It must have been a bit like a social club! Oh, absolutely. There were these "fringe benefits" that were quite common. I even had a colleague who would go on these mini-vacations where he'd be giving lectures on oral surgery while literally sailing in the Mediterranean. The NHS would pay for these trips if it was professional development. That's quite the perk! What was the most memorable lecture given this way? Well, once I attended a seminar on "Dental Health and Civilization Through the Ages" while on a boat in Greece. The sea was calm and we were discussing the dental treatments of ancient Rome while sipping wine. Ah nice! I'd take that over some of the conference rooms we got today any day! Nowadays, we have to be a bit more creative with our "perks". I saw that Prague doesn't come cheap but you can find some fantastic bargains if you time it right. I've heard of concerts and plays where you can get tickets less than half the price if you're willing to sit just a bit less comfortably. Speaking of entertainment, we're organizing this jive event at the converted barn next to the village hall and it's turning out great! We're changing the layout to accommodate more people and making sure they can really let loose. The barn will be fantastic for jive. I've seen some American barn dances, but jive is such an energetic dance! Can we see if we can fit a tiny stage for the band? Good idea! And once this is set up, the barn could be used for more things beyond just events.

So okay let's consider this for a second - if we move into online education, we can really tap into that market and reach students all over the world. Absolutely and we've seen how effective technology can be in making learning accessible. Plus it's scalable, right, we can start small and grow depending on demand. Which is where the business side comes in - we've got to consider subscription models, pricing strategies, and how to keep content fresh and engaging. I've noticed that interactive elements and multimedia materials really help with student engagement and retention. Yes, and from my teaching experience, I've seen that video case studies can be particularly effective for visual learners. But there's also the challenge of balancing individualistic versus structured learning. Some students thrive with personalized plans, others need the structure of a traditional course outline. True. And that's where perhaps offering both - personalized learning paths and structured courses - could work. We could use algorithms to suggest customized content for each student, based on how they're doing in the course. That's a great idea. And we could also make use of social features to encourage community learning, like discussion forums or live webinars. I've found that students learn a lot from each other if they're engaging in conversations and activities together. Yeah, and then there's the whole learning materials development. We can either create our own, or we can partner with content providers. But we must ensure that it's all high quality and current. I mean look at how fast topics can become outdated nowadays. Absolutely. And to ensure quality, we could also get feedback loops in place. So students and users can rate content, suggest new topics or suggest improvements. And how about developing different types of content based on different learning styles? Some people might prefer video lectures, others might like interactive quizzes or gamified learning. And collaborations with other experts or institutions. For example, we could partner with professors who are leaders in their field and have them contribute or even moderate certain sections of our content. That's a brilliant idea. It adds credibility and diverse perspectives. Plus, by working with others, we can spread the workload and also ensure we're not duplicating effort. And let's not forget about accessibility. We need to ensure that our platform is easy to use for everyone - including those with disabilities.

You won't believe this. I was talking to Ella the other day, and she was telling me about her weekend at the sea with her family. What happened? She's not the type to get into trouble. She's not, but the kids sure are. Apparently, they decided to create a massive sandcastle right out in the water, far beyond where people would usually build. You know how seaside sand can be pretty unstable when it gets wet. [laughs] I can only imagine. Ella said they screamed when it happened, but once they realized the castle was gone, they kind of assumed that the sea 'took' it and they started speculating on where the castle might have ended up, floating out to sea or something. They were out by the sea for hours, and all sorts of adventures happened—digging through rock pools, finding interesting shells and things. More now than ever, it seems like we need to foster that sense of wonder and respect for nature. Absolutely. I hadn’t thought about it like that, but now that you mention it, yes. There’s definitely something calming about the sea. Maybe it’s the rhythm of the waves, the vastness. Definitely. Even just the sea air and the sound can put everything into perspective. Yeah. It’s amazing how often we adults forget to look at our world through childlike eyes. A simple thing like building a sandcastle and watching it get washed away can teach us so much about impermanence and the beauty of the moment.

Did you guys see what was on the catwalk at the London Fashion Week the other day? I mean, I love how some designers really understood proportion. I wish I could have gone, of course, but the ticket prices are just exorbitant. However, I do like how they've been incorporating sustainability slowly. It's not just a trend for them but a real commitment. What was your take on the show?      Honestly, I was a bit underwhelmed by the whole thing. I mean, as much as we can appreciate the art of fashion, the prices are just making it an inaccessible luxury. As a primary school teacher, I find it disheartening how children are being exposed to this world so early on, idolizing looks over substance. But I guess it's just the way the industry works now. Fashion has never been so far removed from everyday life, has it?      True, it's a common complaint and it certainly raises some uncomfortable questions about value versus cost. However, I think most of us agree that fashion can also be a form of self-expression, art if you will. And if people want to pay, why not? It's the same with music or movies; there's a range from blockbusters to independent films, and fashion's got its own tier system as well.      Valid points, but we’re missing out on a lot of local designers and brands that can't even get on the radar with such high costs. It's not just about the tickets but the kind of influence and exposure this gives to particular brands over others. We should be supporting more varied voices in the industry.      I just wish, as a primary teacher, I could more realistically discuss fashion's impact on students. Like, we had a class about media influence yesterday, and fashion and beauty standards came up naturally. We talked about the Kardashians and how unrealistic some examples are, but also about finding style that makes you feel comfortable. I'm sure in another five years or so, it might be something taught in schools more overtly, given the trends.      That's an interesting idea. Maybe we can incorporate more about the production process and sustainability into fashion lessons.
