So have any of you seen that ridiculous meme about librarians being social media whizzes? Oh, I saw it and thought, "Well, that's not entirely far from the truth." I saw it and couldn't help but chuckle. It's a bit ironic considering our jobs, right? We're supposed to be guardians of information, but social media can sometimes feel like the exact opposite—chaotic and overwhelming. Yes, exactly! I mean, have you guys seen how quickly information gets spread on social media? It's like a wildfire. One wrong post or a misinterpretation, and before you know it, everyone's talking about it. And not to mention the fake news and misinformation campaigns. It's our job to teach people how to navigate that and find credible sources. Absolutely! We're in the digital age now. It's not just about knowing what's in the books or the databases, it's about understanding how to access this vast amount of online information responsibly and critically. I often tell my students that just because it's on the internet doesn't mean it's true. They often look at me like I'm the one spreading myths! I had one student come to me insisting that all German words are silly because someone shared a list of really unusual ones online. They didn’t understand that’s all part of language variation and some words can look daunting because they're technical or archaic. Oh, that reminds me of this video I saw of a cat understanding and responding to complex programming code in "cat language". Of course, it was satire, but some people took it seriously! Exactly. The line between reality and satire seems to get blurrier by the day. We really do need to be infodemiologists in some way, teaching people not just how to find information but how to evaluate its credibility. I also teach a session for undergrads on using social media for academic research. Most of them are surprised at how much academic information is actually shared on Twitter and other platforms. That's interesting. I've almost gone over to Twitter just for the academic discussions. You'd be surprised how many researchers and academics share their works-in-progress or engage in discussions about their fields. For me, it's all about introducing them to academic hashtags and demonstrating the importance of engaging with the right communities... and staying away from the trolls!

Alright so let's discuss what we need to do for the tape for our meeting. We must make sure it's a compelling case for the questions we're asked. Going over the goals and potential hurdles and how we intend to tackle them.      Absolutely, and of course, we must highlight the rationale behind choosing this location specifically. Plus, we need to stress the benefits of having good relationships with the local hospices. It’s about showing synergy and complementing each other’s services rather than duplication.      Exceedingly important. Patient health and how we can positively impact the quality of life for those at the end of it. This should be at the core of what we present.      Nursing care is a critical component. Integrating advanced nursing care models into our service model would be a distinctive selling point. We should specifically mention plans for staff training and research collaborations in that area.      And then we have to address the elephant in the room, politics and geography. Absolutely. Plus, the visual of the new building. Do we have rough sketches or at least a concept to present? It can really help people visualize what we’re aiming for and how it’s intended to blend in or benefit the local environment.      Precisely. Physical plans or a model would be ideal. I’ve asked the design team to prepare some concept sketches just for this purpose, but we should probably focus on the viability and potential benefits rather than aesthetics first and foremost.      Good. Visual aids can make a significant difference in how this is perceived. It’s about presenting a clear, practical, and empathetic plan, not just an idea.

Oh look at this one! You and your Dad have changed so little over the years aside from more grey hair! Well, the gray is a testament to life experience. Yeah, and I was thinking a bit like what your mum used to make—some kind of fish bake with this new recipe I found using lemon and dill.

So, you've really got to watch A Quiet Place next weekend, it’s supposed to be freaking brilliant! Oh really? I've heard a lot about it. I’ve been a bit hesitant to see it though – I can get very jumpy with scary movies! Oh, I know that! But it’s really good, trust me. The silence thing is really interesting, makes everything feel more intense. That does sound interesting. But I’ve been meaning to try out watching in the dark. Might just do it next time. You’ll be fine! Just grab a cushion to hide behind when the jump scares kick in. I already have one in mind! But seriously, what’s the best scary movie you’ve watched recently? For me, it has to be Hereditary. That film… I didn’t sleep for a few nights afterwards. Oh, Hereditary! I've heard a lot about that one as well. I’m a bit more of a fan of the older horror films. Like The Shining or Psycho. Oh, those are classics! But Hereditary is definitely very distinctively modern in its approach to horror. Hmm, maybe it’s just the new scares that unsettle me more. The atmosphere in films like The Shining is fantastic but it’s slow-burning, I like that. Oh hell yes, The Shining has incredible atmosphere. The slow build-up is part of what makes it so terrifying when it all finally comes together. Exactly! But I just found the visuals in Hereditary so uniquely unsettling. Like, the way they use space and symmetry… It’s just so unconventional. True, Hereditary is very much about visual horror. I think that’s part of why it sticks with you. But sometimes I find those unconventional scares can be less effective than just good old-fashioned suspense. Maybe it's just me, but I think suspense is key to a good scary film. Again, like with the slow build-up. Totally agree. There’s nothing like anticipating what’s going to happen next and not knowing. It’s the best kind of torture. For me, it’s all about the sound design as well. You can often tell if a film will work just by the score or the sounds they choose. Absolutely! Hereditary’s score is definitely unsettling. But the absence of sound in A Quiet Place is actually kind of brilliant too.

Right okay so I think that's all of the emails that I need to have a look today. Oh alright. Hopefully they don't include anything too alarming. Not that I've seen anyway. I did have to sort through this one about a company that's supposed to have some kind of new gadget that helps manage daily routines and stuff. Like this thing called "Pulse". It could probably help us, especially during holiday times or large family gatherings. But as I was saying, I didn’t buy it, I was just intrigued. Just be careful with things like that, it's easy to spend money on something you might not use or need. True, true. And speaking of spending, have you seen the new smartphones they're advertising? I just saw an ad for the iPhone’s latest model and I'm considering getting one. Oh, are they making you want to upgrade? I guess changing phones is something that feels necessary every few years. Not really a need, but I like staying on the current technology for work and for these FaceTimes with the family across the country. I thought they were trying to push the iPads for that sort of thing. They are. And I do almost all of my work on an iPad now. I swear, if I didn't have that, I'd be stuck.

So tell me about that new book you've been devouring. I have heard so many recommendations; it sounds like it's going to change everything. Oh, it really has. You know I've always been quite captivated by exploration narratives but now, this author, who is kind of a combination of Bruce Chatwin meets Bill Bryson but with a twist of mindfulness and contemporary spirituality - quite out of my usual reading genre but absolutely enthralling. Ah, I see. What draws you to it then? It's this whole concept of reconnecting with nature while questioning some of our more 'civilized' ways of engaging with the world. The way he writes, it's almost as if you're right there with him - trekking through the Pyrenees or sailing down the Ganges. But then he also brings in these meditative, observational aspects that really have you rethinking certain lifestyle choices and values. I've read a lot of creative non-fiction lately, too. What really excites me about this author is his deep connection with the landscapes he travels through and the people he meets. It's as much about the places as it is about this inner journey he undertakes. Absolutely. One of the most compelling parts of the book is the way he discusses how certain landscapes can genuinely affect your emotional and even physical health. Do you remember when we went on that hike in the highlands? Oh, yes! A couple of summers ago, wasn't it? The cloud inversion and the way the mountains felt both vast and intimate at the same time... Exactly! I feel like that experience is something that's echoed in the author's passages about the mountains. The way he writes about clarity of mind and perspective, and how one’s perceived problems become surprisingly trivial or less overwhelming against the backdrop of such grandeur. It's like a reminder to slow down and truly observe. And think about it - we've both traveled extensively, but sometimes it's traveling and sometimes it’s just noticing the small details changing around us where we are. Right. I think that's part of what draws me to this book: it's about looking and seeing in new ways. Even in our so-called mundane routines, there's depth everywhere if we just take the time to look. Did the book inspire you to take any new travels or journeys in the near future?

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 , mother and daughter discussing a job application: Hi Mum, talked to you about the job application for the Surrey project. Want to discuss the outline I’ve drafted? Ah, George, welcome in. Come on through. Nice to see you again, Ian. How are you keeping? Ah, great to see you George! Come in, come in. Tea? Ah, yes, please. We were just discussing the news. Yes, I've been thinking... ever since the report about housing came out, I worry about how it will affect us older folks. Can we afford to stay where we are when our homes need constant repairs? Oh, absolutely. I've been there, and I know it's a battle. Exactly. The young ones can't even afford a decent house around here. My son's been trying to get onto the housing list for years now. Now that's politics for you. Where has the sense gone? The gov'ns don't care about the long-term, just about the next vote. Well, they keep promising but promise ain't worth the paper it's written on. Speaking of which, have you two heard about the new policies they're discussing? I've read something about free... um, the name escapes me, but it was something about cars for the elderly. Cars? That’d be a dream, but I’m not sure they’d understand the needs. I mean, I’ve seen them allocate funds for this and that, but personally, I’d rather see support for housing and healthcare. Yes, and we might not even need a car by then if the health services were better for us. Our generation used to take pride in our country’s support for the elderly. But have you seen how health services are underfunded? Overworked staff, long waiting lists... and sometimes you feel like you’re being fobbed off. Totally. My back’s been playing up, and I went in for an appointment for months... still waiting. Just the system's way of reminding us we’re not as young as we used to be. Don’t start, or we’ll make it across the youth of today too. Although, come to think of it, my grandkids watch documentaries about what we might face when living out here in retirement... I hadn’t thought of it that way. Oh, speaking of families, we’ll need to make sure our children understand our situation.

Speaker_1 sounds slightly educated and has the typical Stratford-upon-Avon dialect influenced by her background while Speaker_2 exhibits the Mancunian accent from Manchester. Right okay so I think I've decided I'm going to make bangers and mash but with a bit of a twist. Bangers and mash sounds excellent. You could be doing a bit of a Wales-England fusion. Well, haven't talked about holidays recently. Got any ideas on where we're heading this year? To be honest, I was kind of stuck on questions because there are just so many places we could go. I read that the city’s undergone big transformations. Shops, attractions, even the food scene. And have you seen those beautiful West End boutiques? Haven’t really paid attention but apparently, it’s gotten quite the following. Apparently, they serve the best burgers in Harpenden now. Seriously? Also reminds me, we were supposed to watch that film, what was it... 'Burns the Movie' or something? Oh, weren’t we going to watch the Burns documentary? I actually found it really interesting, even if some parts were a bit slow. Yeah, but it was really rich in historical detail. I think the film takes a more modern approach to his life and poetry. Definitely. It’s these kinds of documentaries/personal interest films that make me feel like I’m learning something new. And speaking of learning, how’s the new work project going? It’s good. Some interesting challenges, especially with integrating this new software. It’s like... harder than solving those math problems we used to work on together. Haha, yes. I remember those “can you solve this?” moments. Math wasn’t my strongest subject but yours has always been impressive. Thank you... I do enjoy any challenge however... I can’t say the same about dealing with arguments at work.

So, you had that hospital appointment again? How was it? Oh, the usual, really. Nothing groundbreaking. The doctor just kind of brushed over the whole thing and then reminded me again about the blood pressure and weight loss. It feels like they just want me to diet right now, as if that's the magic solution. I know that feeling. My sister’s still on about it too. Since her dad passed, we've all noticed she's eating way less. Like, she’s always passing up on family gatherings for some diet meeting or another. Yeah, and then when she’s stressed, she ends up having a big binge night - which we all do, but she feels terrible about it. It’s like this never-ending cycle. Exactly. It’s just... how family dynamics change when someone close dies. Everyone’s expressing emotions in such different ways. My mom’s on this health kick now - she’s never been a fan of green juices, but suddenly this is her new obsession. Oh, I’ve heard of that. It’s kind of assumed now, right? If someone in the family passes, you must at least pretend to become healthier to, I don’t know, honor them or something? Ah, maybe. But I think it’s more about dealing with our own mortality. When someone close dies, it’s like we’re forced to confront our own end, and all the what ifs and maybes come flooding in. But it’s tough seeing your family members struggle. My niece went through this phase of excessive exercise because she thought if she lost weight, she’d somehow prove she was better or could’ve prevented her grandfather’s death or something. It blurred the lines between grief and body image. Same with my son. He was really affected by his grandfather’s passing. He and his best friends started this thing where they’d all try to eat less and less to see how little they could survive on, all because they felt guilty for not being able to stop his grandfather. Kids, they truly don’t process it the same way, do they? No, and it’s heartbreaking. We had those kids come over and almost unintentionally criticize each other’s diets or what they were or weren't eating. They were really young, like 10, 11. It was like they thought they were doing something to help, but all it did was create tension.

Speaker_1's Dad: Okay so today's the big day isn't it boys? Yeah, talked about it all week, can't wait to hear about your skiing trip! Was it scary at all? Oh did you see that old photo you took at the Japan trip? Which one? We took so many! The one with the cherry blossoms and the badgers? Ah, yes! I remember actually, that was a funny day. How so? Well, we were at this small town in the foothills of the mountains and we saw these badgers just wandering around. We were going to take more photos of the blossoms but then we just like stopped to watch them. They're so cute but they can also be quite big, you know? Yeah, definitely! And you have a great shot of one up close, I recall. It looked a bit confused by our presence, yet very curious. Exactly! That photo still makes me laugh because it looks like the badger is thinking "what are you doing here?" But the cute look on this badger just stole the show. I also remember the silly conversation we had that day about how the badgers must organize their social structures in a way that's quite interesting, perhaps even complex, given their behavior. Oh, right! Ah, the badger hierarchy! We imagined badgers having little badger councils to decide on foraging routes and burrow improvements. And we were pretty convinced that there must be leading badgers with real badger power! Yeah, complete badger politics. But the really great thing about that day, was just being able to capture these moments, blurred as the blossoms are but so full of life. Absolutely, nature's beauty combined with animal encounters always makes for some memorable moments. Speaking of memorable, have we updated our photo archive on the cloud? I was thinking we should make sure all our trips are well-organized. That’s a good idea. I can do that tonight. Maybe we can also scroll through them and choose some for physical prints. Physical prints are always nice to have. Maybe we could even put together a small album for when we have guests over or send some to friends who were part of those trips. Definitely. And while we're at it, I might also consider finding that old video of the time we... Oh, not that again? How could I forget? You know how it was; a bit of a mess but definitely entertaining history. Let's save the less professional moments for when we have a laugh party, okay? Deal! And it's also about preserving memories, good, bad, and funny.

Right okay so I've been looking at different options for you getting your own car insurance. Yeah I've been wanting to drive for ages now, so that's really helpful. Of course. It's a big step. So, even if I drive safe, I'm still going to pay more because of where I live? Unfortunately, yes. But there are some things you can do. For one, consider black box insurance. That sounds a bit invasive, but if it saves me money, I guess it could be worth it? It is a bit of a trade-off, but it's one way to prove you're a safe driver. Cars are grouped into categories from 1 to 50 based on things like performance, and how safe they are. For a young driver, generally, you want to aim for cars in lower categories—so maybe 1-15. They're usually smaller, less powerful cars. For example, a Vauxhall Corsa, a Ford Fiesta, or a Volkswagen Polo might be lower-risk bets. Alright, so no fancy sports cars then. Got it. Not for the first few years, at least.

Some days the air is just too bad for people to focus outside or even to come in for class. No kidding, it was really bad today. We could barely see across the street from our office. Exactly. I’m worried about everyone’s health—my own included. Makes me wonder if they’re learning more about pollution than the subject we’re supposed to be focusing on. Well, at least it’s serving as a bit of a real-life case study, right? Yeah, I suppose so. It’s funny, the other day a student asked if we were working on solutions to tackle the pollution problem in our community because that's where the project is happening. Actually, that kind of makes sense, doesn’t it? Maybe we should encourage more community-based projects that could help reduce local pollution. Our research could tie into environmental efforts, right? Absolutely, and it could be a great thing to educate students about while they're confronting it and learning to live with it here in China. You know, after all the focus on theoretical advanced mathematics, it might be time for us to start applying our expertise to practical issues like this. Could actually make our work so much more relevant and impactful for students here. Besides, it’ll add a great dimension to the course. And who knows, maybe we could even involve our friends and maybe even get local organizations involved. That sounds like a great plan. We could talk to Dr. Zhang or Liu.

Right okay so I'm going to make homemade pastry for these pasties. That's brilliant, will you use suet? Yes, I've got some but I need to work out the ratio for this because it's going to be a vegetarian version. Oh that's great! Do you have a recipe? I've got a basic recipe but I may need to adapt it a bit. Suet makes such a difference. Absolutely, and it gives a better texture. You'll need it if you're making traditional pasties. So what's in today's pasties? Today, just like the traditional ones, but with vegetarian sausage, carrots, peas, and a bit of potato. And I'll make sure to put a bit of swede in too. Swede or turnip? Swede, yes. It's traditional for pasties in the Southeast. I had no idea. I thought you only used turnip in Lancashire? Actually, both are used but swede is more common in the Southeast. I never realized that. It's interesting how different regions have their own special ingredients. Speaking of food, are we still on for lunch at that new place in Canterbury on Friday? I've been meaning to ask, have you all seen the photos I took of the Omega trial weekend? I'd love to see them! I'll show you during dinner. And have you all started watching "Archer"? Yes, I started it last week. It's hilarious. I'm right at the end of season one. It's really quirky. So you're planning to watch a season of Archer while making pasties? Haha, exactly. I'm sure we can multitask well enough. I want to make lunch plans for next week. Alright, let's discuss that over the pasties. So what's the plan for next weekend? Ah, I was thinking about going to the market on Saturday. I can take you along. I need to grab some more herbs for my cooking anyway. That’s a great idea. And maybe we can grab a bit of lunch there. Great! That works for me. And then how about a dinner at our place on Sunday evening? Sounds like a plan. So at our place on Sunday with what we get from the market? Yeah, why not? I'll prepare something with the fresh herbs we find. And then Archer for dessert? Perfect. Alright, on that note, should I start making the filling for these pasties now?

Speaker_1    : You know that's what really surprised me at Cambridge or rather, it was more that it didn't really surprise me. Ah, I can't believe I used to teach mathematics for so long. It feels so long ago. Now I'm more concerned with what will be on the dinner table tonight, wouldn't you say, Susan? You're quite right about that. Still, now that you're retired, you might have a bit more scope to enjoy hobbies you never had time for. Speaking of hobbies, have you picked up knitting again now that your students aren't demanding your attention? Erm, knitting. Well, I've got a keepsake jumper still on the needles for my granddaughter. It's taking some time, but she'll love it. However, as for cooking, Veronica, dear, I've been perfecting my shepherd's pie. It just needs the right bit of sweetness from the caramelised onions, but of course, it never goes amiss to have potatoes that are immaculately mashed. That sounds delicious, mum. Maybe you could pass on the recipe to me. My own creations barely excite anyone at dinner these days. Oh, for sure, Veronica. Now speaking of family, have you had any news from the children this week? Your boys are certainly growing up. Brendan is good. He has just started his new job, while the younger one, James, is in the peak of university exams. I'm trying to stay calm, but it's not easy. He's always been so anxious about his studies. A university student now, it feels like just yesterday he was in school uniform, really. Time sure flies when we’re busy, and all that. And what about you, Anne? How's the lads doing? The lads are lads. Busy with their work and lives, but they do come around when they can. Kevin's the one who's into culinary arts now, training as a chef. He's always talking about fusion food. I'm not quite sure what fusion food is exactly, but it seems quite fancy. That sounds nice. From technical manuals to a kitchen changing the world byte by byte. Haha, exactly. I mean, I'm sure some of that fancy language is for show, but it's just impressive when children pursue their passions. Indeed. It does give one a bit of hope for the future doesn't it. Speaking of passions, you know Michael's coming over next weekend? Ah, yes! The boy. It'll be good to see him.

Oh I used to take my first job's passport photos here actually. It's these old buildings, they're still standing. I remember you saying that. It's fascinating how much history is packed around here though, isn't it? It absolutely is. And isn't it lovely how they've integrated the old with the new? Completely. Like this bar right here, it's a modern place, but it still has that old world charm. Yeah, and then you look out and... You see the Thames. I never get bored of it, every time is different. It just never stops moving, doesn't it? Reminds me of life sometimes, always in motion. Exactly. And then you have the O2 Arena out there, which is the opposite, one of the biggest, static spectacles London has. And we can't even agree if it's called the O2 or Millennium Dome anymore. I say this because it was the Millennium Dome when it first opened, but yes, I understand the marketing shift. It’s kind of like, the name 'O2' has taken over. Anyhow, speaking of not getting anything fixed in time, have you seen the O2's lineup for this year? I haven't, no. But I'm glad we're walking here, really. It's one of my favorite things, walking along the Thames. I know what you mean. It's peaceful and you see London from the best angle. Talking of peaceful, it's things like this walk that remind me of why I try not to own a car in the city. The traffic, the costs, it's just not worth it when you have this. Absolutely. We've been meaning to go on a holiday with the family for a while now. Maybe take the train instead? Or even rent somewhere outside for a weekend. Our kids would love it. But planning just family trips without the car... so much easier. It does simplify things a lot. We can show them the world without the hassle. Exactly. And the freedom of movement. Yeah, and philosophically speaking, aren't we thinking a bit outside the box just by walking and not using a car? Sure, it's not grand, but it's a... a kind of rebellion against the norm. Rebellion? I'd say it's more of necessity and common sense these days. True. Though sometimes, youth can get away with things we older folks can't.

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 while house-sitting in Australia: So, what's the latest with your teaching job? Are you still enjoying it? It's been good, you know. I love working with the kids, but sometimes it feels a bit routine. I've been considering further study to specialize in a certain area. That sounds like a good idea. Career development is always important right? Definitely. I was thinking about doing a master's in educational technology. Have any friends expressed interest in starting up something with you? Actually, yes. A few old colleagues and I have discussed the idea of creating an online platform for teachers to share resources and advice. Wow, creative entrepreneurship. That could be big. Knowing someone who did something similar, it's not as easy as it sounds but the potential is huge. Exactly, so we're trying to work out the details. It's a balance between making it professional enough for schools to recognize but fun and accessible for teachers. That's the tricky part, isn’t it? Making things work, not just on paper but in practice. Ah, but if we can make it work, the rewards could be amazing. On that front, we've been discussing it. Truth be told, we've enjoyed this experience so much that we're starting to question our original plans to move back to England. Really? That's a big decision. Yes. The lifestyle here, the opportunities, even the thought of planning a family... we're starting to seriously consider staying if we can work it out. Planning a family could be a significant factor. However, immigration, jobs, and all the logistics... We know. We're weighing up pros and cons. Totally. We've been talking about that too. I've been kicking around the idea of expanding my business here, or even joining up with some friends over here for a new venture.

So speaking of manners, did you hear about what happened to Laura at work the other day? No, what happened? Right, so she had this client that just wouldn't stop talking about herself, and Laura kept trying to steer the conversation to the actual project and ended up having to wait an hour for the woman to stop! Oh man, that sounds like I had a similar situation with Karen from Accounting. Wait, really? How did you deal with it? Well, I just had to be polite and wait for her to eventually run out of steam. And I bet she didn’t even realize she was being so self-absorbed, right? Exactly, that’s what makes it even more frustrating. It's like they have the spotlight and you're just a prop. True. But, you know, it’s all about balance. Some people just don’t get it. Speaking of people not getting it, have any of you seen this video about how people react to Pokémon Go in busy areas? Yeah! I saw it. Some people just stumble around, completely lost in the real world because they're too busy catching digital animals. It’s hilarious and sad at the same time. I mean, can you imagine accidentally crossing in front of a bus while trying to catch a Pikachu? I saw a guy get into a fight because someone else caught a Pokémon that he was trying to catch. Whoa, excessive? I guess that’s fight or flight in the digital world. More like "Fight over a pixelated rat". Speaking of stress, has anyone checked out this new app that helps you meditate? It’s supposed to help with stress and anxiety. Yeah, I’ve seen it on YouTube. Some people swear by it, others think it’s just a waste of time. Personally, I prefer just sitting in silence, but maybe for some people, the guidance is helpful. I tried a free 5-minute trial session and found it was actually quite relaxing. It’s something almost. Wonder if there's a version for those of us who’ve been dealing with camping stuff. Like “Forest Sounds for the Stressed Camper” or something? Someone could totally make that and it would sell like hotcakes. Imagine being hounded by urban noise and then booting up an app to get instant forest ambiance. That’s genius though, maybe a portable version for service stations?

Ah, I was at that football match yesterday. Really? Which one? Yeah, tell us about it. It was the Canary's match. They're doing quite well this season, isn't it? Really? I heard rumors they were kind of tanking. No, they've picked up pace, especially after that manager change. Oh, I don't know much about football but I know Norwich. Ah right, yeah, well, let me tell you. Go on! So the atmosphere was brilliant, you know. The crowd's been fantastic. And they won by a bit, but what really was lovely was seeing some of the new players in action. I should've gone. Speaking of which, I had such a great week looking after the kids again. They're always so full of life, it's just infectious! Did I tell you about this one little incident? No! Tell us. Oh it was funny. So I've got a little boy who's just started nursery, and he just started kind of throwing tantrums over everything. But yesterday, in the middle of a tantrum, he stopped, looked right at me and said, "You're making me feel sad for not liking peas, but peas make me feel happy because they're green like grass!" And then he started giggling uncontrollably. That's cute. That is absolutely adorable. True story is the real gem. You should've been a child psychologist or something. No, but it really was just lovely, you know, seeing him connect it all like that. Oh, by the way, are we making any plans for Christmas yet? We should get a head start on the party. Ah, right, good thought. Yeah, I was thinking maybe we could do like a big meal, something traditional, but also so we can use all the new zero-waste things we've discovered. Oh, good one. I've been trying almost all of those new plant-based desserts recipes. You know, to see if we can make something everyone will love. That sounds brilliant! Let's definitely get something green, I mean plant-based. And while we're planning that, any any of the older TV shows that we used to watch, anyone catch up on any? I've been like really into reruns of Fawlty Towers from the start of the year. I've been bingeing on The Great British Bake Off. Been watching The Crown, though, I have to say it's been quite heavy, you know?

So, I was thinking about what you said to me last night. You know, about dropping out. Yeah, well I don't know, uni just doesn't feel right for me anymore. I need a break, really. I can see where you're coming from. It can be overwhelming, all this pressure to do well and then make a career out of it. Did you talk to anyone about it yet? Not yet, I wanted to talk to you first. You know how much I admire your perspective. Thanks, but I'm just here to listen, really. What was it for you – was it the course, the campus, the pressure to have a plan from day one? It was a bit of everything, to be honest. The course is interesting, but I didn't realize how much I'd struggle to be away from home and everything familiar. And the pressure, I feel like everyone else here knows exactly what they want, and I'm still figuring it out. That’s totally normal. I felt the same way for a bit. Yeah? Did you? I mean, you’re on track to graduate early, how did you cope? Honestly, it took me a while. I had to figure out what genuinely excited me outside of the academic bubble. Do you have any hobbies or interests outside of uni? Ah, yeah. I love drawing and messing around with photography, but it's hard to find time in between all the assignments and trying to maintain a decent social life. That’s so key! These interests can often be a lifeline in times like these. Maybe see if the university has any clubs or projects related to those, to give you a bit of time off from your main studies. That’s a good idea. But I just don’t feel like I should be here yet. Maybe I just need to take a step back, figure out what I want without this next deadline looming over me. I think changing the pace can be really good for you. It’s okay to not be 100% sure what’s next. You make it sound so easy, but I’m scared. What if I end up stuck or regret dropping out? That fear is natural. But the regret you might feel from not listening to your inner voice could be worse. Whether you take a break or complete your course, it’s about finding what’s right for you right now.

Oh Grace gods it's been too long isn't it since we last caught up. Yeah! I know unreal! Life just keeps getting busier. Still working at Pearson then? Yeah, still there. I can totally see it with you... lots of team sports themed decor.

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 while browsing the internet for shopping purposes:   Background:   The conversation takes place in the living room of a home in Malton, where Speaker_1, who has various family connections and long-term friendship with Speaker_2, is guiding and discussing the process of internet shopping, specifically focusing on questions and concerns related to Ebay and Amazon. --- Wow, look at this watch! Oh, is that on Ebay or Amazon? Ebay, but the prices are all over the place here. What's the best way to figure out if something is a good deal? Ah, that's the million-dollar question isn't it? First, make sure you check out the seller’s ratings. That'll give you an idea of how reliable they are. Okay, this guy has 98% positive feedback. That seems good. 98% or even 98.5? Those are really good. Second, check if the item is new or used. If you want a new watch, make sure it's listed as new. This one is used but in good condition. What if I want something new? Then look for sellers who clearly state it's new. And then compare the price with the original retail price. If it's significantly lower, be a bit cautious. But how do I find the original price? That can be tricky if it’s a less known item. You can google the product name and try to find it on the official website or other trusted online shops. That should give you a comparison. If it's a unique or collector's item, that's more complicated. Makes sense. Also, I see some items are listed as Buy It Now, others as auctions. What’s the difference? Auctions are when you bid against others to win the item. Buy It Now is when the price is fixed and you can just buy it without bidding. So auctions can sometimes get cheaper if no one else bids. But if I really want it, should I bid high to make sure I get it or wait and see? That's a good strategic question for auctions. If you really want it and can afford it... generally it's better to set a limit you're comfortable with and stick to it. Don’t get caught up in the excitement of bidding higher than you want to. Don’t worry, I’m pretty good at setting limits.

Thanks for coming over today, particularly since you had a long day. Want a cup of coffee? Oh, yes, please! That sounds fantastic. Especially because this kind of chilling isn't possible often due to my tight work schedule. I wish I could have helped you more at the production meeting earlier. Seems like there was a lot of pressure for improvements. It was a bit stressful, but routine for my role. Management expects us to stay on top of things. However, the part that seemed out of place today was the sudden questioning about the monthly trends. We’ve just been dealing with a new supplier. Right, but from what little I understand - which isn’t much, to be honest - your team has been doing a great job so far, right? Yeah, we’ve hit our targets mostly, but there have been little hitches with the new supplier. It seems their quality standards aren’t matching what we need, which has led to a bit of rework and time lost this month. That must be frustrating. I’ve heard about similar issues in logistics. Sometimes it’s the new kids on the block don’t quite understand the existing workflows. Exactly. They’re trying, but we’re used to very specific standards and deadlines. The reworks take up more time than expected, which can throw off the whole schedule. Well, speaking of schedules and deadlines, how’s the planning for the family gathering at Mum’s in a few weeks? Going to manage the logistics and the clashes? Actually, that’s part of what I needed time off for today. I’ve been trying to piece together the availability of everyone together. It’s proving to be quite the puzzle with all the different work hours and preferences. Yeah, planning for family can be just as intricate as a production schedule! Especially with so many relatives changing plans last minute. True. I’m thinking maybe we need a bit more structured approach for this time. A shared Google doc or something where everyone just inputs when they’re available. That’s a great idea! And maybe an option for the more tentative folks to say they could be available “sometime during this window?” So we can fill in slots as we go. Yeah, plus then the more decisive people can make decisions. Otherwise, we’re thinking everyone else will sort it out while they’re kicking it about for another two weeks.

So, I was browsing on Flightradar24 last night and noticed that there are actually still flights operating on Christmas Day. It's not as empty as you'd think, actually. Really? Are you kidding me? I guess if you're on the other side of the world though, it makes sense... Oh, hell no. Flying on Christmas Day? I'd rather take a boat. I guess some people can't actually spend Christmas at home. Like, service staff, pilots, and stuff. But even so, it must be depressing. Well, some people, like the airline staff, might have to choose to work that day, but also I saw that airlines do offer 'Christmas Eve' or just late night flights purposely for those who wish to spend part of the vacation on Christmas Day at home or another destination. Hence the late-night departures? Because if they flew during the day, it'd be missing the whole family dinner, breakfast, etc. Exactly. Off-peak times are their best chance to avoid the family chaos. And it's not cheap, I’m sure. I mean, who wants to fork out extra cash for that privilege? Unless you're super entitled or have priority airline status, I guess? Strikes me as a terrible time for delays, though. What if weather is bad and you’re stuck at the airport? Ah, the thought of Christmas at an airport is grim. True, but sometimes the really early Christmas Day flights can actually be quite leisurely. Empty airport, quick check-in, no baggage claim delays... unless, of course, the flight is full and you're the one with too much luggage. And then on the other hand, who wants to fly the next day? Seems like the whole logistics of it would be a nightmare with so many people departing right after. If you think about it, maybe it's not about being stuck alone, but traveling and arriving early to spend more time with relatives who'll arrive later that day. Or maybe it's a family on the way back from a pre-Christmas holiday. Exactly, or people with different cultural celebrations, or for whom Christmas is work-related and not family-oriented at all. Ah, I suppose so. Though if I had to choose, I'd take Christmas in bed over Christmas in a plane, any day. Likewise here. But I can't help thinking of all the food that’ll go to waste at cafes and bakeries that day.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new car that's almost as fast as our current one but it's got super cool technology like talking navigation and stuff? Oh yeah, I've seen that one. It's got quite a different voice compared to other cars, though. You know, kind of futuristic and clinical. Yeah, I'd totally go for that. I mean, my current car has the most boring voice ever, right? It just reads off the directions, no personality whatsoever. True that. You know what's weird? My mum still has her old Ford and it's got this really '90s robot voice. Always cracks me up. Haha, yeah. I've got a colleague whose mum uses a GPS with what can only be described as the most butch, ex-military voice ever. Every time it says "turn right," it's like a drill sergeant ordering him about. That's hilarious. I wonder how they select the voices for these? Do they do focus groups or just pick something that sounds sleek and modern? I hope so. A friend of mine once tried to set his navigation on his phone to sound like a Jamaican tourist guide. Not sure why, but apparently it was kind of neat, while the system was still working. Haha, that's a great story. So, speaking of different voices and accents, have you guys noticed how your own accents have changed since moving to Cambridge? I feel like I've picked up more RP since coming here. Oh, definitely. And it’s not just the geographical influence. Just spending time with people from different areas changes the way you speak, even if you try to avoid it. True that. I've definitely noticed the different accents in clubs or just around town. Cambridge’s got a real mix, isn’t it? You get the traditional Cambridge accent but also all the students from everywhere else. Absolutely. And it’s not just the technical features of the voice or changing accents. Accents are also tied to identity and sense of place, don’t you think? I mean, some people deliberately hang onto their accent to maintain connections to where they’re from. And it's not all zero-sum gain with accents, either. You can keep the core of your original accent but be aware of and adopt bits from elsewhere. Like, you hear people here use words or phrases that aren't from around here, but they've adopted them.

Did you see that new movie that just came out? No, what’s it called? It’s called "Another Universe". It’s about parallel universes and stuff. Oh right, I heard about it. I didn't know you were into sci-fi though. Me? I'm into anything that's interesting. That stuff about alternate realities is pretty mind-blowing, actually. Totally, right? And the physics behind it – it’s fascinating. Though, let’s be honest, even if you try to explain it, it’s still a little impossible to fully understand. Agreed. But what about the music from the movie? I heard it’s got a pretty good soundtrack. Yeah, there’s a song by that artist, “Echoes of Eternity” or something. I can't remember, but I’ve heard it’s pretty deep. It is! I listened to it last night. It’s got a bit of a mysterious vibe to it, while the rest of the music has this futuristic edge. It matches the concept perfectly. So, what music do you usually listen to? I know you’re into some less mainstream bands. Yeah, I’m a bit of a fan of experimental indie rock and lo-fi electronic. It’s all about mood and atmosphere for me. Like, have you ever heard of “The Softest Dawn”? Yeah, kind of. It’s good, but I've been listening to more folk lately. Maybe next time, how about a word that's more directly about youth? Good idea. How about "Precocious"? I helped you win last time! And it's my turn to stifle your emotions!

I talked to my supervisor the other day about various sociolinguistics theories. It really seems to highlight the drastically different language styles even within a small region – do you find that in your research? Absolutely, and it extends beyond regional variations into accent and even grammatical structures. I've been working with some researchers looking into the use of 'ma' in North-Eastern England alongside verbs. It's fascinating how distinct it is compared to other parts of the UK. Fascinating indeed. I've been studying some of the northern Midlands varieties. Sentence-final particles like 'aye' or 'y' - so much variation in usage but little study on why certain demographics use it more than others. Ah, you’re diving into the particle study - I’ve seen some studies suggesting it’s linked to how formal/informal the context is, but it could be even more nuanced. It’s like, for example, older folks use it more or as a marker of expertise in certain domains. Precisely, and that's what overlaps with what we're seeing. There's this kind of assumed 'overuse' in media depictions of the North; the particles become a kind of exaggerated defining feature - but the real use is far more complex and varied than that. Right, like 'getting the bin out' or 'goin' to the shops'... really, it's about pragmatic functions of discourse, not just 'dialect markers' that caricatured analysis often treats them as. True analysis is the goal now. For my thesis, I’m looking at cross-generational use and if younger people are abandoning the more marked forms or not. More variables than just age, I’m finding, like socioeconomic status and marital status playing a role too. That’s solid. For us, we’ve noticed that certain constructions seem to be being levelled out over generations but changing according to where in the socioeconomic spectrum you are. Like, certain markers may be perceived as 'lower class' so are less likely in more professional spheres. It's always class - so much influence. I've spoken to a few Cambridge locals here who report that even within the city, depending on which neighboorhood you're from... Clearly, regional and socioeconomic dynamics are intertwined. The problem with many studies is they don't account for fine-grained connections. And all these variables seem to affect where and how strongly you see these features. I wish there were more corpus-based research on the issue.

Well, maybe not the healthiest choice, but a bit of fun can be part of it, as long as we also do things the right way. Speaking of fun, weren't we going to the school tennis tournament soon? I need to remember to sign the form for either practice sessions or just attending. Right, and it's important to decide if you want to participate or just watch. We need to confirm that by next week. I might participate. I like playing tennis. That's great! We just need to make sure you're fitted in with everything else like homework and the circus workshop you're helping with for the school event. Ooh, the circus workshop! We get to be clowns or trapeze artists. I'm not sure I can be a trapeze artist. Oh, funny thinking you could just swing from the ceiling like that. But there's another workshop that might interest you more – dressing up as historical characters. We could look into the ancient Romans for that.

I talked to [Name of Teacher-friend who attended the debate] this morning, and she had some interesting things to say about the debate on teaching history – do you remember we were kind of discussing that? Yeah, I think the thing that really struck me was how they were arguing about whether history should focus more on individual stories or broader societal movements. As someone who works in advertising, I see how both can be really powerful but in different ways. For a campaign, you want to connect with people on a personal level but also understand the larger context. I remember when I was in school, history was all about kings and wars. I never really understood the broader context until much later. What do you think is most important, individual stories or big historical movements? I think both are very important. Individual stories can make history more relatable and engaging for students. But broader movements help students see patterns and connections that might not be as obvious otherwise. The challenge is finding a balance. That's very true. When it comes to advertising as well, I often find myself recommending that we incorporate personal stories – maybe a customer testimonial or a case study – into our campaigns to make the product or service more appealing. But at the same time, we need to consider the broader trends or societal issues that might be affecting our target audience. It's all about relevance really. For instance, when I was at uni, we were always taught through a broad analysis first – doesn’t matter what subject, it was always about "how this fits into the larger picture” and then we'd drill down. Did they do that when you were in school, or has that changed much? I think methods have blurred a bit over the years. The curriculum now tries to strike a balance between content knowledge and skills, but sometimes it feels like it leans too much towards skills-based learning without sufficient depth in the content. You know, it's all about analysis and interpretation these days, which is great, but sometimes I worry students are missing out on some of the fundamental knowledge. That's true. I mean, in advertising, if we don't understand the history of an industry or the broader social movements and trends, we can miss opportunities for really impactful campaigns. It's about understanding the context in which our audience is living and making decisions.

Ah terrible weather we're having now. I remember when it used to be like this but today's like every day. Well it's winter, Milton. We can't expect sunshine all year round. Indeed. Speaking of the weather, this old armchair – do you remember grandpa bought it from the auction years and years ago? Yes, I do. It's been through a lot, right? Through two wars and it still remains. Sturdier than most furniture today. I always wondered if it had any family stories hidden in its history – who had sat in it before, what kind of conversations it had been a part of. Maybe it was owned by someone who was in the navy, or a soldier during the wars we talk about. That's a possibility, Richard. It's a piece of history just looking for its story. What about police, you know? Did police officers ever sit in it during inspections or for whatever reason? That's an interesting angle. We could research it if we wanted to learn more. I doubt the police would have any records on that though, Milton. True. But think of all the people it might have welcomed, stories it might have heard. It's a part of us now, sitting here in our home. Speaking of, I still can't believe how different the police are today compared to when you were a kid, Richard. Oh, they've changed a lot. More formal, more… wary, maybe. I always wondered how they judged the seriousness of crimes. Did they really make decisions based on things the way we hear about? As a childminder, I always wondered about that. The little world our kids lived in was so different from the bigger world outside. We've had our fair share of disagreements with the police, changing rules and all that. But on the whole, most of them are just trying to do their job. Yeah, fair enough. I suppose it's like any business, they've got their challenges. It does bring to mind, though, the world our kids are growing up in. So much conflict, so many ups and downs. We can only do what we can. I believe in teaching them about peace and understanding as much as we do about history and reasoning. Absolutely. And while we're at it, I must say this armchair has seen a lot of peaceful times too.

So how are we going to deal with this? We can't just let everything slide, right? I know and I agree. But we need to talk about something else before this mortgage situation and the extended family visit next month. True, my throat has been absolutely killing me and I'm worried I might be getting a bit unwell. Oh that's terrible to hear. You should probably see a doctor. You can't be teaching English when you're struggling to speak. Exactly, and I've been relying on that income. This illness is just like the worst timing. It's never good but we'll manage. Shall we discuss the mortgage arrangements then? Yeah, okay. We're looking at rates and options with Halifax right? Yes, and the advisor said we should visit the branch in Bedford if we want to sort it all out smoothly. I hope so. The whole process is giving me a headache. I've been through it before. It's manageable with good advice. Where did you get the idea for this house in the first place? You know, it's the one we saw last weekend while visiting Dad. It was near the university, nice location, nice size. Oh right. And you fell in love, didn't you? Yeah, kind of. And with the deal they're offering now, it seems like a good price considering. That's great. As for the food and entertainment, you planning to do all the cooking or hire a caterer for the family gathering? Probably a mix. I can do the basics but for the larger gathering, a caterer would definitely help. Plus, we can focus on other things. Makes sense. Have you thought about what movies to watch during that time? Hmm, I was thinking of renting some old classics or maybe some new releases. I know extended family visits can be a bit stressful so we need something light. Light and easy to agree on. Maybe have a pick and choose session. Yeah, or just stick to the classics. Everyone can have their say. I also thought about showing my old videos from school days or the ones we made when we were kids. Oh that could be a great way to lighten the mood! I remember those videos. They were hilarious. Exactly, and it can help stir up some good memories. Anyway, back to the mortgage, I really hope we can get a good rate and not make it too tight for us, given my, well, health situation right now.

So, for tonight’s birthday dinner for Gran, what type of food are we thinking? Right, well, I think we've already decided the general idea. We're planning a buffet style with a mix of dishes she likes and some new recipes to keep it interesting. Yes, exactly. She loves her fish but the question is, where are we getting it? Do you want to check out that new fishmonger down the High Street or just get it from the supermarket? I was thinking we should opt for the fishmonger just to ensure quality. It's only a short walk and they’re known to have the freshest fish around. Brilliant idea. And then we can also get some candles and maybe that smell of the sea which Gran loves. It's all about creating the right ambiance. Agreed. Setting the table too might be a little tricky given her dementia. Maybe we can just have a few strategically placed pictures of family around, light some candles, and keep the table low? Maybe a few familiar items on the table to make it feel comfortable. Exactly. Simple but effective. And maybe we can print out pictures of the kids so they can easily recognize them. Speaking of which, we also need to think about the seating plan. She can't remember everyone's name at times, so maybe we can have placemats with pictures and names? Great idea, really helps with easing any anxiety around not recognizing people. We might also want to limit the noise and keep conversation at a comfortable level since things can get overwhelming quickly for her. Definitely. Perhaps we could also consider rearranging the cupboards if it’s feasible so things are more easily accessible and familiar. More accessibility equals less stress for her. That’s a good point. I remember when she tried to find the sugar and couldn’t because it wasn’t in its usual spot. It was really upsetting for her. Yeah, and on that note, maybe we can also check her condition over the past days? If she’s feeling particularly fatigued, we might have to adjust our plans a bit. Wise, indeed. And have we decided on a dessert? We can show her pictures and let her pick. Maybe Gran’s favorite cake or something similar? I was thinking we do her favorite Victoria sponge with some fresh strawberries and cream.

So, I got my wisdom teeth out yesterday. Oh, gods. How did it go? It was actually okay, I talked to my dentist the whole time. Made it not as scary. That's great! Did they give you a lot of painkillers? Yeah, they gave me some pretty strong stuff. But they said I could still take paracetamol if I needed it. Good. Tablets can be your friend in times like this. Yeah, they really are. Speaking of... my parents are being a bit, um, overbearing about it. As usual, or am I mistaken? As usual. They keep checking in on me every hour and asking if I'm okay even though I've been texting them updates. Parents want to make sure you're alright. I know, but sometimes... it feels like they don't trust me to take care of myself. I hope you remember that it's coming from a place of love. They just don't want anything to happen to their little girl. I know, and I appreciate the worry. But sometimes I wish they could let me just do my thing and not worry so much. It can be hard for them to let go, especially when it comes to important things like health. Definitely. And in all fairness, I do need to take it easy for a few days. But they're already asking me about going back to uni on Monday. Oh no! You're not even out of the dentist phase yet and they're already planning for you to go back to studies. I know right? But I guess that's their way of ensuring I keep on track with my studies. It's classic parental behavior. My mum's always been like that too. Yep. But in my defense, my flatmate mentioned something about her parents offering to help me move house when I go back. That's thoughtful. But, do you think you'll need help? It's not like Cambridge is huge. Yeah, but it depends on the flat. If it's in a less accessible area, maybe. But I've got a pretty good place lined up I think. Well, if your parents are offering, why not take them up on it? It'll just make everything easier for you. I suppose so. And while they're there, we could even sort my room out already. That's a good idea!

[speaking to Speaker_2] Are you still enjoying playing with that money game we set up with the chess pieces, dear? [in kindergarten/adolescent voice] Yeah! But last time I wanted to make a "village" with our cookies and I ran out of "money". Now I'm out of "money" too and it's hard to trade even if I want to get another colour. [jumping in, slightly overlapping] Even lazy king can't get more cookies! [chuckling] You two are certainly industrious with your "baking" efforts. [thoughtful] Oh, like helping share your "money" next time or even better, making some more "cookies" this week. You could give some to a neighbor or grandma if she needs some "cakes". [intrigued] Can we do that for Chinese New Year? It feels like the right time for kindness coins! [smiling] A nice idea! Chinese New Year is indeed about being kind to others. We could bake in batches: some for our generosity, some for the "village", and maybe even some for "chess market" events leading up to it. [animated] Oh, that sounds so fun! Can we colour the cookies red for good luck? We could. And who knows, maybe we'll learn about a few real Chinese New Year traditions and weave those in as well. [to Speaker_3] Like sharing oranges for good fortune or creating little animal statues from clay. [cute and curious] What’s that? [explainively] Well, for Chinese New Year people sometimes give oranges and make or buy little animals, like dragons or pigs, because those animals are lucky symbols. Maybe we could do that as a craft project leading up to February. [interjecting] Can we make the oranges from clay or paper? [thoughtfully] We could make some oranges from paper — that’s a fun idea. [excitedly] And I know! I can paint some red clovers and dragons and share them with friends for luck! [grinning] I'll make the "cookies" and give them as gifts with the clay oranges! [contentedly] That sounds like a very thoughtful plan. And we could also plan a small family act of kindness for Chinese New Year — maybe something like making a gratitude card for someone who supports us or helps us, like our downstairs neighbor or a local charity. That’s like catching two fish with one acting of kindness cake!

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 :   Background:   It is a Sunday afternoon and Hannah and Sue are home after having been talked about Hannah's car accident and the various conversations that followed. They are having a quiet time together chatting and catching up. ---   Speaker_1 :   So, mum, have you thought about what I said last week about the theme of Alice in Wonderland for my costume?   Speaker_2 :   Oh, I had almost forgotten. That’s a great idea. But remember, keeps it subtle. You don’t want something too complex for a school dance.   Hannah:   Yeah, I thought I could wear a blue dress with a white apron and a hat. Maybe add a clock on my wrist just like the White Rabbit.   Sue:   That sounds lovely. You’ll be impossible to miss but also very creative. What about music? Are you still thinking of playing a certain song on your phone?   Hannah:   Yeah, looking for a nice version of “Just Like Fire” by Pink. It’s upbeat and fits the theme a bit. It’s also on my playlist these days.   Sue:   Sounds good. It’s a cute song. I don’t know if it’s suitable for school but it’s appropriate for a dance, I think. You’re becoming quite the music curator.   Hannah:   Haha, thanks. It’s just that we were discussing the accident, and music helps me feel better. Well, actually, it’s not just the music but also the Internet. I love how there’s always something new to find and learn, even scar-related stuff. Did you see those really cool, custom prosthetic covers they’re making now?   Sue:   I did. How they can turn something that might make you feel bad into a positive, kind of fashionable thing. It’s like art, isn’t it?   Hannah:   Exactly! I was thinking about the scar, and it’s weird but I’ve actually seen pictures where people are turning it into a design —like getting a tattoo or something unique around or on it.   Sue:   That’s courage and creativity, but also healing. I’m proud of you for thinking about it in that way.   Hannah:   I was a bit nervous when some people would stare or ask questions. But I figured if we’re talking about it, maybe it can help others too.   Sue:   It might help others, or it might show them that physical differences don’t define us.

Speaker_1 :   I talked to that group the other night down by Surrey, remember? They're quite idealistic, almost romantic about protecting their countryside. But I told them – research is key. You can't just throw emotions around and expect it to win points. A good strategy starts with solid data and understanding the planning laws.   Speaker_2 :   Ah, absolutely. Our very own council here can be...shall we say, unpredictable with how they support local opinion versus national energy goals. I've seen it with the solar panels in the nearby parishes. What seemed like a simple approval process turned into a big battle.   Speaker_3 :   Indeed. And beyond planning laws, there's the big picture – the whole "renewable transition" that governments keep touting. The amounts they throw at research are a drop in the ocean compared to what they spend on subsidies for these...some might say, outdated tech solutions.      And it's not just money. The politics between the local councils, the energy companies, and these protest groups – it's a minefield. One side blames the council for being pawns of big energy, the other side says the protesters are just anti-progress.      Exactly. The research we need is not just to argue against wind turbines but to present viable alternatives. For example, how do we improve energy storage to make solar or wind power more consistent? That requires serious R&D investment, not just political lip service.      Alright, and let’s not forget the 'informational warfare' – the ease with which misinformation can spread, especially in today’s digital age. Groups need to be on top of the science, the policy, all of it. I once suggested to the protesters creating an info sheet of measured, verified data points about noise pollution, bird impacts, etc., but I noticed a lot of them weren’t even looking at peer-reviewed studies.      That's what I'm saying! Emotional appeal has its place, but when you present solid facts and aren't just screaming "Think of the views!", you make a real impact. I teach global issues now, and I see it in my students – when they truly understand the context, the viability of various solutions, they can argue a policy or a plan.      Speaking of policies, what do you think of the Scottish referendum in two weeks? Whether Scotland stays or goes, we’re all watching to see if there’s a new energy policy direction across the UK.

So Grace, today we'd like to talk about your driving. How is it going? Grace, we've noticed you're still driving with the L-plates. How are you finding the process, dear? You've been driving now for about three months, I believe? Yes, and we're hoping you'll soon be able to take the test. Grace: Erm, yeah, it's okay. I'm just keeps coming across loads of new people in town who don't seem to be aware of the rules. It frustrates me because sometimes I'm unsure how to react. Well, that's understandable. But let's remind you to stay calm and patient. Everyone makes mistakes, even the best of drivers. It's important to remember the L-plate means learners on the road. And I think you're going a bit too much on your own yet, maybe stick with the instructor a little bit longer? Grace: I thought I was doing okay, but yeah, maybe I should keep practicing or even take some extra lessons. Also, have you sorted out car insurance yet? Grace: Not yet. I was wondering if we could discuss the best options. We thought about adding you to our policy or getting you a separate policy, but we want to make sure you're not spending too much for what you need. And you need to consider all the details like whether to have comprehensive or third-party only, and all those extras. Grace: Like what? I don't know much about it. Well, comprehensive covers you more broadly, including damage to your own car, while third-party only covers damages to others. And there are those extras like breakdown cover, which can be very useful. But it can drive up the premium if you're not careful. Grace: So which is better for me? As a learner, third-party could suffice until you've passed the test and gained some actual driving experience. Then you can reassess for something more comprehensive. Grace: Alright, okay, that makes sense. And on the topic of driving—how about a holiday? We're considering a break this summer. Yes, we were thinking maybe to Devon or maybe somewhere a bit different next year we could aim for Scotland or Wales? Grace: Sounds good. Scotland could be really cool. So, have you all thought about it more? I know sometimes choosing where to go can be difficult with three...

Pa, I was browsing on Facebook yesterday and I came across an app that uses AI to predict the winner of horse races. You would've loved it! Oh really, that sounds quite handy but I'm not sure I'd want to bet on it now, the odds are tricky enough as they are. Exactly! But sometimes it gives tips and says the horse has about a 95% chance of winning. I'm tempted to try it, just for fun I mean, not seriously. Oh, I'd want to get alongside with something like that if it were my time again, but you, you stick to your books, sweetie. I will, don't worry. You know, back when I was young we used to bet without any fancy apps. Just the newspaper tips and odds from the races. And you had to physically go to the bookies. Yeah, that was a lot of work. A lot of effort, but people trusted it more back then. Now it seems like everything is online and sometimes I worry you don't know what you're getting into with some of these online apps. I know, I understand the risks. I hope so. And what about driving in Brighton? I heard parking can be a nightmare there, right? Yes, it's crazy. Parking prices are through the roof and even if you do find a spot, it's always tight. I've learned to time my journeys based on when I think the spots will be available. Brighton's changed a lot since I lived there in the 50s. We didn't even have cars for most of the family then, but I do remember walking everywhere or just catching buses. More green methods those days, weren't they, less of the traffic we have now. If only we still had more of those environmentally friendly options today. Technology has moved so fast, changing the world. Speaking of which, my Facebook notifications are driving me up the wall. Every time I try to do something, they pop up saying someone’s liked my post or commented. I thought they might be useful but honestly, some of that stuff can be very distracting, and it’s one of the reasons I avoid it as much as I can. I know, and I try to turn them off when I need to focus but sometimes it's really hard to resist.

So tell me about that Shakespeare thing. You're pretty passionate about's it? Oh, Shakespeare. Yeah, I've always been fascinated by his work, especially Macbeth. But you know who's not? My mum. A Shakespeare skeptic, huh? Yeah, she once asked me what’s so bad about a guy who just murdered people and got away with it, but my point is that it's not about the guy, it's about the play. The complexity, the structure, it’s all so... Shakespearean. Right, let me guess, she just blunders in, points to a random line, and says, "What's with the old English nonsense?" Exactly! And then says, "I’ve got better things to do than trying to understand Shakespeare when I could be watching the Real Housewives of... wherever." Haha, yeah, classic. The language barrier and cultural references are too much sometimes, I guess. It's crazy, right? But I love it. It's like a different world, a different language, and I’m learning it. Kinda makes me feel like this is a skill I’ve mastered, which is kind of funny since I’ve spent hours just "winning" at video games, while the Bard was mastering his craft in a more... worthwhile way. Ah, ‘winning’ at video games. Is that like a job or something you boast about? "Oh, I totally dominated that silly game. I’m a pro." Yeah, almost. But you know, joking aside, I feel like doesn’t everyone in our generation subconsciously see "winning" at anything as this huge achievement? It's like we've been trained to compete or just to do things the ‘right’ way to the point where any small victory feels like justifying our existence. You're right, it’s funny how we equate small victories with self-worth sometimes. Back in uni, my friends and I used to make bets on stupid stuff just so we could sit there later and be like, "I bet I told you so." Right? I know a guy, let's call him "Dave" for anonymity’s sake, who once bets he could learn to play golf in a week and then he took the whole campus hostage until they agreed to this ridiculous challenge. Dave's little escapade? That’s priceless. So, he actually managed to play a full 18 holes? He did alright, I suppose. More importantly, he won... a pint of cider from us for agreeing to stop harassing the golf club staff.

Yeah so this week was crazy. I nearly missed the deadline for that conference schedule and had to pull an all-nighter. Oh no did you finish on time? Yes, but it was touch and go, let me tell you. Oh wow, that's rough. I feel like my week was pretty chill compared to that. I was just digging up some garden beds for a new project. Now, that's hard work, but at least it's not as pressure-filled as your job must be. [laughing] Well, I guess pressure is relative! Even though I have to keep all those factory machines running smoothly and on schedule, at least I get to walk around a bit and not sit at a desk all day. That does sound better than conference organizing! [chuckles] Though I have to say, seeing the room finally set up the day before and knowing it's all ready is a great feeling. Yeah, that's rewarding in itself, isn't it? You know, for all the stress beforehand, at least you get to see the fruits of your labor. Exactly. Now, have either of you tried intermittent fasting? I just started and it's been... interesting. [interrupting with a mix of surprise and curiosity] Oh, really? What makes you do that? Well, I've heard it's good for weight loss and some health benefits, but mostly I'm doing it for productivity. Less meals mean less time thinking about food and more focus on work. Except, when you're starving... [laughing] Oh no, have you had any [mimics holding stomach] moments of weakness? Yes, plenty. Last night, around 11 am when my fast started... seeing all the food in the fridge was torture! [laughing] That does sound familiar. But do you think it's sustainable for you long-term? I mean, as much as I hate changing my habits, I also know consistency is key. True. I was on the fence before but I'm trying to give it a full month before deciding if it's for me. It's been tough but I've noticed I have more energy some days, which is nice. I could use more energy. Got any tips on that? Like, healthy snacks or stuff? I started bringing nuts and dried fruit with me. They're light and don’t spoil easily. And you can always turn to tea if you need something to drink but not to eat.

Right okay now I'm going to show you around the garden and I've got some things today that I want to talk about. That sounds excellent. You two are always making changes out here. Just trying to make things nice for when questions come in the days and nights isn't it? Indeed, Maud. And aside from that, I've been thinking... of actually looking into getting a TV licence. And why is that dear? Are you planning on putting a TV in your shed? No, no, not at all – but with all the talk about the new programme I heard on – you've heard of it, the one that talks about the cosmos and what not... Stars, space, the universe... yes yes, that's the one. Yes, the astronomy show. It's excellent, isn't it? Absolutely. And I've recently been wondering about things like black holes, how it all began, that sort of thing. So, I'm thinking maybe that a TV licence this time isn't such a bad idea. Well I can't say I disagree. Where did you get the idea for this show, actually? It was on the other day when the eclipse was on. Someone mentioned it. Ah, the eclipse – I saw it through the telescope in the shed. Quite impressive wasn't it? Indeed it was. An event like that – you feel tiny and yet expansive all at once. Exactly! And the presenter is the one that I kind of – Dr. Brian Cox or was it someone else? No, it’s that other gentleman who’s... Oh, Professor Brian Cox? Different show. The one you're thinking of is probably by Professor Cox or maybe Dr. Cox but from a different science perspective. You mean Dr. Alice Roberts? I think you're thinking of Dr. Alice Roberts. She often covers broadly scientific programmes. Right, right! That's the one – the painting one No, the one about the cosmos. Oh, the cosmos programme. There are quite a few. I believe you're thinking of a certain show with Professor Cox but Dr. Cox is more into physics and popularizing it. You might be thinking of David Attenborough presenting something but that's... No, no, the one talking about the cosmos and origins of the universe. Is it the BBC’s “Space: A Horizon Guide” series? I don’t think so. It's more recent and I think it might be what you get with a TV license subscription.

Have you got the voice guide sorted for the trip now? Yeah, I set it up this morning. Going to take us through Nottingham then Derby and Lincoln. Good, that makes life easier. I'm just hoping the traffic won't be too bad. It should be okay, given it's a Sunday. Though if we hit any roadworks we could be late. Right, we should just keep an eye on the signs. I don’t think we’ve ever had that kind of experience with beer and the brewery. It could be fun, and if it’s not what we’re in the mood for, we can always try another place. That’s a good plan.
