I’ve always heard it’s worth seeing, especially the views from the top. Oh, it’s stunning. You can see for miles when you’re up there. I’ve taken friends often, and everyone loves it. That’s what I've heard. It’s a shame we won’t have much time in Lincoln this trip though. Maybe next time then. We’ll still have a little time to see some of the highlights, and maybe there’s a quick bite to eat at one of the little places nearby.

You know, I overheard ANON talking about her birdwatching the other day, and I couldn’t help but think of Mrs. Jenkins. Remember her? The way she could identify any bird song and tell you the type and sometimes even the history behind it. Oh absolutely, Mrs. Jenkins was incredible! I used to love how she'd point out even the most subtle differences in their calls. She had such an ear for it. Yes! Even when I visited her house, she’d have the windows open and you'd hear this beautiful song early in the morning, and she'd point towards the window and say, “Now, that’s a robin,” or “That’s a song thrush.” She knew them all. It was amazing. And she used to be so particular about feeding them the right things too. I remember she was always concerned about the healthiest options for her feathered friends. Yes! And then there was her alarm clock. I mean, it was the birds outside her window! “They're my wake-up call. Always on time,” she’d say. I often thought about that when I couldn’t sleep or was early in the mornings. Her dedication was inspiring. Definitely. It also reminded me of visiting the dentist last week. The new one is much more efficient but lacks that personal touch we’re used to. Shows you what humanity can do when they care, doesn’t it? Agreed! On the topic of human touches, have you heard from our mutual friend Margaret? She mentioned she had a nosebleed recently. She did, worryingly. But I just sent her a message to check in. She said it was stress-related, nothing serious. Just proves we’ve all got our weak points regardless of our age, and it’s always good to check in on people. Indeed. It’s one of the things I love about gardening, actually. The physical work sure is nice for stress but also the quiet contemplation. Sometimes, when I’m out there, I can’t help but think about our elderly women friends who are often the backbone of their communities. Absolutely. Even Mrs. Jenkins, though she wasn’t as young anymore, was out in her garden every day, even after her husband passed. It kept her going, gave her purpose and connection to nature. You know, it also makes me think about this throat cancer that seems to be more prevalent.

Right! Emma, isn't it? It's lovely to see you! You look fantastic. Oh, thank you! It's been ages, hasn't it? I feel like a lifetime has passed. How have you been? Busy, but good. All very secondary school stuff. But even that keeps changing, loads of new regulations to get my head around. You know, it's funny when you're in a profession for a while, you start thinking you've seen it all, but then trends change. It just like the whole bit about digital platforms for learning. It's good in places, but then you also have to deal with the well-being side of screen time and all that. It's a whole new challenge. That's so true. I mean, thinking back, when I was in school, it was all physical books and pens. Now it's so much more sophisticated. Yeah! Now the kids are learning this coding, on computers, from early on. Exactly! I often wonder how it'll shape their world. You know, speaking of kids, I've been meaning to ask you, how is the family life treating you? I remember you were going through some tough times with IVF a couple of years back. Oh, it's all good now. We've got a lovely little boy. He's fantastic, keeps us busy all the time. I'm so happy for you! It's a hell of a journey, isn't it? Oh, it really is, but oh so worth it. But the thing is, now I'm looking at single parenthood from a different angle, as a friend is going through it. It's a different kind of challenge. It's one of the hardest but most rewarding jobs out there, I think. Definitely. It’s all about resilience and juggling a million things at once. I'm sure you see that with your work too, just in a different context. Absolutely! My work with social work, it's all about adapting to new situations, and strengthening individuals. Do you ever almost wish you could just escape digitally? I mean, I swear sometimes social media feels like a little too much. Oh, don't even get me started on that! I mean, as a teacher, I'm always on there for resources and whatnot, but sometimes it feels overwhelming with all these platforms and the pressure of presenting a perfect online life.

So, how's life been since retirements? Any grand new hobbies now? Ah, you know, it catches up with you. Just trying to keep up with my garden and the grandkids, but my wife keeps saying I need to get out and do something more active. Oh, I hear that! keeps coming up with new things. She's always suggesting volunteer work or joining book clubs, but I'm a bit lazy I guess. Well, at least your garden is looking good, though. Thanks, actually needs a bit more work but I'm getting there. What about you? How's your health been? The usual arthritis and things, but nothing major. The worst part is thinking about the state of the world these days. Politics these days are just so stressful. I know what you mean! It feels like every day there's a new crisis. One moment it's the crime rate in this city, and the next it's the cutbacks in education and health. It's hard to stay positive. Especially the thing about the new library closing down. It's a bit of a central hub for so many people in the community. I wonder what they'll replace it with. True! I'm worried about all the young kids who used to use that library all the time. It’s so important for their education and development. Well, maybe things will pick up. As long as they don’t start cutting back on schools, that would be a disaster. Agreed wholeheartedly. I just tried to get my niece to come for a little while since her school's library is tiny now, but she had too much homework already. That's the thing, they pile them up with so much homework and then we wonder why they don’t do it all out of curiosity. They're just overwhelmed. Exactly, when I was teaching, so much focus was on exams and grades, but the real learning happens outside of that. That's almost gone full circle, isn't it? I used to say the same thing when I was actively teaching. Well, I suppose change is constant, but we have to make sure we’re not losing essential parts of our education system in the process. True. We also need to focus more on mental health in schools. It's such a big issue nowadays, especially with the pressures these young people face.

Right okay so I'm going to make homemade pizza first time's a charm I hope. You guys want any toppings? Well maybe some olives wouldn't hurt. Yeah olives and maybe feta. A Greek style pizza sounds good. That’ll work. I just hope it isn’t a disaster. But hey, it’s going to be fun regardless! right I’ll be sure to report back on the success of my culinary endeavours. So alongside this food adventure let me ask, has anyone watched anything good lately? I did finish “The Social Dilemma”, that was quite a watch wasn’t it? Oh yeah, I saw that too. It really made me think about my phone use. Me too. It kind of hit you with just how much we rely on these things and the impact it’s having on our lives. But, you know, it’s hard to give it up Mm. I’ve tried to cut back but even as I talk about it I’m probably checking this or that on my phone. I’m sure we’re all guilty of that. Speaking of phone guilt, have you all seen the Facebook documentary “The Facebook Dilemma” by PBS? Yeah, that was quite insightful as well. Though I feel like we all know the basics by now, it still shocked me how much they blatantly disregard privacy for profits. I guess that’s a conversation for another time doesn’t it? Exactly. What about music? Anyone hear any new tracks that they can't get out of their heads? More recently for me, it’s been the new album from The 1975. I’ve been listening to it non-stop since it dropped. Oh, really? I must check it out! I’ve been listening to a lot of classical music lately to change things up. I’ve been stuck on some soundtracks. There’s something about Hans Zimmer and Tyler Bates that just gets me. I’m all for film scores too. They completely enhance an experience. Speaking of which, you guys want to plan a movie night after the pizza? Maybe pick something from a recommendation or something we want to rewatch? That sounds great. Could we watch "Inception" again? I’ve been meaning to see it again but never got around to it. Inception is a classic. We could also consider something a bit more recent like "Tenet".

So, I hear you've seen some of the latest first-person shooters. What do you think; have they improved anything? Well, they've talked about refining the mission structure and improving visuals but I still think there's room for better exploration and storytelling. I kind of agree. Storyline-wise, it’s starting to feel a bit redundant. Don't you think they're starting to miss out on some genuine character development? Absolutely, and I think it's partly because they're still trying to cram so much into each game. Think about something like Skyrim; it had this massive world, and you really had time to breathe and explore. These new shooters, they feel like you have thirty minutes from getting your mission brief to just trying to survive. I read that one of the developers said they wanted to encourage "streamer-friendly" gameplay. As much as I love watching streams, sometimes I want a game I can just play at my own pace without feeling like I'm trying to create a highlight reel. Did you grab a look at the proposed roadmap for the next few months? I think some of the updates they're rumored to be coming out are actually pretty interesting. Like, finally addressing balance issues that have been keeping the competitive scene on edge. Yeah, that's true. If they can get the weapons and abilities dialed in to the right balance, it could make a big difference. And they keep talking about adding more varied multiplayer modes, perhaps even bringing back some classic maps. I just hope they really focus on quality over quantity. Some of the maps they've released lately feel like they were rushed. I don't want to see them start sacrificing polish for the sake of churning out more content. And then on the music side... did you listen to the new releases from that one band? I’ve been diving into a few albums, and they're really exploring new sounds. It feels like they've taken risks and come up with something quite unique. I’ve heard it’s supposed to be quite a departure for them. I might need to give it a listen after work today. I played basketball with them last week. They said they’re trying out a new gym that just opened down by the river. I thought it might be worth a look; the description of their community vibe was quite strong.

So, I hear that your weekend was quite eventful huh? Yeah, you have no idea. Jeez, I was slumped out after the match talked about that chicken supper, unreal. Made my own stuff though, got the wife involved. That sounds great! How did she do on the wings this time? Oh, she got them crisper this time, took my advice and used that thermometer thingy I told her about. Now, don't start, I know she still says she doesn't need it, keeps coming out soggy, but hey, baby steps, right? Well, she's lucky you're there to guide her. Yeah, well, let’s just say my research into dehydrated chicken was slightly less successful than usual but hey, it’s all part of making the perfect wing. Speaking of research, I heard your university has a pretty good sports team, didn't you play in a scrimmage over the break? Yeah, we got together, old teammates and new, it was quite the turnout. A bit rusty, but it was good fun. Also, reminded me how much I miss being out on the pitch. Yeah, I can imagine. You must have been one of the better players back at university. Any other sports events on your radar this season? There's the university cup at the end of the semester, hoping to make some time for it. But really, it depends on how much time I have with my research looming over. I know that drill. Just don't let the PhD consume you, it's good to keep the balance. Exactly, like my mum would say, "All work and no play makes Jack or Jill or in this case, a burnt chicken sandwich a dull person." Your mum has some real gems. Speaking of which, how's Easter planning going? We're thinking a small family get-together, nothing too big. My wife’s got a knack for making these amazing hot cross buns for Easter. Makes me wish we celebrated like that back in my family. Oh, those must be delicious. It's so nice to hear about traditions being kept alive in different family ways. Yeah, it’s just nice to have those little remembrances of home and tradition even if you're far away. Definitely. And with our family get-togethers during special occasions, it’s a way for us to keep connected too, no matter where we are...

Oh look at James here he was running around like mad at your birthday party. Oh my goodness yes he was the life and soul of that party. He was literally bouncing off the walls. Still brings a smile to my face. And isn't that one where he got totally covered in cake at his fourth birthday? Yes, and I had to laugh so hard he almost didn't notice! Yes and then there's this one here, this is the picture from Iceland. Oh dear God I can't even believe that's our child. He just looks amazed to be surrounded by those natural wonders. And the look of dismay when his ice cream fell over. That was so hilarious. He was so upset, then he barely let us visit anything else because he was on his "hop on, hop off" ice cream watch. For a moment there I thought it was maybe worse than losing a limb for him. The priorities of small children. Speaking of priorities, I found it quite interesting during the London marathon. So many people carrying on through pain and exhaustion just to finish, to support charity or perhaps for their own personal goals. True, and sometimes as parents we need that kind of spirit too. It’s all about the love and the "finish line" even when the road doesn’t look ideal ahead. Definitely. It’s good that you bring that up, Mum. Looking through these pictures really puts things into perspective. All the milestones, the laughter, the adventure... And even when we were at the cinema last time for his birthday, he just loved it and wanted to go sit with you in the changing seats. Yes, and he was more impressed by the cinema’s snack bar than any of the movie trailers we showed him! It does bring back sweet memories. Ah, and this fun fair he went to just over the summer... Ooh yes. The joys of the Ferris wheel and the “spinning teacups” as he calls them. And... Oh my, his birthday coming up again? Time certainly flies. Very fast now. Another year gone by. Yes, youth is fleeting. But it's nice to see him grow and enjoy these times. Truly, these are the moments we'll cherish. I was just thinking... We should make a memory book just for these occasions. Adding to it each year.

So, I was browsing on Amazon yesterday and I came across an eBook that was called “Neighborhood Tables: A Journey Through Shared Meals and Tales”. It sounds familiar, but I don’t think I've ever read anything like that. A book about people sharing meals, huh? That does sound intriguing. I wonder if it’s about the kind of community spirit where everyone knows each other and shares cooking? Exactly! It seems to capture moments around the table with various people, talking about food and life. It reminded me of how my grandmother used to cook Sunday lunches for our whole family. Oh, how lovely! My mom did the same for us when we were kids. She made sure we all sat together, even just for the meal. She would sometimes knit while we talked. Was a good way to bond. Yes, and the meals were always so wonderful. My grandma made a special potato and leek soup with crusty bread on the side. My mom made similar comfort foods. And it wasn’t just about the food – it was the time together. I remember playing board games afterwards, Forbidden Planet and this game where you had to collect roundels to make it "home". Roundels! The very word makes me think of Scrabble. Kids in my day loved playing games like Ludo or Snakes and Ladders. Now, people have become too technology-focused for board games, don't you think? Hmm, maybe. But I find that eBooks are kind of like a modern take on sharing stories. It’s all about the love of storytelling. That’s true! But it loses that face-to-face warmth. I’ve noticed my grandchildren prefer their tablets and e-readers but I do try to set aside sessions to read together the old-fashioned way. Our children and grandchildren, they live in a completely different world. Speaking of which, have you watched anything interesting on TV recently? It’s all repeats these days, or maybe I’m just turning into my mother who watched “It’s a Small World”. Haha, I was actually reading a review of a book for work and in passing mentions of TV shows and it just hit me how similar our childhoods were despite different times. It feels like we're talking about a small world indeed, minus the Disney ride. And there's almost a bittersweet feeling in all these shared meals and memories – it’s as if we're trying to bottle up a certain “it”.

Speaker_1 :   "Blimey isn't the weather just lovely today? It's a shame we couldn't have gone for a stroll. You remember when we used to go and walk down the Wensum walk? It was our favourite pastime."   Speaker_2 :   "Lovely indeed. You know, it's funny, those memories. Like when we'd have sandwiches like we are now, chatting away about everything and nothing. Seems like just yesterday we were just like you, out and about, not stuck in here."      "Indeed. Now we're the oldies keeping each other company. Speaking of which, you remember when we thought we'd do all these grand things after retiring? I thought we'd travel, learn something new, maybe even visit those places we always dreamed of. But life got in the way, didn't it?"      "Oh, it certainly did. But it's funny, life's taught us that sometimes it's not about grand gestures or long travels. It's about these small moments. Like right now. Having sandwiches, talking about everything and nothing, that's what life really is, isn't it? Small pleasures, small comforts."      "Small comforts indeed. Speaking of which, did you see that in the paper about the whales that washed up? I couldn't believe it. Such big creatures, and they end up on our shores like that doesn't seem right."      "Well that reminds me of the time we were at the coast and saw all those seagulls. Never understood the fascination with them but there's something about seeing those creatures up close."      "True. Speaking of creatures, did you ever think we'd end up like this, retired, just living life in our own little ways? It's funny how plans work out. You dream big, but sometimes life has other plans."      "Life certainly does. I always imagined we'd have a small cottage by the sea, something modest, but comfortable. But here we are, in our own cozy little space, making do with the simple pleasures. It's not the dream maybe, but it's ours."      "It's ours indeed. Makes me think we should make more of these moments. Like planning a little day trip or something. Maybe visit our old haunts, reminisce about all that?"      "Now that's an idea. We should...we could even look into the blue badge thing. You're eligible, if you'd like to consider it. Not that we need to, but it could make exploring a bit easier.

So how was your Christmas? It was really nice. You know just relaxing at home with the family. That sounds lovely. I kind of regret not doing anything this year. Just worked right up until Boxing Day then got sick and had to take a few days off. Health is important of course, but sometimes you just need a break. True! I've given loads of thought to taking time out. You know just before we had that long break. Like not lazy time but actual holiday time. Idk if I can stomach another year of just fitting in 10 days to Spain or something. Definitely needs a good balance. I mean, I cherish those 10 days in Spain but it's just not enough. Exactly! So looking for alternatives. But then work comes in and it's like, "Oh right, no Spanish holiday for you!" I've always wanted to try driving around the UK. But that seems so... this year it just didn't happen. I’ve heard some good things about exploring the coast of Cornwall while driving. Stunning. But the car thing is a bit daunting for me. I used to have a car but after it broke down a couple of times I just gave up. Now I take public transport or taxis. Yeah, car troubles are the worst, and they always seem to happen at the worst times. I've had my share of headlights that don't work or engines deciding the day after I've washed it to stop working. Talking of car troubles reminds me of the time I got into a scrape with my dad's car and I just tried to... erm, "solve it" on my own. Which ended up with me having to get a tow back home. That's a great story! You know, my cat could sit on your lap while we're chatting, though. Oh! Would you like to talk about pets? I’ve just got a new rescue dog, it's been an adjustment but he's so loving. That's lovely! I’ve been thinking of rescuing a dog too. Our family just got a new cat though. She’s tiny and we’re all obsessed with her. Aww, pets make everything better! Except cleaning up after them, but I suppose that's just part of the job. Totally. But they’re worth it.

So, I hear that your sister might be moving out soon, isn't that right? Yeah, she's been thinking about it for ages, but now she's actually got a place lined up. It's a bit of a scary thought because it's going to change things around here quite a bit. Oh, isn't that house where her friend Tom used to live? The one with the really tall trees in the garden? No, this one's a bit further up the road. It's nice though, keeps changing as you approach it. You'd never think from the front it's got that long garden to the side. [Chuckles] I used to know a couple in London who lived in just like that house. They had what they called their "secret garden". It was big enough to host whole family gatherings without even needing to go inside. [Smiles] That sounds lovely. Speaking of houses, have you all seen the new developments happening around here? I heard they might be changing up the look of Chamberlain Street. Yeah, I heard something about that as well. They're rumoured to be building some apartments on the corner by the old flower shop. It's different from anything we're used to but who knows, maybe it'll bring in some new business and younger families. [Quietly, not sure if he should chime in] Well, they keep talking about installing better lights to tackle the crime... Maybe it’ll feel safer walking around at night. [Looks at Speaker_4] That's true. We all know this area and we like our community, but yes, doesn’t hurt to feel safer. Exactly. It's finding that balance between maintaining our community feel and also keeping up with modern needs. Speaking of balance, do any of you still watch the news? The stuff about ISIS is just so concerning. It's hard to keep up, isn't it? There's always something new each day. I try to stay informed but it's overwhelming at times. Absolutely. It’s important but it can also be mentally exhausting. I often find myself just reading about it in articles because watching the news can be quite draining for me. [Looks up, a bit shyly] I don’t know, Dad almost makes us watch the news sometimes. But sometimes I just put Harry Potter on and pretend I don’t know about stuff.

Planning a trek to Nepal? Are you still considering it? I remember telling you the other day, the mountain air is supposed to be fantastic for questions like this kind of adventure.     Indeed, I am still considering it, but my biggest worry is the altitude sickness and the language barrier. Although I've always wanted to see the Himalayas and especially Everest. But even if I don’t get to walk to Base Camp, Kathmandu and Pokhara are worth visiting on their own. Have you heard about the new altitude acclimatization schedules they recommend nowadays? They say starting in Pokhara then moving to higher altitudes to avoid sickness.     You two were always big on trekking - oh we used to trek everywhere when we were your age. I never progressed beyond the local hill walks but oh do I remember the fun we had! But, your talk of altitude sickness takes me back… my mother-in-law once told me about his mother coming from Siberia to Africa during the war - she said she barely took sick ever. Now that was resilience! But Nepal, on the other hand, it's a whole different story. I’ve heard they advise tea and rest on day one, while the Nepalis swear by their local garlic and ginger concoctions. Any other recommendations?     Tea, rest, local remedies - exactly right. But back to Nepal, I'd recommend avoiding meat as much as possible to help with acclimatization in high altitudes, really. And you should book with a reputable guide - many have local knowledge and they help with permits and fixing the trek doesn’t come in handy.   Thanks for the advice. Just last weekend our village shop had some terrific sausages - I thought ‘this could really be great for a trek, sausages are light and a good source of protein. But do you think it would be wise to take them? What about food preservation and all that?   Oh, and the local butcher! I often pick up a pack from him for our family picnics. They do a fantastic job. But on a serious note, for trekking in Nepal, freeze-dried meals and lightweight grains like quinoa or rice are probably your best bet. Though, if you're going to a town or village, the local food markets and dairy products could be interesting. I heard they even have cheese climber over there?   I love cheese, but I need to be careful.

So tell me about your week how was it. To be honest today's been a bit of a relief after what was clearly the most chaotic two hours of my working life yesterday. Oh dear, what happened yesterday? Oh the usual, three late deliveries, a client questions scope which they'd never had any issues with before, and then our external printers going down so half the materials for the conference aren't where they should be right now. Oh, that sounds very stressful. Are you still on top of it? Yeah, I'm okay. It's just ... sometimes I wonder about the planning stage, like if I could have anticipated some of these issues. That's what contingency planning is for, isn't it? But it sounds like yesterday threw even the best plans out the window. Speaking of which, I had a string of meetings yesterday that went on forever. One client kept switching the discussion to their personal life, and another wanted to spend an hour discussing their grandkid's dance recital. That's the worst, isn't it? I mean, it's nice they're happy, but when you're running up against deadlines... Exactly. But how about outside of work? Stills at all the social stuff going on, or are you all work, work, work? Ah, actually yes. I did manage to grab a drink with Alex after work yesterday, which was nice. But as for social events this week? Not really. I'm planning a get together at the weekend, but realistically that's it. Last week was the lads' night out, and this week is just settling back into the normal routine after vacation. Nice. Vacation? I’ve been thinking about a weekend away, maybe hitting up some of those new little wineries around here. If you're free, we could do a trip together? That sounds lovely but honestly, I'm trying to avoid commitments right now until I'm sure this conference is all sorted out. Plus I'm sure you're busy with your prep and all. I can't imagine how much goes into organizing one of those conferences. Oh, it's a lot, but I like it. It's engaging. And this one's actually been quite rewarding in terms of the content. There are some great speakers. I'm particularly looking forward to the session on fault lines.

So, I was browsing on the local council's website last night. Did you see that today's the last day to submit suggestions for council's development plans for the Moore area? No, I didn't. Is that right? That seems to happen so quickly now, the council’s decision timeline... It kind of sneaks up on you, doesn't it? I mean, we've all been a bit busy but now I think we should make sure we have our say. I was thinking, why don't we start a petition to save the local library? A petition? You mean like an online one, or actually going around and getting signatures? Both, actually. I think we need to get a good groundswell of support. Online is great for visibility but the council always seems more responsive to actual physical signatures. That might be a good idea. I’ve heard talk about the council wanting to redevelop that whole area, maybe into flats or something... Exactly! And the last thing we need in this already overcrowded area is less community space. I mean, a library is not just a collection of books; it’s a hub for learning, for community activities, for kids' homework club, even just a place for elderly people to meet while the kids play. They don't even realise how much that space means to so many of us. It’s a bit concerning, how often community facilities seem to be the first things to be taken away in these redevelopment plans. But starting a petition, that’s really putting your money where your mouth is. Exactly! Plus, it’s not like we’re asking them to keep it the way it is for no reason. If we can come up with a solid proposal for how the library could be modernised without falling victim to demolition, that would be great, wouldn’t it? Perhaps we could suggest they partner up with local community groups or businesses to fund upgrades? Oh, that’s a good point. Maybe we could also argue that a modern library should include a digital media space, where people can borrow things like e-books, or access video editing tools, or even just use some of the better computers people have at home. If we just keep saying it’s about books, we might miss the point that for a lot of people, a library is a safe place with free internet and quiet spaces.

You know these Jehovah's witnesses that come round. I always find it hard to deal with them. What are your thoughts? Ah, well isn't it just now, the Jehovah's witnesses were at the door yesterday again. I just feel so bad because sometimes they're just so young and they have this look in their eye, like they absolutely believe what they're saying, but I just can't bring myself to listen. I always wish there was a polite way to get them to leave without feeling like I need to enter some kind of discussion. Like how do you have that conversation where you try not to be rude? Yeah, it's a real skill. Sometimes I just say, "Thank you for your time, but I’m not interested." or "I already have religious beliefs, thank you." It’s kind of blunt but I want to be clear. That sounds like a good approach. I often just say, "I’m busy at the moment. Perhaps another time?" It gives them an out and me a moment to breathe. But have you ever noticed how some of them seem quite aggressive or condescending? It’s different from when the Salvation Army come round. They seem more friendly. Yes, absolutely. The Jehovah's witnesses can sometimes come across really pushy. It’s a bit like they’ve been taught certain phrases and they keep repeating them without really listening to what you say, you know? Yeah, it really is. One time they started talking about Armageddon and I said, "Oh that can't happen because the world doesn’t work that way, it's not just about the people that believe in it." And the guy just kind of gave me this look and repeated something about "The world of Jehovah’s witnesses". Oh dear, they often don’t realize how it can feel condescending to keep repeating things to convince you. But personally, I find it less confrontational than those ones you mentioned who talk about Armageddon. It’s like anything, you just have to politely but firmly set some boundaries. For me, saying "No thank you, goodbye" usually ends it. That’s true for most things in life, isn’t it? Like setting boundaries in marriages and friendships. Yeah, definitely. It’s like any relationship. Boundaries are key to keeping things amicable. Speaking of relationships, have any of you ever taken our family to The Old Meeting House down by the coast for Sunday lunch?

Oh did you two finish decorating Alison’s room while I was out? Yeah, we painted and hung some new drapes. You gave us a pretty clear plan and the materials. It’s looking lovely, I must say. I was just discussing with Charlotte how to deal with budget increases for the school academy this year keeps coming up due to changes. That’s a challenge, indeed. I spoke with our new neighbour Bob about it, his business is going through some outsourcing to India. Sent him a log I cut up recently, as he’s looking to get a good log burner for his place. That’s very kind of you. I made fudge last week, did I give you each a piece before you left? Oh yes, thank you! It was delicious. You’re so talented. I heard Bob also opened a new restaurant nearby. For a time, this town has been lacking in variety. I’ve heard mixed reviews. You’re right about needing more variety though. Suppose we need to support local if they’re at all viable. Well, at least there’s some excitement about the new place. Speaking of local, I saw my contractor earlier today about the antique furniture. It’s coming together in time for the family visit. I’m glad you mentioned that. I hope the cats and dogs behave during the visit… We can train them. As for the family, did we confirm the menu for the family dinner? I thought we agreed on a simple meal but with exquisite touches, perhaps those mashed potatoes you like, and of course, a good pudding… Absolutely. And by the way, I found an old family recipe book. From your grandmother’s collection, actually. We might use that for inspiration. You know how much everyone loves her traditional dishes. I hadn’t looked for that in ages! Bringing it out will surely take us all back. Reminds me, we should see if there’s a good local shop for the ingredients we’ll need. Right, and perhaps we should also prep the living room. The cushions are complete and I’ll just need to finish the upholstery for the armchairs. I’ll help if you need it. You know I’ve taken up upholstering as a hobby after... well, retirement. Remember also, if anyone needs a distraction during the visit, there’s that log I gave Bob if they want to come over to see it.

So, I was browsing Rotten Tomatoes yesterday and came across that new's film. "The Truth About Christmas." What did you think of it? Actually talked about that recently. Got some of the family together. We watched it together and found it quite enjoyable. A fresh take on Christmas traditions and kind of a bittersweet story. Yeah, I saw some people talking about how it unexpectedly moved them. It wasn’t the big blockbuster, right? More of an indie film. Exactly. And it got some really solid reviews for its portrayal. It’s not too preachy but it definitely makes you think. I was impressed. Makes me wonder what's next for similar topics. You thinking of watching any other holiday films this year? Maybe something for the upcoming Chinese holiday? There’s the "Two Dumbbell Bian Lian", have you seen it? It's more of a comedy but its scenes during the Spring Festival are quite hilarious. It’s nice to have something light when it gets busy around the festive season. I’d like to watch something like that, especially now that we’re away from home this year. You and the others planning anything special for Christmas here in China? Either for the dinner or just fun activities? Actually, we've been considering a more English-style Christmas dinner and perhaps a small, local group movie night. We have an English language meetup club here, and a couple of us thought we might organize something thematic around holiday classics or even indie films. That sounds great, actually. Or maybe we could do all-night watches or sessions with "Home Alone" or "The Santa Clause". I love that idea. Who wouldn’t? We could even mix in some Chinese holiday movies for the local flavor and meetup's cultural exchange purposes. True, and changing the movies to something more widely known could help include friends who might not be interested in a series of unknown films. Also, we should consider any local customs. For instance, it’s quite popular over here to have a large lunch on Christmas day if anyone decides to mark it. Good point about the customs. And maybe we could even organize a potluck.

Imagine these twats complaining about the bread not tasting home-made enough. It’s like, congrats you've found out we're not a five-hundred-year-old craft bakery, but we’re a modern café – do you want a status update with your overpriced kopie coffee? That’s my point! It makes me so mad – they ruin it for everyone else with their pickiness. Like, if it’s not homemade out of wood and baked on a medieval fire, it’s not good enough for them. Tell me about it – I saw someone complaining that the Birch and Bagels' service was slow in London. Like, have you ever been to London city centre during rush hour? Four in the afternoon, impossible. Then they go "Two hours wait, that’s unacceptable", and you’re sitting there thinking you’re going to the dentist, not grabbing a coffee before class. Exactly! It’s ridiculous. And the thing is, it’s often the same people on every review platform. I swear I saw the same person give one-star to a different café this morning. One-star for no soy milk when they’re not even vegan. And they often don’t even provide helpful feedback. They just say the food was nasty and the service terrible, but what, really, can we do with that information? It’s like they forget we’re real people trying to run a business. And you know what’s worse? If we try to respond, they just get even more snarky. I saw one person was complaining about the design of a café in Margate saying it was too “corporate and soulless”. I mean, come on! Margate has gone through so much. They should be grateful there’s a new place that just tried to make a nice spot for people to eat and drink. Oh, and have you seen that one new place in Reading? The one with the great concepts but they changing the menu every week. I love that restaurant’s sense of adventure but some of my customers – I know because they are also my friends – say it’s too much. Either it’s too expensive or they don’t like the changes. I had a friend who started a café in Dulwich and he’s been tweeting about the struggle almost daily. The most common complaint? “It wasn’t as Instagram-worthy as expected.”

Look Grandma what Oisin is doing, he's pretending his spoon is a bike! Oh dear, Oisin really does love his bike doesn't he? He's going to be just like his papa then isn't he? I remember when he was your age, he'd spend hours spinning his wheels. But why are there raspberries on the dinner table? Are they for us? Yes, indeed. Raspberries are not only delicious but also really good for you, full of vitamins and such. You need to eat your vegetables, they're good for your body just like biking is good for your legs. But can we have some ice cream now? They say eating vegetables helps us grow big and strong and have energy for biking. Well, you've had your vegetables, now let's talk about ice cream. What flavour would you like? Strawberry or chocolate? Chocolate! I love chocolate ice cream too! But why? Is it because of the chocolate ice cream that we can bike? Well, funnily enough, while the ice cream doesn't help with the biking itself, eating a balanced diet does help give you energy for all sorts of activities. But tonight, it's a treat after a job well done with your vegetables. Also, did you know that in our garden, we have bird eggs? They're really cool, and they come in all sorts of colours and patterns. Bird eggs? Like the ones from "The Very Hungry Caterpillar"? Exactly! We can go look at them later if you want. Can I see the eggs? And the birds? I really like birds. Yes, we can take a walk around the garden later if you'd like and maybe you can see some birds. What about my gerbils? Did you check on them today? I brought them some chocolate chips - they love those. Ah, yes, the gerbils are fine indeed, thank you for remembering them sweetie. And they could use some fresh veggies too. Maybe some carrot or apple slices? You could help cut those up. Yes! I love helping with the gerbils' dinner. I like helping in the garden too sometimes. You can find all sorts of interesting things like bird eggs and strange bugs. Exactly, there's a lot to learn from nature and taking care of animals is a big responsibility but it's also very rewarding. Speaking of learning, I've got exams soon.

So okay I thought we could perhaps arrange something for mom first or's Dad have you thought about what you want to do for Father's Day and for the holidays coming up? Well I've thought about but I need to discuss with her first isn't it because now she's got this care plan and everything so... Or maybe just like a nice home-cooked meal. Do you think she'll be up for that or does she prefer going out? We can phone around, find someone and arrange everything for you. You know, it's things like this that can really make her feel better. She does miss her independence. I just want to feel like myself again, you know. And we're here to help with anything that can make that happen, and even the smallest things can make a big difference. On a different note, have you two discussed any meal out arrangements? Perhaps a family day out?

Yeah's Dad's coming over today so we might just have to take the baby and go then. Oh really? What time? He's arriving around 4. We thought the morning, but he's actually coming in after his football match. That sounds like a good plan. It's been a while since they've all been together. Yeah, I know! He'll be very excited to see his niece again. How is she doing today, by the way? She's been a bit unsettled. Slightly teething perhaps. But she had a good morning, despite that. I hope so. So, what about sign language classes? You mentioned wanting to start or something earlier this week. Yeah, that's been on my mind lately. It seems like such a beneficial thing for her and for us, too. Do you think there are any around here that are good? Offline, I mean. I've been looking online, and there's a local community center that offers baby signing classes. That sounds promising! Do you know when they start and how often they are? They start next Wednesday at 2 PM, and it's once a week for six weeks. That's great! It would be really helpful to have some structure as well, especially during this weaning process. Absolutely. For the baby, and for both of us. I'm a bit nervous about weaning but doesn't seem ideal that she's not back to her old sleeping habits. It's completely normal, and if one day goes well, the next might not. But the class could be a good distraction and also a nice break for you. Exactly. And once she gets used to solid foods, hopefully, she'll start sleeping better again. Fingers crossed! You've also been meaning to catch up with friends, right? Yeah, there’s this small group of friends we used to meet up with regularly, but it's been a while. Maybe later this week or over the weekend we could plan a catch-up. That could be lovely. And what about your sister? Has she heard from the folks in Scotland about the upcoming meet-up? Yes, apparently things are looking good for their visit in a few weeks. They're really looking forward to seeing us all. That'll be fun. And while they're here, we could also plan a family day out somewhere interesting?

I love it out here, don't you? It's wonderful. The fresh air, the open spaces… reminds me of why we love living in the countryside. I know it's so different from London. There's a rhythm to life here that I find so soothing. Absolutely. And the villages – so intimate and close-knit. It's almost like stepping back in time. I love how friendly everyone seems. True. In London, it's all about rushing to get somewhere, right? Out here, people actually talk to you. They stop and chat. And the landscape, of course. I love these rolling hills. They remind me a bit of parts of the Dales we went on holiday to when we were younger. I always find them so evocative. There's history here, so much history. You can feel it in the earth and the air. And the mud. Don't forget the mud. Someone should make a village sign saying "We Welcome You… But Our Mud Forgives None." Well, that's Norwich in a nutshell. You know, I sometimes think the countryside is misunderstood. People think it's all bucolic and unchanging, but there's so much more depth and variety. Absolutely – like the different types of soil, the changing light as the seasons shift. There's beauty in that, and character, really. It's not just fields and farmland. And the villages! So quaint on the surface, but each with its own unique story and personality. Look at that one ahead – what's the name? That's probably Wicklewood. It has this beautiful old church and a few lovely tea rooms. The local history there is fascinating – battles were fought nearby, and there are signs of early settlement. I've always loved the way these areas feel so steeped in the past. You walk around and you can almost sense all the lives that have been lived – all the stories that these villages could tell. Stories, yes. And the way they all seem to know each other's secrets, too. It's good for us, I think. Living in this way reminds us of the importance of community, of slowing down. Very much so. It's not always easy, of course, but the quality of life… it's worth it for sure. Definitely. Do you ever feel like you just want to pick up and move into one of these old cottages and never leave?

So, I was browsing Rotten Tomatoes yesterday and I came across an interesting film review. Oh? What was it about? It was for the film "There Will Be Blood", directed by Paul Thomas Anderson. You know Daniel Day-Lewis is in it? Yeah, I've heard of that film. I haven't seen it, but I've heard it's quite good. It's actually very good. The reviewer talked about how influential Day-Lewis's performance was and even how it affected him personally. I've noticed that some people, especially actors, can be quite influenced by certain roles or performances. Absolutely. It's almost like they leave a part of themselves in those characters sometimes. Speaking of influences, I've been thinking about how well that might apply to your friend Sarah's new job. What do you mean? I mean how her work in the non-profit might be changing her perspective or even her goals in life. You know, she's always been passionate about making a difference, but now she's actually doing so directly. That's a fair point. I've noticed a change in her. She seems more motivated and driven now than ever before. It’s the kind of influence that can be truly impactful, right? More than just an acting role or a film review – it’s real-life work. Yeah, it’s interesting how one area can influence another. For example, the other day when we’re driving, I noticed there are more cyclists. That’s true. I think that's a good thing though. More people are cycling which is environmentally friendly and good for fitness. Definitely. And you know, some cities have done a great job in making sure there are bike lanes, which makes it safer for cyclists. Exactly. It's all about infrastructure and awareness. Some places really seem to get it right. Yeah. It's changing the culture and encouraging healthier lifestyle choices. Definitely. Speaking of influence, I've been reading about public policy and urban planning, and it's fascinating how so much of it comes back to influencing behaviour through design – like making bike lanes or designing safer public spaces. That's really interesting. I had no idea just designing the layout of a city could do that. It's amazing how much of a difference it can make. It can encourage more people to use public transport, or just to walk or cycle.

Isn't it just beautiful? Definitely. I've never seen more wildflowers growing in one place. It's just incredible the diversity, isn't it? Yes, and so many of them are native species, and they're thriving out here. I've been reading up on why the UK's biodiversity is plummeting. All these secondary uses for land — like agriculture keeps changing, especially with the focus on cash crops. You'd think it's about economics, but really it creates this cycle of disturbance for wildlife. I used to teach a module in our economics course that just focuses on this. How development sometimes means sacrificing biodiversity, even though places like here in the English countryside are making strides in conservation. And yet, still, it's a balance. It's all about finding that balance. It also links to how we conceptualize value, whether it's economic or ecological. I've been thinking about writing a paper on this. That sounds fascinating. What's your take? How can this balance be achieved? Well, for one, I believe in rewilding. Where possible, returning areas to their natural state. Allowing nature to flourish without as much human intervention. Of course, there are always concerns like the wolf reintroduction in Europe. It's not a straightforward decision for people who live nearby. There's also the aspect in economics regarding externalities. The costs and benefits we’re not always accounting for. For example, preserving some areas can also impact local economies but doesn’t always show up clearly in the data. Exactly. It’s about understanding those indirect costs and benefits. We can't just look at the immediate economic value. Take the value of ecosystems: pollination, soil creation, water regulation — it goes on. But it’s hard to put a direct value on it. It's also confronting species and habitats you might never see if they're changing. You know, reading about all the diverse dialects of UK wildlife… Like, I was shocked to learn there’s even a specific dialect for Seahorses and a different one for Salmon, isn't that fascinating? Haha, yes! And yet, it makes sense. Just like languages, they evolve in response to their environments. Wonderfully complex stuff. Yeah, and languages themselves are facing challenges with the way the economy is. Language change — whether it’s from outside influences or just adaptation — it’s interesting to see where it goes next.

Ah, right. So tell me, I couldn't help but notice you had a job interview last week, how did it go?      Honestly, I’m not sure yet. I was just looking to switch things up a bit, you know? My current role’s fine but I’m finding it a bit monotonous.      Yes, completely get that. Before you started, we talked about how the English curriculum was changing and that could lead to various roles. Did this one align with those ideas?      Well, yes and no. It was quite different than what I thought it would be. They were looking for someone to take on more of an interdisciplinary approach. It was intriguing but also made me realize how much I enjoy the structure we have now, really focusing on language and literature.      Ah, the lure of change can be tricky. Sometimes it looks great on paper but then...      Exactly! Plus, they didn’t seem to understand the importance of phonics in that interdisciplinary model. I found myself wanting to explain but then I thought, maybe I just don’t fit the bill for this role after all.      Well, it’s good you’re taking your time. What about another job interview couple of months ago? Didn’t that one also have something interdisciplinary and tech-based?      Oh that one. That was a nightmare. They asked for so much in terms of technology integration I barely understood half of it. And my current school isn’t set up for all that fancy tech stuff yet.      Again, timing and fit. It’s like they almost want teachers to be tech whizzes overnight. I swear, next they’ll want us to code too! How is your little one adjusting to school?      Oh, she's doing great. She loves it, but it’s been an adjustment for me not being there all day with her.      Honestly, I felt the same last year when Henry started. This past year has been so different. Less time but seeing them grow every day makes it worth it. But yeah, it’s a constant juggling act.      Exactly. This time of year with all the new back to school stuff and then job searching...I feel like I’m either being pulled in too many directions or not moving at all.      You know, it might help to focus on one thing at a time for now. There’s no need to hurry into something that doesn’t feel right, or to feel guilty about taking time to figure out what does.

So have you given much thought about what you want to do after college? Yeah, I talked to my tutor the other day and we discussed a few options. Right now, I’m torn between trying to get into journalism, maybe a traineeship at the local newspaper, or looking into starting an internship with a bigger firm in London. That’s quite a spread out choice, journalistic right? Yeah, but I love writing and I always enjoyed English at school. It's just the competitiveness in the industry right now is quite high, and I'm a bit worried I might struggle to get in initially. But that’s natural in almost any field, just like my job. There were times when I thought production control was really tough when I started. Right, right. And you said what made the difference for you? Well for me, it was really trying to get practical experience even when it was just an unpaid internship. And also trying to network, talking to people in the industry at events or even just over coffee. For me, it really paid off. Networking is different for journalism though, right? You’re kind of relying on the right assignments and publishing. True, but even in writing, there are events and workshops where you can connect with people who can become valuable contacts or even editors in the future. That makes sense. I’ve been trying to write more articles for the student paper to build up a portfolio and all that. And you mentioned London, if you do end up moving there, how’s your side of things, any preferences where you’d like to stay? I’m not entirely sure. I mean, inner London will likely be quite pricey but I want to be central enough and close to potential workplaces. I’ve looked online and there are some good areas that aren’t too pricey if you’re willing to share a room. Shared accommodation is definitely a must if you want to manage your finances better. I’ve always found zero-obligation rental platforms to be quite helpful when I was looking for shared flats when I moved to Cambridge. Yeah, I might look into that as well. Did you move to Cambridge for work or was it the university initially?

Ell now, have you seen Sarah’s new Instagram? She’s gone full-on Rom-com with this new lad. Aye, I’ve seen it. She’s absolutely smitten, isn’t she? Erm, yeah. It’s all a bit... weird how quickly she’s leapt into something new. She’s always been quick to move on. I’ve always found it quite nauseating, to be honest. I mean, let’s not be too hard on her, she’s just genuinely happy. At least for now. True, but it does leave you wondering what’s happening with Tom then, doesn’t it? Oh, she’ll be trying to pretend she’s over him already, that’s the thing. She couldn’t even give him a proper goodbye, just ignored him for weeks after. For Pete’s sake, don’t start that again! Anyone can see she’s just trying to move on for her own sanity. And maybe for this new guy. Look, I think the issue is people get so caught up in other people’s relationships. It’s like we’re all analyzing every move Sarah makes while Tom’s just trying to get his own life back on track. You’re right, really. But it is annoying, innit, when all of a sudden someone you thought you had a connection with is all over someone else in public. Connection? [laughs] You and Tom had like one good coffee, and you’re talking about ‘connection’? More like one good night, weren’t we, Rach? [laughs] Oh, let’s not go there. But yeah, people are just too confrontational about everything these days. Especially with social media, changing partners is like having a new profile pic now. True. But sometimes I do wonder what these Instagram relationships are like for the people actually in them. I mean, if every second of their life is an ad for their relationship, does real intimacy even exist anymore? [sighs] IDK, but it makes us all feel like we’re in constant comparison. Like we’re in some weird game, and everyone’s competing for the “best relationship” or whatever. Exactly, it’s toxic. And seriously, who even has the time to live up to that kind of expectation? I guess that’s why I’m always left thinking we just need to focus on our own lives, our own relationships, whatever form they may take.

So okay I mean money laundering. I don't think I fully understand how that works. Can you explain it to me? Well it's essentially using financial transactions to make money from criminal activities look legitimate. It's complicated, really, but think of it like this: if you've got dodgy income, you can't just put it in the bank and call it a day, right? So you get into real estate, stocks, businesses - anything that you can ruin actually - and then you hide the trail. It's very difficult for law enforcement to trace because it can be done through a whole network of shell companies and fake accounts. So you're saying there's always a risk of getting caught? The risks are huge. Sentences for just trying it can be up to fourteen years. And if they prove you were involved in a large-scale operation? You're looking at decades. It's not worth it. Hmm, I didn't realize it was that serious. What about fines? Oh, fines are just the beginning. Offshore banks and institutions that facilitate it can get penalties in the billions. But what's even worse is the damage to your reputation. If you're caught, it's game over for your business and possibly for you personally too. And the banks? Don't they have systems in place to prevent this? They're getting better at catching irregularities. But it's an arms race – as regulations tighten, people who want to launder money get more creative. It's a constant battle. I never thought of the ethical side much. But if you're in business, you need to be mindful doesn't you? Absolutely. Look at cases like the Panama Papers. People who were part of that, even if they just worked for the law firm or banks involved – their careers, their reputations, everything just tanks. You want to be in a job where you can look your family in the eye and say "I did something good today". That makes sense. But I guess changing the business environment itself would take a lot of work. It's a societal problem. Education for kids about ethics, for one. I've started just talking about it in my classes so they can learn from the start what's right and wrong. Legislation's getting tighter too, so maybe it'll become even harder to launder money in the future.

So, have you all had a chance to read over the latest academic journal from our press?
