Oh the tea is ready isn't it. Want a cup?      Yes please, thanks! You've always been the best at making it so quick!      Can I have some too?      Now, shall I start with your tea first before pouring for us adults?      Yes, please!      She's such a tea lover! I used to be just like her when I was a kid, down to drinking tea with milk.      I remember making you an invitation to our little tea party and you'd serve out the cups so diligently.      Yes, I was the little waitress! And now I help Mummy with the tea.      That's so cute. So on the topic of helping, how's it going at work?      It's going. Been so busy with the new stock and the shop's been quite chaotic lately.      Oh, keep it up! I know it's always chaotic around holiday seasons.      Yeah, but chaos is better than no customers. Although I'm glad it's weekend and I can finally get some rest.      Well, you deserve the rest. You're off on your Easter break soon, right?      More days off together! I'm going to paint lots of Easter eggs this year!      That sounds fun! And we should plan a little family outing. Maybe a picnic on the green?      I like that. It's been ages since we had just family time without planning something too big. And it's always fun for the little one.      Absolutely! And speaking of big plans, you know what we almost forgot about?      We're getting closer to New York. I started reading up on places to go.      Oh, yes! I've been reading travel blogs and seriously considering trying to get tickets for the Statue of Liberty.      Statues? Like big dolls?      Something like that. Very big and very famous.      So if we go, we’ll take you to see some big statues and maybe even a big carrot cake.      Carrot cake? Really?      You've got her hook, line, and sinker with that.      Now, before we delve too much into deep planning, let’s talk about something I’m a bit upset about.      What’s up?      I couldn't get to buy that fabric I wanted.      Oh no, that's a bummer.      What fabric?      It was this really nice one for a sewing project I was planning. But they ran out of it at the store.

So okay so I had this thing for educ maths first year's assessment. Oh, okay. Right, and they wanted us to complete these booklets on various concepts. I remember that now, the old booklets with all the pages on questions. Yes, and one of them got me. Like this question: "Determine whether the following statement is true or false and provide a proof or counter-example: 'The sum of two odd numbers is always even'." So, I thought, "Alright, let me write down my proof here." I started, okay. Right, so proving the statement by first understanding that an odd number in binary is represented as something like ... Ah, right. Well, from that concept, I thought "Two odd numbers, that means two ones in binary. When you add them together, it gives you 10." Which converts back to 2 in decimal. Exactly. So, the sum is always even. Perfect. That's a nice proof using binary. Yeah, but then I thought, "Wait, they asked for a proof or a counterexample." So, maybe I need to provide the other way around as well. What? A counterexample? Yes, like a specific case where the sum of two odd numbers isn’t even. Like, maybe, 3 and 3? That's 6, which is even. So that doesn’t work. True, indeed the sum 3 + 3 equals 6, which is even. So, if one’s looking for an odd sum, that doesn’t fit. I just tried to think of the smallest odd numbers possible. 1 and 3, perhaps? Good call! 1 + 3 is 4. Which is even. Exactly. So, for a counter-example, you actually need to show a case where two odd numbers’ sum is odd. That seems impossible given that 1 + 1 = 2. Right, and if you keep adding them like 1 + 3 or 3 + 5, you inherently end up with even numbers. Because odd + odd = even. So for a statement that says the sum is always even, that seems... True. But the question asks for either a proof or a counterexample. So from what I remember, a counterexample would be a specific instance that disproves the statement, but in this case, you can’t seem to find one. Exactly, that’s what I thought too. So I left that part blank I guess because I couldn’t come up with it, but maybe I missed something.

So okay let's talk about what we could buy if we won the Lottery. Assuming the Lottery prizes are still there even though the odds are like minuscule. Exactly! But let's just have fun with this. If we – hypothetically – won some kind of life-changing amount, what would we do? A DOG! A big friendly dog! Oh that's keeps coming up. You two love dogs, don't you? Yes! A big one. Something like a Labrador. Or Border Collie. They're so clever. Yeah, but would you help take care of it? You know, feeding, walking... I promise I'll help Dad and Mum! Me too! Alright then, a dog would definitely be part of it. Maybe even travel and visit all the dog-friendly places. Yeah, maybe a cute little cottage in the countryside. It'd be so lovely to have somewhere to call our own where the dog could play. And maybe paint all the walls the favourite colours. I was actually thinking we could use the money to travel more. I've always wanted to spend more time exploring different parts of the world. Like, take months off at a time, not just the silly two-week holidays we squeeze into because we're too busy. We could go to France and eat all the delicious food! Or play in the gardens! Whoo! That's right. And who knows, maybe we could learn French a bit better, learn more about local cultures. If we're going all out, maybe educate ourselves further in certain areas. Volunteer globally and learn some new skills. You know what would be interesting is taking some classes or courses on things we've always wanted to learn but never had time. Like, for me, I've always wanted to learn more about art. Taking art classes. What about going to Legoland? Again and again! There you go. Maybe set up a little trust or fund to support causes we care about. Like animal welfare or conservation. Can we do that while having the dog? And while playing in Legoland! Sure, why not? It's our dream, let's not limit ourselves. Another idea, from a different kind of dreaming, make sure we share this kind of security and good fortune with others in our community, help out at the school or maybe set up a scholarship fund for kids who want to pursue art or other interests they might not have found otherwise.

So, you had to go to A&E this past weekend didn’t you? Yeah, I was kind of hurt on Friday night. I was trying to move some heavy machinery at home and, you know, overdid it. I thought it was just a normal muscle strain, but actually, I fractured my forearm. Oh my god! That sounds really painful. How on earth did you manage to move those machines by yourself? Shouldn’t you have had someone help you? Honestly, I just thought I could handle it. Sentences of Pride and accomplishment to myself, but clearly not the smartest move. Was a little stubborn, wanted to get the job done on my own. Big mistake. Well, bruised ego aside, you’re lucky it wasn’t worse. How was your experience in A&E? I barely go to those places, but I always hear horror stories about waiting times and service. It was actually much better than I expected, considering. I went there on Saturday morning, early, and there was a surprisingly quick turnaround. I think most of the heavy traumas were coming in later that night. The nurses and doctors were all very kind and efficient. Do I wish there weren’t so many people waiting and the waiting room wasn’t so crowded? Absolutely. But I’d say A&E did okay, all things considered. That’s really good to know, considering we’re always worried about the worst. And what’s the prognosis? The break is in a good position, so no need for surgery. I have to wear a cast for a while and then do some physio when I get the cast off. The worst part is the lack of mobility in my hand right now. I feel so clumsy without my dominant hand. That must be so frustrating. Do you think you’ll need to take time off work? I’m changing the way I work for now. Doing more things on my voice notes and using my left hand more intelligently. I’ve asked for some remote work accommodation, and my team is being very supportive. That’s lucky for you. Not everyone would understand such an unusual work arrangement. No, you’re right. Mobility and flexibility at work are just not things everyone gets. I’m counting my blessings there. Definitely. And hey, maybe it’ll push us into our thinking about how we execute tasks more safely.

You heard the news about the new immigration policy from the government? Yes, I saw it this morning. What a mess, eh? Absolutely. It makes me think about how quickly things can change in our lives. Just last year, we were set for expansion. But with these new restrictions, I'm not sure if it's worth the hassle. Same here. I was hoping to hire someone from overseas with specialized knowledge but I'm not sure if that's feasible now. It just adds another layer of complexity to what we do. Business owners like us have been dealing with enough uncertainty already. This just makes it more complicated. I know what you mean. But on a positive note, your book seems to be doing well. The last sales figures were good. You're thinking of writing another one, or maybe expanding that series? Yeah, the feedback was so encouraging this time. I've started making notes for a new installment. But I have to be careful. You know how it is, the market can change. Still, it's good to hear that people are enjoying what I write. Absolutely. And it must be fulfilling for you too, creating something people enjoy. In business, we don’t always get that feedback as directly. Exactly. For me, that’s a big part of why I started writing in the first place. Plus, it’s a nice change of pace from the usual stresses of running a business. Speaking of changes, I’m considering a small pivot in my business. The market trends suggest people are more interested in sustainable products. I’ve been thinking of adding a line that meets that criteria. That’s a solid strategy. The demand is definitely there for eco-friendly products and it aligns well with consumer values these days. You’ve always been good at forecasting market shifts. Thanks, that’s reassuring to hear. But it does mean I have to do my research. I’m looking at local suppliers for sustainable materials. It’s a bit of an investment, but it seems like it could pay off. It could definitely be a growth area. Plus, if you’re passionate about it, that’s half the battle. The other half is solid market research and a clear plan. How’s your thinking going with that? I’ve got a few leads that look promising, but I’m also considering some... let's say, unconventional approaches.

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 at the Guardhouse pub in Woolwich, an evening drink. The conversation touches upon several casual topics: planning what to eat, discussing a TV show, and general surroundings, including the local university.      You know, Happy Valley is on tonight. Wonder if we should try and catch the new episode.      Nah, we can watch it later. This pub's just cosy to sit here for a while.      The décor here’s quite nice, isn’t it? Much better than what they used to have when it was The Ram.      Definitely. The changes have worked out well. Next to the university, it must get a lot of students coming in.      I was thinking about enrolling for a short course at Queen Mary next year. Not sure if I’m busy enough with transcripts.      Oh, that sounds interesting. You could do with a break from all the typing.      Yeah, it’s monotonous, but it pays the bills. Though, I do miss university days.      Affording life around here is getting tougher. What do you think about that place round the corner for dinner?      The Indian place? That would be good. We need to pick something on the menu though.      Let’s see... How about we get something light, maybe a starter and a main?      Yeah, or just have some pub food here if it's good.      Right. Speaking of good things, this pub’s got a great atmosphere.      I like the music they’re playing. It’s casual without being overdone.      They’ve got a good mix. And have you seen the cat they have roaming around?      Oh right! I saw that when we came in. It’s so friendly.      Yeah, funny thinking a pub would have a resident cat.      It adds to the charm. You know, kind of like our own little feline at home?      Definitely like that though. Straying back to food, what do you think about getting some fries here?      Maybe. If they’re as good as everyone says.      Alright. Shall we get some fries and a couple meat pies?      Sounds good to me. And maybe another drink?      Absolutely. The conversation’s flowing as least as well as the drinks.      Right. So, deep dish? Or stick to lager?      I’m cool with lager. Let’s just enjoy the evening then plan for dinner later.      Sounds like a plan.         You ready to see if that TV’s worth catching up on?

So how are you enjoying that new camera? It's been great! I've been taking some shots around Edinburgh. There's so much to capture. Still trying to get the hang of all the manual settings though. Oh don’t worry, it gets easier with practice. I remember getting out into the countryside and just experimenting. The best lessons you learn right there, in the field I'd say! Yeah, exactly that! I've been meaning to get out to Fife. You know, before we had that rainy spell. Right, the weather had been quite unpredictable, hasn't it? I almost gave up any thought of taking my camera out. But as you say, there’s beauty in the rain, if you can capture it right. Definitely. I’ve actually tried some shots with the rain and they’re surprisingly good looking. But sometimes it can be a bit tricky, you know, with the lighting and everything. Absolutely. Sometimes it's all about those unexpected light conditions or even the mist. Now that we've moved this side of summer, it might get a bit clearer, but who knows? You’re right about that. I was thinking maybe going up to the Highlands if the weather improves. You know, trying to get some landscape shots? Though I’ve heard the highlands can be quite treacherous weather-wise. Oh, you’ll love it. But do take precautions, right? Can be quite unpredictable, especially around the peaks, and all that. And don’t forget that the conditions up there can change in minutes. True, I will be careful. I’ve heard some great stories of photographers who’ve managed to time it just right during those sudden changes. Yeah, timing is everything with photography, isn’t it? I once took a trip to Ireland specifically for chasing sunrises and sunsets. Just the timing and patience, really. That sounds fantastic! Maybe something for me to add to my bucket list. You should, it’s worth it. Though in these parts of the world, we usually have to be prepared for anything. I mean, look at the weather we’ve had last week! It would have been a disaster for landscape photos unless you could have captured the drama of it all. Maybe I’ll just try to capture more of the everyday, then. Not just the landscapes but the city too. Edinburgh has so much character.

So, what's on for this week? You got the usual squeeze time at the nursery and then the usual after-school drama with the nipping questions and the kind days and the hellos and the goodbyes and the settling in and out? Oh, actually, I've got a bit of chaos planned this week. Emma is doing this project on keepsakes for history and they want something from our family for it. I swear, every week there's a new project or a new volunteer day at the school. I remember that phase with Rachel. "Mom, can you help me make a model of the Solar System? No, no - not a model planet, but a whole system with orbit lines and everything." She wanted it so real I had to consult Google maps looking for how planets orbit. Yeah, it's crazy. Next week, I think it's a sports day. Someone should make a roster for us parents too or a 'how not to embarrass your child' pamphlet. I can't even. Remember how fun it was though, while the kids were still small and they genuinely thought you knew everything? It really was fun. Though now, they're starting to realize how little I know . Honestly though, this week, it's the silly things. I've got a really good recipe for a slow-cooked beef stew and all the grocery shopping is done. That sounds lovely! I've got that new series from last year the one that everyone talks about on Netflix. It's like a mystery and all these twists and it's really tense. You should check it out if you’ve got the time. Netflix’s got a lot on their mind these days. I've been meaning to watch that but between work and school stuff, it's hard to find time. But a dinner changing the pace and having some adult interaction is exactly what’s needed. Definitely. What’s for dinner tonight then? I said I'd do something easy, like spaghetti Bolognese with a side of garlic bread. Hope the little one will like it. Or at least let me eat in peace this one time. You put in garlic bread and you’ve got my vote! Speaking of garlic bread, I saw something on TV the other day about making garlic bread from scratch. Someone said it's way better than using the pre-made stuff.

So have you heard the new team lead is kind of a nightmare, right? Yeah, I'd heard rumors. But have you actually dealt with them yet? Not yet, but from what people are saying, they’re set on micromanaging even the simplest tasks. It's gonna be a challenge. Definitely, and on top of that, there's been a reshuffle in the department, and I’ve been questioning if staying in this role is the best for me long-term. Really? You haven’t started talking about it yet? They making any sense with the organization stuff? It's all very unclear, to be honest. We’re looking for growth paths, but they’re not offering any training or support. That’s frustrating. Especially when you’ve got potential and can see where you could take the company. Maybe it’s time to start looking outside. I've been meaning to polish up my CV for a while. You’re always on top of the job market news. Any tips? For sure. I’ve been getting on with rewriting mine. The key is highlighting soft skills – like team management or whatever you’ve done that's impactful, even if it’s not directly related to your current job. That makes sense, and it’s what I’ve been working on. But I don’t know, sometimes I wish there was a better balance between work and life. I feel like I’m always behind on something – either on work or on my own stuff. Yeah, true enough. I’ve been trying to focus more on my hobbies when I’m not at work. It's hard when you’re physically demanding job, but even just 30 minutes a day of something you love can make a difference. Definitely. I've been struggling to find that balance too – I feel like I’m always either in work mode or I’m so exhausted just from work that I can't think about anything else. And on that note, have you guys heard about the new sustainable clothing brand that just launched? I saw an ad online and it’s like...everything I’ve been into these past months. Yeah, I saw that too. It’s really inspiring – they’re thinking about both the planet and fair labor practices. I’ve been considering switching to more sustainable fashion. Same here. We should look into it together maybe?

Right, now I'm going to make a pot of tea, would you have a cuppa? Yeah that sounds alright, sweetener please? I'll just be on my second one of the day, really indispensable isn't it. Can't go without it, questions are always asked when one decides to decline a cup. You're right there. I've heard this one of why the English drink so much tea, and the joke goes it's so we always have a reason to have a sit down. That's a good one. I've always thought there's more to it than just the need to sit down, though. There's a certain comfort in a good cuppa. Comfort food, in a way. And it varies so much from person to person, too. Some like it strong, others weak. I recall when I was working, the school staff room was always filled with different types of tea, it was like a tea shop within a school. Exactly, and at home or with friends it's more about the time spent than the tea itself, isn't it? Absolutely. It's often the start of conversations, no matter the time of day. Early morning, mid-morning break, afternoon, evening... there's rarely a wrong time for tea. And it's not just the tea, it's what you have with it, too. A slice of cake, biscuits... really sets the scene for a nice chinwag. I always used to get the kids to make tea for myself and the other teachers. It was great for them to learn how to make a decent cuppa, and for me, it was one less thing to worry about in the day. Ah, the joys of teaching. Speaking of which, did any of you see that recent news thing about traditional tea rooms being more popular again? Seems like it's coming back into style. Yeah, I read that. It’s a good thing. I for one don't like the automation of tea everywhere. You lose something when it's just a button to press. A good brewer's skills can make all the difference. There's an art to it, I swear. Now, shall we wait, or would you like me to top up your pot while it's fresh? Actually, I'd love another. And could you bring a plate of that lovely cake you made this morning?

So tell me about that pub you mentioned yesterday. Oh yeah, it's The Red Lion. They've got this amazing new chef, he's been experimenting with traditional Essex dishes but with a modern twist. Sounds interesting. What kind of dishes exactly? Well, one of the things they serve is this herby chicken pie, but the crust is made out of shortcrust pastry and there's a side of pickled green beans. It's quite surprising and it works. Pickled green beans, how would they taste with a savory dish like a chicken pie? They're actually quite good, add a little bit of a crunch and a tang. But honestly, just like the whole experience, you have to be slightly open-minded about it. I'm intrigued. I should try going there sometime. Speaking of openness, I had to go through a CRB check recently for a volunteer role. It's quite rigid, isn't it? But good for safety purposes. Yeah, these checks have become quite standard now, especially in fields like education and customer facing roles. I'm curious, what was it like for you? It was pretty straightforward. The application process, while time-consuming, was clear. The check itself was thorough but respectful. It feels like the right balance between individual freedoms and public safety. Ah, but have you ever considered what prompts such checks in the first place? It wasn't always this way. True, we’re always talking about the contexts that lead to these measures. Like when I saw that protest in Norwich last week, it was about the redesigning the city center. Some of the concerns were about public safety and protection. It’s hard to balance these issues. I just got back from a weekend in London and visited the V&A. The new exhibit on modern architecture is fantastic. Circling back to what we were discussing earlier, some of the protest art there really caught my eye. It speaks to so many of these social topics. It’s great that venues like museums are using their platforms more thoughtfully. I also saw in the news there’s been an uproar about circumcision and so-called 'excessive' zero-tolerance policies at some of the city's hospitals. Yes, those debates can go to such extremes. Sensitivity and cultural understanding are key. Whether it’s about food, traditions, or personal beliefs, it seems dialogue is the starting point.

Oh okay so I need to tell you about this stupid story but today when I was at work and I overheard this conversation between two older women and they were just talking about their unrealistic expectations of life. Like what? So there was one woman who had this whole scripted life where she and her partner moved house every 5 years and at that point they had a big barbecue and threw away all their old stuff and bought everything new. Right, like in a sitcom. Exactly! It was so ridiculous. And she seemed so serious about it. The other woman was listening in awe. Must be nice to have that kind of money or free time or whatever excuses they have for that kind of lifestyle. Totally, I mean do they also sell all their children on the next move and then replace them? Or just stop owning pets for the same reason. "Sorry, Daisy, but we're moving to a house with this new kitchen on the 3rd and your fur is not matching the new aesthetic." I know right. Anyway, so in other news, I was thinking maybe we should try the new Indian place on the high street. Ah, the one that opened like two months ago? I've been meaning to go there. Yeah that one! I actually passed by and they have really good reviews and they're having a two-for-one deal doesn't come in handy. That sounds perfect. When would you want to go? Wednesday or Thursday would work for me. How about we finalize the plans for Wednesday evening? Great, yeah let's do that. And by the way, are you free for a catch-up with some friends from uni next Sunday? That's on my calendar already. Where do you meet? They're thinking of grabbing brunch at that new café near the park, but it's not fully booked yet. Oh perfect! Can I get a spot cleared for me? Of course, no problem. Good job I put my name in when you told me. I should remind you of that earlier, but hey, just made sure. Yeah, because that's crucial. Well, that and also, I finally realized it's better to just make plans like these in the first place rather than trying to catch up over a million messages. Planning ahead can be surprisingly liberating.

So, I hear that Cassie's health has taken a turn for the worse. I'm really worried; her cancer is quite aggressive. Yes, I talked to her husband the other day. He said they're still hopeful about the new treatment, but the prognosis now looks quite grim, unfortunately. Oh, that's so tough for them and their children. Cassie and I have been friends since uni days. It's always heartbreaking to see this happen to someone so young and with a family. It really makes you think about how precious life is and how much we take our health for granted. I suppose seeing someone you care about go through this also makes you check your own health more. Definitely. I had a quick check just last week to make sure everything was okay. That’s a good idea. And speaking of things that might be unpredictable, have you had a chance to look at those houses for sale in Oakwood yet? Not in too much detail, no. I saw the ad in the village newsletter but haven’t had time to look into it. What's your view? We were thinking maybe that area would be more feasible for us and the children than some of the others. I think most of those houses are older, but the village is so charming. If the right one came up, it could be a great opportunity. But the planning side is always an issue, isn’t it? You’ve got to be mindful of what you can do to the property. Exactly, and I heard there have been some concerns about the new development they’re proposing. Yeah, there was a community meeting about that a couple of weeks ago. Some people were quite vocal about wanting to preserve the village character. I don’t blame them, it’s such a lovely place. We do want to keep the village feel, of course, but we also need somewhere that works for us practically. Yes, it's a balancing act. There’s one house that came up a few months ago, and it was large enough and on a decent size plot… but it was out of our price range. I suppose we’ll just have to keep looking and see if anything that fits our needs comes up. That’s the plan for now. It's not ideal to have to pick and choose right now, but circumstances aren’t perfect for us either.

Right okay so I'm going to declare something. Go on then. I really hate waiting in queues. Oh God, unreal. Especially if they're long and you've really got time. It feels like people queue for everything now. Everywhere you go now it seems like a queue for something. Supermarkets, cinemas, even just normal public transport... it's unavoidable. And don't even get me started on the ones where it moves really slowly, or someone's in front of you just tapping away on their phone. It's like, you have to check your damn social media before ordering food. Or someone just talking away to the person next to them. I had that today at the post office, for goodness’ sake. I just hate being held up like that. Like, you have somewhere to be, and you're just standing there. I know, right? What about overcrowded places? Can't stand it. Especially at popular events or festivals. I went to a festival last summer and it was a nightmare. I mean, it was fun, but being squashed into a field with thousands of people is just not my cup of tea. Exactly! And the noise – you can’t even hear yourself think over the music or the chatter. Ah, and to make it even worse, people who don’t know how to use silly things like in and out arrows on roads. One car blocking a whole lane because they don’t know which gap to go into. Or they come in the wrong lane at a roundabout. That’s just so infuriating. Honestly, I just hate people not thinking ahead or being considerate of others, you know? Totally agree. Okay, now it's your turn. What is one thing you’ve had enough of lately? There must be something. Yeah, something that really bugs you. It might be something small but it gets to you.  thinks for a moment  Alright, just because it's small but truly frustrates me – people not covering their mouths when they cough or sneeze. Oh right. Disgusting and almost rude in my opinion. I swear, if I see someone do that near me again, I'm going to remind them politely but firmly to use a tissue or at least their elbow. Fair enough. I guess that is often overlooked but it's basic etiquette... and COVID made us even more aware of that habit.

So, I was browsing on Instagram yesterday and I came across an account that uses AI-generated pictures. The artist is combining people's faces with portraits from the past Renaissance period. It's fascinating! Oh, that sounds quite captivating. I've seen some AI-generated art exhibits in Antwerp – they're questions the status of 'originality' and 'authenticity'. Interesting! It links back to the Language Learning class where we discussed the impact of AI on translation and voice recognition. Have you seen how some of these AI keeps changing the accent and intonation when translating English to languages like German or French? Yes, actually! I've been trying to learn French with one of those language apps. Sentences that have been translated to English then back to French sound so different. It really shows how tricky language can be - the nuances, the context. Speaking of language, have you thought about language learning during retirement? I met a fellow in a botany group in Dorset who picked up Spanish just to read Spanish scientific texts on his carpentry hobby. I never thought about it. But maybe that could be a project for my next birthday or something. My grandkids are always asking me to "talk silly" which funnily enough, while I may not master a new language in a year, at least I can try some basic phrases or rhymes with them. That's a brilliant idea. I imagine teaching my niece to say "coucou" , maybe with some funky rhymes. You know, I also saw a program on how they're using language learning to help with Alzheimer's patients. There's something about holding onto language that's deeper than understanding words, it's about identity and connection. More reason for us to keep challenging ourselves with language. For sure! Listen, did you all catch the Christmas markets this year? The one in Herne Bay was really charming and it got me thinking about how they're changing. You can buy these huge amounts of plastic decorations now. Sadly, that seems to be the case in most popular places now. But there's always something special about Brighton Seafront during Christmas. I've heard the dogs’ nativity play has become quite infamous. Oh, have you seen? It's gone bigger and bigger every year. And yes, I swear those puppies are more entertaining than the human performances sometimes. Oh, funny thinking about that.

Did you hear about the Ireland thing they've been talking about? You mean about equal marriage rights? Yeah, isn't it great though? Really? I heard questions were asked if it was going to bring a flood of gays and lesbians over from England and the like. It makes me so mad. Yeah, I know! It's like they don’t think gay people even exist in Ireland right now. Ugh, let me tell you my school friends were talking about it. Some of them thought there wouldn't be any real difference because, in their words, "what do two guys or two girls even do together?" It was embarrassing to hear them say that. That type of ignorance is just making me mad, hearing such stuff. What's even more frustrating is that some want to treat this issue as political bargaining rather than as a basic human right. Exactly! It's funny because we're in this stage where people will share posts on Facebook about racism and inequality or even attend Pride marches but still won’t support this because it affects maybe someone they know, or their beliefs. I think most of it comes down to lack of education and exposure. If kids grew up learning about all different types of families, it wouldn't be a big deal. I used to have this friend who was super homophobic, but then she met my friend's family and, you know, saw firsthand that they're just as normal as anyone else. Yeah, I know. It’s about that simple. Just meeting people and seeing they're not that different from you. Then there the parents that say they're fine with it but then, in private, all these assumptions or negative stuff. It’s like they don’t want to be thought of as “that kind of family.” Embarrassing really. Totally! And then there's also the issue of parents who are supposed to support you but actually make things worse. My friend had a birthday party where one of the partygoers’ mom was there and when some of us were discussing this equality vote she just chimed in with something so backwards. Oh, I can tell you a real embarrassing mother story. This happened at my daughter's birthday. One of the kids asked my daughter if she had a boyfriend yet and she said no.

I've heard of hamsters in the oven but not in the microwave. It's true, though. Young folks these days. They don't think twice about putting a pet in a microwave. That's quite an anecdote to pass down the generations. I hope it serves as a cautionary tale about the dangers of technology and the importance of reading instructions, right? Absolutely. Reminds me of when I was a childminder. Parents trusted me with their precious cargo, and I always made sure everything was okay. I can imagine. It's similar to managing a team of young learners, like I have to do sometimes. You're right about following instructions though. I recall making a similar mistake with a lathe tool once. Didn’t read the manual properly and thought I could do it by intuition... Did it make a similar ‘pop’? Almost, but fortunately, not as dramatic as the microwave hamster. Just a lot of frustration and wasted time. Well, that's a valuable lesson. Attention to detail and respect for instructions can save us from all sorts of mishaps, whether it's with machinery, pets or even the food we prepare. Well, speaking of food – are we serving soup for lunch or perhaps some of that lovely, fresh baked bread from last night? I think soup would be nice, and a slice of that bread you baked would be perfect! I second that. Let me just get the soup warming on the stovetop. And let the bread rest for a bit longer, I reckon. I'll pour the water. It's great to have us all together like this. While we’re on changing subjects, any plans for the garden? It’s mid-spring and I was thinking maybe some more planting? Ah, I was meaning to tackle that this week. We could probably use your help, indeed. And maybe we can include a small plot for some herbs too? Again, health and the importance of fresh produce... almost as important as not putting hamsters in microwaves! Perhaps a reminder to follow instructions applies across the board. For sure. Now, shall we wait for the soup and bread to be ready? It’s a while yet, but I can already smell it. Here we go, everyone. Bon appétit! --- [There ends the conversation as the speakers focus on their lunch, likely transitioning to more topics such as garden plans or other family matters.]

Did you see on the news that cat that figured out how to use the self-checkout? It’s hilarious. Yes! I couldn't believe it. It must have seen its owner do it enough times to pick it up. People forget how intelligent animals can be. We do far too much anthropomorphising and don’t credit them enough for their smarts. It did seem quite intentional. I guess modern technology can ruin things, like fracturing out simple human service jobs, but it can also create these oddly charming moments. Fitting. You know, it's funny, those new plastic bag fees. I heard about a woman at the checkout, she got into a heated argument because she didn’t want to pay just for the bag. She said, “Why should we pay for something we can reuse?” Then the shop assistant said, “Because that’s what it’s supposed to do.” It's all about encouraging the right behaviour, but some people seem confused. While technology can cause such distress over something as simple as a plastic bag, it also fills our lives with far more sophisticated challenges. I’ve never gotten into cryptic crosswords, for instance. I don’t understand the mindset involved. I’ve tried them, but I find them too convoluted. I prefer straightforward puzzles. However, I think the secret is seeing the wordplay rather than the literal meaning. Well, technology is certainly changing banking habits, isn’t it? I recently had an issue, trying to pay back my personal loan in advance, but because I wrote it off as “Marcia, my sister,” they didn’t know what to do with it. It ended up being a bit of a saga. It’s like the bank’s system can’t handle such straightforward directives. Yes, technology’s intended to simplify, but it can also create new sorts of complications. As for banks, I remember when they were local institutions. Now, it feels like they’re multinational corporations with little interest in personal service. And what about those cryptic crosswords? Do they actually benefit the brain? Or are they just clever time wasters? I think there’s some scientific evidence that they can improve cognitive function, like memory and problem-solving. But, as someone who struggles with them, I might be biased! Speaking of cognitive function, I found it quite concerning the other day. I heard about a study that young children being given phones and tablets are getting less adept at writing.

Alright, let's make this a fun, family-friendly baking night that matches our love for building and creating. This conversation is a mix of discussion about the activities, the skills being learned, and enjoying the time spent together, with a playful nod to involving all family members, highlighting how technology, creativity, and real-world activities can complement each other.

Oh, so how was your first year's holidays? I bet you're nearly over the excitement by now. It was amazing, thanks for asking! We had a great time, just relaxing and enjoying the usual family time. We had a wonderful time at the beach, and the children really enjoyed it. It's moments like those that make me feel like maybe all the chaos at home is worth it. Yo, you hear about that new sandwich shop that opened last week? Yeah man, I was thinking about going there today. Have they got any good deals? But did you hear that they're hiring and you can get a free meal every shift? That's a sweet deal! Maybe I should apply for it alongside my part-time job. Definitely, you should. Speaking of school, have you guys seen the latest episode of ‘Stranger Things’? It’s really good. Spoiler alert, the Demogorgon is back and stuff. I know, right? I was totally into it. And while we’re on the topic of fun, planning a trip already for summer?

You wouldn’t believe the physics teacher we've got this year. What’s he like? He’s so questions students in front of everyone. You’re sitting there, and suddenly he’s pointing at you and "What did you think that was?" Eeew. That’s harsh. And he even made us watch that really old science video in class. Yeah, I remember that. We can choose, but I’m thinking something like rewriting the story from a different character’s point of view. That sounds interesting. I’m thinking of exploring the novel through poetry. Yeah, the one that compared Hemingway’s minimalist style and some over-the-top modern author. Exactly! I actually found it helpful. Yeah, it was good. Did anyone mention what’s happening during the English reading lesson this week? No, I just know we’re discussing the themes in “To Kill a Mockingbird”. Oh, right. Totally. Speaking of fitting in, there’s this girl in school who really stands out. Like, she’s always so herself, and it’s kind of cool. Really? I haven’t noticed her. She has this crazy hair color and always wears these unique clothes. But she’s happy, you know? That’s a good take. Maybe we all need to be a bit more her. Agreed. Anyway, I heard our form tutor might be showing us that new "School of Rock" film next week.

But yeah, I’ve been wanting to check it out too. Might just sneak down to your place for a while before you leave, in case we can do a little pre-tour briefing. That’d be awesome, mate! I’ll email you some prep stuff if you want. It’s going to be an amazing trip, I barely sleep thinking about it. Let me know. Where did you get that from? You seem so into it. Honestly, it’s the stories, myths, and the people. The local culture is so distinct – like a patchwork quilt made from many different threads. Speaking of which, have you tried pronouncing any of those really hard-to-pronounce Hungarian or Romanian words I learned? No way, man. How do you even say them? Uh,  attempts to pronounce a word  Let’s just say if I say it right, the locals will mistake me for the king's personal translator. You always were a charmer. On a side note, did you hear about Sarah’s accident at work? She’s okay, but it really scared us all. We should check in on her, make sure everything's alright. Yeah, definitely. I’ll give her a call when I get home. Hopefully, she’s recovering well and it’s not something serious. Reminds me, I was thinking of going for a laser eye surgery next month. Anyone done it? Thoughts? Mine was just a couple months ago and honestly, I’m over the moon with it. No more glasses! The first week was a bit tricky

So, darlings, we were thinking about having a little celebration for your birthday. What do you think about it?      A party! Yeah! Can we have cake and balloons?      And can we play games? Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 : Now listen, let's talk about government policy and taxes. Okay, go on. You know, back when I was just starting as an accountant, things were quite different. That means more money in people’s pockets. And the thresholds for higher tax brackets have been adjusted. But I thought that only helped a certain group? It did, yes. It's often those on lower-to-middle incomes who benefit most from increases in the personal allowance. And those on higher incomes or even business owners might feel the squeeze from other changes. Interesting, I see. So, different policies can significantly impact different income groups. Precisely. And don't even get me started on the recent corporation tax increase. It's caused quite a stir among businesses. Ah, the corporation tax policy. I've taken an interest, especially after studying how it affects different sectors and companies' strategies for expansion or staying competitive. That's good. You're paying attention. The corporate sector is always talking about it - "affects competitiveness," "encourages investment," or "it's excessive and makes us uncompetitive globally." The debate rages on. I’ve noticed that too. Some argue the increase was necessary to fund public services or counteract tax evasion, while others think it will stifle growth. Exactly. And then you've got the entire business of the government trying to balance the books and reduce the deficit. It's a juggling act – more tax revenue, but also not putting people off. I always take issue with how tax policies are presented to the public. It feels like a blunt tool when often the intentions are more nuanced. Haha, well, politics isn't known for its subtlety. But I think you’ve got a good point there. People often misunderstand or don't see the fine print until it affects them directly. And then there’s the issue of tax avoidance. Big companies, sometimes, they find... let's say, creative ways to minimize their tax bills.

So tell me about that conference you were at. It was actually really great. The speakers were super knowledgeable and insightful. I particularly enjoyed the session on using literature in the classroom. They had some great ideas for making reading more accessible and engaging for students. That’s really interesting! I’ve found that kind of material so useful in my own workshops. Absolutely! It links so well with what we teach and it’s great for getting students to think critically. But, between you and me, I got a little frustrated with the whole “everything must be tech based” approach they were pushing. I thought there was a bit too much of that, too. I mean, technology is great in moderation, but we can’t forget the importance of hands-on activities and human interaction in the classroom. I feel like sometimes the conference organizers get caught up in this whole techno-fetishism. I couldn’t agree more! There was one session on creative writing and it was all about using apps and software to guide the process. And it struck me that it was so far removed from the actual act of creating or even thinking. It was more about using a tool than it was about the process of writing itself. Exactly! I spoke to a few other teachers in the coffee breaks and they felt the same. It’s as if we’re forgetting that sometimes the best way to learn or teach is by doing something or through discussion rather than just relying on a screen. And don’t even get me started on the talk about monitoring students' progress through apps and spreadsheets. While I understand the need for tracking and assessing, some of these tools seem to intrude on the real essence of learning and the teacher-student relationship. Yes! It's like we're equipping ourselves with more tools to do things the way we’ve done them before, just electronically. But what about just talking, questioning, debating? I worry we’re losing the human touch. There was one session on collaborative learning though, which was fantastic. They had some great ideas on group projects and peer to peer learning. That was more on the spot, you know? Ah, I would have loved to have seen that. Sounds like just the kind of thing that truly engages students and fosters meaningful learning. The problem is that often the software and tech-heavy sessions are those that get more attention and funding.

Oh, did I mention my first move's online banking was so frustrating? I swear, they asked me to click and drag the picture of a rabbit into this little circle. What is that about? I’ve been noticing that a lot of the times when I’m feeling good it’s because I’ve done something useful, not because I’ve checked all my fitness tracker's achievements for the day. There’s a campaign we should start - #LookForTheImpactNotTheNumbers. Brilliant tagline! You know, that also ties into our travel. The experience of exploring new places, meeting new people... it changes your perspective on fitness and health, on appearances even. It’s about being capable and enjoying the world, not just looking a certain way.

On the road these past two weeks. It’s been a mad shuttle from one north east firm to another. Got some of the best tech talent in this country up there–and also the best mugs . You know, the questions they ask are just so refreshingly simple and yet so damningly revealing. “This app, can it make me a ghost?” “How does broadband ruin my life?” Oh my god, that’s keeps coming up, right? The tech support in Newcastle... I mean, we’re all about innovation but sometimes I think there’s a misconception that just because we’ve got some of the northerners in London now, the ones that stayed up north are still stuck in the 90s. But from what you’re saying, they’re just as savvy. Exactly! It’s the best and worst at the same time. But you also get this very... practical, hands-on approach. They build and they fix. And it’s this kind of heritage that’s so strong up there, from shipbuilding to industry. It really shapes the way people view technology, as something you can touch and fix, not just software and pixels. Reminds me of when I was working in Birmingham. The Midlanders, they have a similar industrial heritage, yet approach tech in a different way. More about making tech part of everyday life, without the fuss. But the North East... I always love visiting, especially Newcastle. The energy is different, and the music venues! Had you heard much of the Newcastle music scene? Oh absolutely! I mean, doesn’t everyone start with Stereophonics and then move to The Libertines?! Except, we've got our own bands too. Alt-J, the Arctic Monkeys–they’re all kinds of “Northeast made me”. And of course, we cannot forget Maximo Park. Their music really reflects the gritty yet hopeful spirit of Sunderland. Maximo Park! “Apply Some Pressure” is one of my favorite songs. I mean, who doesn’t love a good angry indie song for motivation? But you know, I often find that in my research, when I’m diving into different communities, the North East has this unique blend of resilience and an understated kind of pride. It’s not about boasting about what they’ve done; it’s just in the way they recover from setbacks or celebrate small victories. Yeah. It’s a spirit you sense everywhere.

Yeah's things have changed so much since I was your age, lad. Do they, Grandma? What do you mean? Politics. It's all so complicated now. People have all sorts of opinions and debates – it's not just about the party you agree with or not. Like how about Brexit? You seem to talk about that a lot. Ah, that's a big deal, innit? Now there's so much to think about – the economy, trade, border control... It must be hard to make sense of. It can be, but it's important to understand even if you don't agree. Aye, that's when people only hear what they want to hear. Nowadays, it seems everyone's talking to the people who agree with them, and no one's listening to the other side. If they do, it's just to argue. Yeah, like at school. If someone says they don't like the current government or something, everyone's either for or against, no one's really listening to why they think that. Just like the old days, only now it's on social media and through videos on the computer. When I was young, you had the local newspaper and the radio. There was more balance, and people would hear differing opinions on the same page or radio show. Seems like the world's gotten a bit smaller but also more divided. That's a good way to put it, boy. But it doesn't have to be that way for you. You and kids like you can make a difference by changing the way we communicate – listening more and shouting less. Grandma, what do you think about the people saying we should just "get on with it" about Brexit? Well, if that meant people would actually come together and agree on a plan, it might be the right thing. But "getting on with it" in the sense of just doing what the government decides without everyone's input, that's not democracy. It's important for voices to be heard, even if they're not the loudest.

So, I was browsing on the news yesterday and came across an article about the blood moon today. Did you hear about it? Well, I did talked about it with the kids at school. You know how they can get excited about anything new. A blood moon, the eclipse, all those things – they love questions like why the sky turns red. Blood moon, what's that? Ah, right. Excuse me, I'd better fill you in before it starts. Yes, please. So a blood moon is a lunar eclipse where the Earth comes between the sun and the moon. Because the Earth is in front of the moon, it blocks most of the sun’s light from hitting the moon but some red light does sneak around the edges of the Earth and reflects onto the moon, giving it a reddish hue. That sounds so magical. Why would it want to sneak around the edges? It's not the light that's sneaky; it's just the way the light bends through our atmosphere. The Earth is quite big so it can block all but the red light from the sun. Exactly. And because of that, the moon looks red at the peak of the eclipse. It's why people often call it a "blood moon"; it's quite dramatic. Wow, I didn’t know that. So in our book, it's more than just a full moon? Much more than that. It's quite rare because it doesn't happen every month, it depends on the position of the moon, the earth, and the sun. Yes, and seeing it can be quite a sight. Now, let’s get back to dinner. So, I've been going over the structure for my first move's application at the council today. The committee will have a wide range of experts and local stakeholders, not just planning ones. So it's about making sure our case is not just legally sound, but also commercially viable and socially beneficial. Right, so not just technical justifications but making a strong business case as well. You're in the right mindset then. Also, have you considered the visuals? They can be pretty influential. Any slides or plans you want to share with me for feedback? That's a great point. I intend to have some visuals to help illustrate the project's layout and the proposed changes. I'm thinking something simple, like a before-and-after sketch. But I suppose I can make it a bit more engaging with some bullet points on why it's beneficial for the area. Yeah, the 'so what?' factor is key. Stakeholders and council members might not know the intricacies of your project, but they want to know how it'll affect them, or the community at large. I remember one application we did together for another project where we framed the environmental improvements as a key selling point, and it really helped shift the discussion in our favor. That's a good example. Going back to the structure, I'm thinking to open with the contextual setup—what's the current state of the site and what’s the vision for the future? Then into the specifics of the application: the proposed changes, the benefits, the impact assessments. I've also included some potential questions and answers to anticipate what they might ask. Good strategy. Anticipating questions can really help you control the narrative. You've also got to be prepared for some curveballs though. Absolutely, and in these sorts of public forums, there's always someone pushing for more green space or sustainability. I've included some points on how our project aligns with those goals.

Ah, do you remember when we all moved into the area back in the 1960s? It was quite the adventure, wasn't it? I think I'm right in saying that three of us had just finished our teaching training and one of us was even on an interview for a job as a dentist when the first day of the military dictatorship began in Athens. Can you believe it? Oh my, dear! I remember that day so vividly. Richard [Speaker_3] was on his way to the interview at the dental school but when he arrived, the whole place was in an uproar. And you were joining me here in the school system? That was my case, yes. I was in quite the mix when it all kicked off. Did I grab a taxi or was it a bus ride? I recall the taxi driver was terrified as much as the passengers. The time change this side of the Mediterranean only added to the disorientation. [Chuckles] You’re right about that, the time change was a small but memorable hurdle. For a week or so we were all trying to figure out if we'd gained an hour or lost one. It was like a perpetual jet lag without even leaving home! Meanwhile, I was still in Britain, trying to find a place to live around Almondsbury. Landlords were scarce and the few houses available were often in a state of disrepair. I remember spending hours scrubbing out one place to make it habitable. Yes, and I had similar experiences around Ramsgate. Rented accommodation was extremely hard to come by. I recall, for a time, we had to share a house with several other young professionals. It was quite the communal living experience! That's right, and we all faced a common challenge: finding something that was within our new salary bracket after graduation. Buying was next to impossible on our pay, but I managed to find a decent small flat near the university in Manchester. Renovations became our weekend hobby. For me, it was Birmingham that became home after dental school. The city had its own set of challenges and almost as soon as I started, the entire deanery was in a fluster. I recall, there were not nearly enough qualified dentists for the population, so we were almost immediately in high demand. Decent housing wasn't that hard to find for me, but I often worked long hours to accommodate that demand... and occasionally had to turn patients away.

So Jeannine, how was Australia when you were growing up? I've always been fascinated by that side of the world. It was wonderful, Marion! Growing up in Sydney was fantastic. So, did you always know you wanted to be a speech and language therapist? Not at all, actually! Growing up, I wanted to be an artist, like you! So, I pursued art in my early years. But, it wasn't quite what I expected. Indeed, artistic aspirations can lead us down unexpected paths. How did the transition happen for you? I realized that helping others communicate effectively through words and gestures might achieve something even more meaningful than through art alone. That's quite a realization! Your work must have been incredibly rewarding. It was incredibly rewarding, yes. Seeing children or adults gain the ability to communicate and connect with others was truly fulfilling. But it wasn't without its challenges, of course. Every case is so unique. I can imagine. As an antique dealer, I've always been intrigued by the stories objects hold. I find my own work often requires a bit of detective work, too, tracing the history of a piece. Absolutely. Stories, pasts...blending different threads can indeed be a challenge but also the sweetest part. Speaking of blending, how did you end up as an antique dealer? Was it always a dream? No, not at all! I came into it by circumstance, really. After retirement from teaching art, I wanted to keep my hands busy and my mind stimulated. My husband had a bit of a collection, and I started selling some pieces...and then I got hooked on the hunt for the next great find.

I reckon if anyone could give them a good lecture on that it's you, given your background. Yeah, plus it’d be nice to officially pass on those old PCs to someone who might find some use for them.

So, I hear you've seen the new neighbours who've moved in next door. Yeah, they seem alright. Strangely silent though, so far. Ah, probably next weekend if the weather holds. I could use some help with the beds, actually. I’m in. I love gardening, it's so therapeutic plus it feels good knowing where your food comes from. Agreed. Though, I did buy a bit too much this time, I think. Should’ve asked for a second opinion. Remember that literature course you mentioned?

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 are sitting in the bedroom, chatting about various topics.        You'd think online shopping companies would get their delivery times right by now. I ordered a pair of those new AC DC T-shirts two days ago, and still haven’t received them.      Yeah, I know what you mean. I ordered those new speakers, and they said it'd be there last Tuesday. Still waiting!      It’s just frustrating. I was planning to wear that T-shirt to the concert.      Well, maybe you could try pre-ordering next time. I heard they’re a bit better at deliveries with pre-orders.      True, but sometimes it’s also about how you order. I might have picked next-day delivery and then cancelled because it was too late. Speaking of which, have you noticed how often these companies say things like “usually arrives within 5 days”? It’s always a “usually,” never a guarantee.      Well, technology companies are just like that, aren’t they? Always promising more than they can deliver.      True, but really, if they can’t consistently deliver on time, they might as well say it’s a lottery when it arrives.      But it’s not just technology or delivery times. Yeah, or you find a job that looks perfect until you realize it’s not in Whitehaven.      Exactly. It feels like online job platforms are designed for bigger cities.      But have you tried looking for jobs on those government employment sites? Sometimes they post jobs that you won’t see advertised elsewhere.      Ah, that’s a good idea. I’ll try that.      Also, have you seen that new company that’s hiring here for tech support? They’re actually based in Egremont.      No, I hadn’t seen that. Ooh, thanks for the recommendation.

Right okay so I've been looking at heating options for the new house. I was thinking gas central heating but considering all the costs and what not, perhaps we should look at electric panel heaters. I’ll check it out and we can make a list for the essentials that are needed on those days. Excellent. Thanks a lot. Also, I’ve been thinking about buying a new set of dining room furniture. So tell me about your week? It's been alright I suppose. The new system is still giving me some grief but I'm managing to keep up with it. Had the usual unrealistic targets set but I'm making sure I voice my concerns. Still it's all part of the job. Those targets are just so over the top sometimes. I've got a similar issue with the grant proposal I'm working on. I wish I could give you some advice, as I'm sure someone in your field could help me navigate my challenges. I wish I could too. This new one just seems prone to glitches every step of the way. What's new with the family? The kids are doing well. Emily has started going to ballet again and Ronan loves his swimming lessons. I've been trying to get more involved in life around here. I mean, work is good and all but sometimes I get home and feel like I’ve been in a bubble all day. You ever feel like that? Absolutely, especially with the amount of time I spend in front of the computer or in meetings. It’s strange because in my field I focus a lot on the impact of digitalization on mental health, but it's hard to prevent yourself from getting caught up in it. Exactly! Especially now with all these digital tools supposedly making our work easier but making us work harder at the same time. Right? Like, sure, these new automation tools should save us time, but what they actually do is just mean we have to work faster to compensate for their existence!

[The dinner arrives, and everyone begins eating and chatting.] Well, haven't talked about this in ages, but remember when we were kids and tried to teach Daisy to say "mommy" instead of "mummy"? Oh yes! [laughs] I remember my mom tried to have us all switch but my grandmother just couldn't do it. She kept using "mummy" and I'd correct her till she said it for a day and then forgot again. But there's still room for improvement. And financially, we're lucky this semester because we got a grant for that equipment, which was a huge help. Speaking of finances, I had to bid on a small job the other day. It's been slow coming into winter, you know? But this job should bring some much-needed income. It’s a residential property in Whitstable; [starts talking about the job details] Well, they want it all renovated in a nice coastal theme, so I'm thinking about how best to use the old wood and bring in some beachy touches. I'm glad you said that 'cause that reminds me, I need to look up recipes that use that avocado from last week. Maybe we can make some tasty guac or something for dinner over the next few nights. [Looks around the table] Seems like the food's pretty universally enjoyed, right? For certain. Speaking of food, I tried making [insert couple's traditional family dish here]. It's supposed to be from your side, but I think I might have missed a key ingredient because it came out a bit dry. Anyone know what I should've added? Let me think. I remember my mother always used [something related to moisture or binding agent]. Could it be that? It does sound like a classic mistake for that dish. Or perhaps you needed more liquid in the beginning stages of the recipe. Maybe let's look it up together after dinner.

So tell me about that trip to Italy again. Oh yeah, that was nearly 50 years ago now. We went to Florence, Rome, Venice. It was the first time I’d traveled abroad. We rode bicycles and trams. A bit of a grassroots, minimalist kind of trip. No grand hotels or anything like that. That must have been quite the adventure at the time, with no guidebooks or modern conveniences of today. Oh absolutely. We had to navigate with a bit of a keepsake guide book and a lot of sign language. You learned to be quite flexible, you know. Like when we found a little trattoria in Milan that had these amazing prosciutto and melon slices. Sent us away just like that, even though we spoke very little Italian. But the pasta places, oh, the pasta places. And the gelato everywhere. Did you guys ever get turned into a meal by some overpriced trattoria or wandering too far into a sketchy part of town? Nothing too dramatic. Once got ripped off for a couple quid by a taxi driver, but he was more cheeky than threatening. And there was that one time we accidentally ordered a whole fish thinking it was enough for two, when it was really for 10. We left with a belly full in good humor though. Sounds like a bit of local culture right there. Yeah, no, no complaints. It was a different era, much more about the journey and the people than the outcome, I think. What was the best food you had there? I would say that it wasn't just about the food itself, which was all incredible and fresh, but also about the experience of sharing it with your traveling mates. We had this impromptu picnic in a vineyard one day just because the sun was setting and we had bread, cheese, and wine from a local shop. It was simple, but utterly memorable. There’s something to be said about a dinner changing the course of a trip. I was on a motorbike trip in Eastern Europe a few years ago and we had this incredible meal at a local’s house where we just stopped by. The hostess made us such an incredible spread—meat stews, breads, homemade spirits. It was like stepping into a family gathering. Yeah, authenticity over the fancy stuff. Did anything surprise you when you were there, food-wise or otherwise?

Ugh, I hate working these late hours here. It really seems to never end.      Oh, come now. You’re a lecturer, remember? It comes with the territory. Plus, the students here are brilliant. They’re so eager to learn, it’s infectious.      Infectious or overwhelming?      A bit of both, probably. But seriously, the enthusiasm makes it worthwhile despite the hours.      You’re right, I guess. I just wish we could do this all from the comfort of our living room here rather than the library/office.      Well, maybe in the future when we decide to fully remote. But for now, this setup does have its perks - like those dumplings or hotpot we had last night?      Now that’s what I’m talking about. Chinese cuisine is something else, while the rest of the world can just stick with their generic takeaway.      Ah, sentiments shared by many expats here, I presume? I mean, look at the line for that one stall outside the university. It’s like the queue for a One Direction concert, minus the screaming and all.      Exactly! Okay, where were we? We were supposed to review our lesson plans for next week, right?      Yeah, and I just thought, maybe we could do it a bit more fun since our first class together was such a hit.      What did you have in mind? Some new interactive exercises?      Oh, much more than that. I’ve been thinking, for our next topic, we should involve something from pop culture. Maybe we can use an episode of a popular British TV show to discuss censorship or representation?      That’s actually a genius idea. The kids here are all about Bridgerton and The Crown, so that could definitely work.      Exactly! We just need to choose the right episode for the topic. Plus, it might make the lesson feel less... archaic.      I’d rather say it might make it  more  relatable. But, how do we actually go about it? Do we need to get permission, or...      I’m sure it’ll be fine. We’ll just apply the educational principles and make sure it ties back to our curriculum. If anything, it could be seen as more engaging and innovative.      Okay, sounds like a plan. But let’s make sure it doesn’t turn into “Let’s binge watch under the guise of ‘researching for the lecture’.”      Well, if it means both of us have to watch every new episode of Line of Duty for ‘research’, I’m in.

Ah terrible I thought that broken coffee machine could at least last a couple more uses Grace but no surprise no surprise. I was thinking we could look up the cost for a new one and perhaps see if we can get a discount with one of our neighbors or other people in the area, maybe share one? Oh no no don’t do that it’s just one of those things that’s outlived its purpose. I wish I could get rid of more things, I still don’t know what to do with all the stuff from when we moved here keeps coming up every time we touch something. I know what you mean. I was looking at our old photo albums the other day and had to laugh thinking of all the things we did thinking they were ‘essential’ but now ... well, what can you say? But seriously, we do need to declutter soon. And the storage costs ... Yes and the removal costs were so high, I didn’t realize it would be that much. But then again, thinking about the politics of the past and now ... removal costs galore on so many levels! So true, politics. Now that we have a chance to actually listen and view from outside, it's all so ... different from when we were in the midst of it. Exactly. The idealism of Labour’s leadership over the past several decades - the core values seem so distant now. Absolutely, like a different world. I remember my early days as a teacher, so idealistic about making a difference ... sometimes it really felt like you could change the world through education and all that. That’s why I loved my work, helping in the industry where you actually see the impact of your effort, even if it’s behind the scenes. Nowadays, it feels like everyone’s so caught up in career politics and side-stepping any real progress. And the Labour leadership’s so focused on winning the right wing arguments rather than standing up for grassroots values ... It's just so confronting to see it all from afar. Right, sure, things are always complicated, but the party of working people becoming so middle-of-the-road, so uneventful. I often wonder if we’re just idealistic fools for thinking anyone could make meaningful changes within the system. We can’t give up on it.

Yo, anyone hear about that new craze using river names as pseudonyms? For real? Like, what’s the reasoning behind that? Oh, I read somewhere it's a nod to one's roots and perhaps a reflection on the flow and unpredictability of life. Cool! I'd go for "Tempe" then, referring to the river of the same name in Sydney. That’s right actually, I've always liked Australian river names. Our very own River Thames here in England has an interesting history, alongside it. You ever take a canal boat ride along it? Actually, yes – it’s quite peaceful. But, have you guys heard that pub just above the London Bridge is actually just by the original line of the river? Was it from before the changes made to the river's course, perhaps? Yes exactly! It claims they still have a historical piece of the actual river as part of their room... very peculiar and cool. Next holiday, I’m on it. Now, onto kosher laws - ever had trouble at a restaurant because of strict laws? Oh, totally. We had a close call at this one place once. We wanted to try a special dish but it had cheese while another of us had a label saying they follow kosher rules. Turned out it was the label we followed but apparently the cheese wasn’t part of the specific certification – close call, but the staff were very patient explaining it. Good on them for explaining. Reminds me, have any of you been to that new club popping up in Shoreditch? Word is it’s like nowhere else – real innovative with their approach. Yeah, kind of intrigued. Apparently, they have this policy with no specific dress code but people end up really creating these unique outfits, almost as if it’s a competition. I might check it out. Speaking of unique things, I tried this pasta dish last night with this crazy condiment. It had sesame oil but also some sort of pepperoncino – where did you even find that restaurant? Oh, that was on Brick Lane. Specifically, this little place that only appears at lunch because of crowd control. The owner truly believes in his dishes, so all the condiments are real mixtures of international influences. Did the owner actually let you try almost all of the condiments with the pasta? Yeah, and I ended up loving it! It was like a flavor explosion but in a really harmonious way.

So okay I got this match with this guy on Tinder and he’s like ‘D'ya fancy grabbing a pint or something?’ Omg, talked to someone recently and he just invited me to a party in Colwyn Bay. I had no idea it was going to be this huge thing, flooded with people and his status was just like "meeting new people" ugh, felt forced. Haha that's so normal, I'm just actually looking for chill dates or meet-ups, not huge social set-ups. Right right, agree with you. Sometimes you just want to like, grab a coffee, talk to someone one-on-one – without the pressure. I used to try to get in early with Tinder just cos it's like, easier to text before you meet, in case it's a total flop or whatever. But then I met this guy properly and we chatted online for like weeks beforehand so the meet-up was more like a fun extension of our already established chat. That's actually a good idea. I've been so caught up in uni and assignments I haven't really prioritized any or even really used Tinder that much this term. Yeah uni life is busy. I’m busy enough with just trying to balance my subjects and still have time for everything. Like, my housemates are cool but sometimes I wish we could also not be on different schedules all the time. Exactly. The whole matching with someone is fun but then you still have to translate that into in-person interaction, which is a whole different ball game. Agreed. Plus, even when you do meet up… sometimes it's a no-show or they cancel last minute. That's the worst. Yes! I just had that happen the other day. Seems like the ease of swiping right has a downside, blurred expectations matched with digital disconnect. True. It’s also weird how before meetups you’re supposed to act all confident but then you sit there thinking, “What if I say something really stupid?” Oh completely. I think that’s part of university life for us - cultivating new social skills, and figuring out dating culture. But it can be exhausting. It does get tiring, especially when the guys’ conversations are like, super one-dimensional. “Hey, you busy this weekend?” Like, dude, tell me about anything else! Haha. “Hey, you wanna grab food?”

[speaking with a well-worn but deliberate Norfolk accent] Ah, did you see the coverage of the election? It's a right mess isn't it? [chiming in with a softer, more relaxed Norfolk accent] Oh, it certainly makes ye think, doesn't it? [modulating her own accent slightly, with a hint of Middlesex due to her birthplace] Yes, it's just all so confusing, isn't it? I mean, who’s supposed to be helming the ship now? [leaning forward, with a hint of bitterness among the folds of his accent] Well, from what I can tell, nobody’s got a grip. And to be honest, it's all talk talk, no action, no action. It's just endless promises and no meat on the bone. [nodding in agreement, his voice fills with a rustic resignation] And those benefits they keep talkin' about cuts, that? I’m more worried about what they might actually do next. [considerately interrupting] You’re right to be, but I’ve been watching these debates, and honestly? They make me laugh and cry sometimes. [smiling wistfully] I used to have quite the knack for keeping toddlers engaged. Politics is like my new toddler show, all chaos but wanting it to work in the end. [skeptical, but a grin plays on his face] Politics is a toddler show alright, but who’s the parent and who’s just throwing the toys out of the pram? [chuckles, shaking his head] [bemused] You’ve got a point there. But weren’t we better off when it was just a straightforward “yes” or “no” on things? Not this endless dithering. [jovially) I agree but changing the world takes time. We forget that we might not see the effects of our votes for years, let alone what these politicians actually achieve after they get elected. [slightly nodding, reflective] True enough. Maybe we just need to remind them that the little things matter – health services, schools, decent wages... [interrupting gently) As long as we don’t get too caught up in all the showmanship. We've seen those before, “making Britain great again” sort of nonsense. [shrugs] It’s the substance they often miss out on. [thoughtful) And maybe that's where we also have a part to play? Not just voting but maybe reminding these politicians of real life, of our own communities? [rising from his chair, going to window, looking outside with a contemplative gaze) Speaking of real life... did either of you manage to get your TV subscription sorted finally?

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 at home in Lichfield having an evening meal. Both of them are partners and family.   So how was your day out at work today? Oh, okay. Nothing too out of the ordinary. Had a meeting with the team and we are making good progress on our project. Though, we did have to deal with some unexpected delays again. You know how it is when you're working with third party contractors... Yes, I can imagine. How did you manage that? Persistence and a bit of good old-fashioned negotiating. It's never easy, but we can't let it derail the whole project. And how about the fundraiser plans? Did you manage to make any progress on that today while I was out at the kids’ school event? Actually, yes! I had a really productive chat with the charity representative this morning. We're getting closer to finalizing the gala event in February. It's going to be a big one, and I couldn't have done it without you. That's great to hear! I'm sure that effort will pay off. You always do such a wonderful job with these events. Thanks, I try.
